"Which one is it?" eagerly inquired his auditors. "The dumb-waiter,' answered the young man. WHEN Rufus Choate first began to practice law, be was intolerably bored by an old lawyer who was always getting off stale jokes at the bar. At last. when the venerable lawyer told a very old joke at Choate's expense, he at once arose and said to the judge: "May it please your honour, the counsel's jokes are like himself; their age renders them respectable." Fifty thousand copies of General Booth's book have already been sold, and another ten thousand have been printed. Messrs. Routledge-say that this rate of aelling is unprecedented in the, publishing trade.

The Queen returns to Windsor towards the end of next week, and the Council at which the Speech will be approved is to be held &t the Castle, on Mon- day, the 24th. The Queen will- stay at Windsor for four or five weeks, and she then goes to Osborne for two rmonths.

The Queen visited Ben Mac Dhui on Monday. Ben is not a Highlander, but , a mountain. Ben is covered with snow, and it is very cold about Bal- moral now, but nevertheless her Majesty still drives long distances in an open carriage. She loves the cold hills and glens in winter. The climate is brac- ing and invigorating, but few women of seventy could stand it. Her Majesty, however, enjoys it, and her good health depends a great deal on her prolonged stay in the land of Ben Mac! Dhui and the other Macs.

Mr, Gladstone unknowingly gave the prisoners in the County Gaol a treat when he spoke at Carlisle. Ile spoke with his face towards the gaol, and those whose position caused them to look in the same direction could see the prisoners, with their faces glued to the bars of their cells, peering wistfully at the Grand Old, who, bareheaded, was speaking in front of the County Hotel.

I mentioned some time ago that Mr. Smith's health, though much improved. was not such as to lead to the belief that he would long lead the House of Commons. This statement, though denied at the time, is now acknowledged in Conservative quarters to be accurate. Mr. Smith will lead the House of Commons till Christmas, but whether he will con- tinue to fill that position next year is doubtful. The utmost that his colleagues expect is that he will be able to hold on till Raster.

One of the most delicious letters in the whole col- lection is that from Mr. Chamberlain in which he abuses the Reform Club up hill and down dale, for daring to blackball his brothers. Mr. Chamberlain evidently had in contemplation a campaign headed by the estimable Larry Mack. "I find," he says, "the good people of Birmingham are furious. They will come up and stoma the club if something is not done." Well, the Reform Club is still standing, and brother Dick is still outside it.

By the way, one of the playful letters of Sir Wil- frid Lawson to Mr. Rylands, in the astonishing col- lection which has just been given to the world, is almost too good to miss quoting. Mr. Rylands was apparentlyunder an engagement to speak at a tem- perance meeting at Manchester, and Sir Wilfrid Lawson writes to say, "Do not get drunk and forget the right day, as you did last year." Of course this is merely playful humour, but it is a queer sort of thing to be published cif a man after his death. Per- haps the most amusing part of the correspondence are a number of letters. which deal with avowedly private matters, and in which the writer requests that his name should not be mentioned in connec- tion with them.

We hear that Lord Wolseley is qualifying himself, in accordance with the most approved Castle tradi- tions, for the duties he will have to perform when he is sworn in as one of the Lord Justices to admin- ister the Government of Ireland in the• frequent absences of the Lord Lieutenant and Chief Secre- tary. His tour through Ireland has not been confined exclusively to the inspection of barracks. r He has found time to, Isobnob with the landlords and land agents in districts where there is severe tension between the landlords and i>heir tenants.

I hear that the Maharajah Dhuleep Singh has made a humble request that the Queen will be graciously pleased to restore him to his position as a Knight Grand Cross of the Star of India. When the Maharsjah kicked up his heels so egregiously he formally returned the insignia of the Order, and ex- pressed a wish that his name might be forthwith erased from the list of the Knights. I suppose Lord Salisbury and Lord Cross will presently advise the Queen to reinstate her flighty subject, as there appears to be a general desire to deal very tenderly with him.

The Lord Mayor's Show drew a vast crowd, on Monday, and the streets were thronged as thickly as if the pageant had been of great national impor- tance. Calculating the distance traversed, and with fair allowance for windows and house tops, the totalnumber who looked upon the Show must have been more than half a million, of whom nearly a third, perhaps,were children. The Crimean soldiers wereiloudly cheered. The crowd asked no incon- venient questions as to the absolute propriety of these veterans being thus made part of a show together with emblematic cars suggestive of Ast- ley's and Drury Lane Theatre.

Sir Edward Ebenezer Kay., the new Lord Justice of Appeal, has a severe face and a sharp tongue. Like judges in general, he has faults—of temper; but he has one great compensating virtue. Be is the " bogie man" of the fraudulent, pettifogging, or blood-sucking solicitor, and of all that class who live in a shady way by the exploitation of public justice. 1% judge ever sat who looked at the vital question cf " costa" more from the- point of view of the suitor and less from that of the legal practi- tioner. kt sixty-nine years of •age he is old to go to ' the Court of Appeal, but he is not too old to strengthem•eonstderably the Chancery side of that tribunal.

Perhaps It is worth noting that •the ,victim of the recent murderous assault, the master of Univer- sity College, tOxford. has a namesake at, the. Unive- rsity in the parson of the Rev. Mr. Bright. of Christ Church, who also is a Don, a Doctor ,of Divinity, and an authority on historical subjects. The Christ Church Bright is Regius Professor of ?Ecclesiastical History, and is a charming exemplar of Oxford courtesy. He delta elderly gentleman, with short grey beard, whiskers and moustache, ,and hair standing up from his head. Dr. W. Bright wears steel-rimmed spectacles, has deep sunken eyes, and knows every inch of his beloved Christ Church. He is shy and retiriagtin manner.

An illustrated biography of Isaac Pitman, ol Bath, inventor of phonography, by Thos. Allen Reed, will be published on Ist December by Messrs Griffith, Farran, and Co, Mr. Pitman still presides over the Phonetic Institute at Bath, which he has superintended uninterruptedly for more than half a century. He is in his seventy-eighth year, yet he supervises a correspondence of twenty thousand letters a year, besides editing the " Phonetic Jour- nal " and compiling the numerous books which he annually publishes. He is a staunch vegetarian, teetotaler, and non-smoker, and is to be found at his desk every morning at six o'clock. The:wonder- ful extension of his system of shorthand is due to the energy and perseverance with which he has worked for over 50 years to perfect his system of phonography.

The Maori chief who demolished Sir John Gorst's editorial office a quarter of a century ago, and used up his type as ammunition against the British troops under the late General Sir Duncan Cameron, is still alive. Rewi is his name, and he is, indeed, the one heroic figure left in New Zealand. Most Maoris are very volatile, but Rewi has always been just the reverse. He once sent to the New Zealand Premier one of the briefest and most enigmatic dis- patches on record. It contained just four portentous words—" The potato is cooked." The Ministry sat up for two nights with wet towels round their heads, trying to discover the hidden meaning of this mysterious message. On another occasion he for- warded to the Governor an enormous chest, which, on being opened, was found to contain nothing but a blown egg. By this graphic piece of symbolism he wished to call attention to certain large pro- mises which had been made to him by the Queen's representative, but which had remained unfulfilled. A grim humorist is Rewi,

The latest revolution in Honduras, though it ' seems to be going along merrily, need not eclipse the gaiety of nations. Artezztus Ward, or some .other humourist, said of the Central American, that, when he is tired of laying on his back and smoking, he gets up and " revolushes" a spell. When he is tired of revolushing,he lies down again and resumes smoking. To all appearances the Central American has not changed materially since that description of him was penned.

Sixteen families out of the two hundred and fifty under sentence of eviction were cleared off Mr Olyphert's property on Tuesday—the total number of human beings cast adrift being close on a hun- dred. Look at the following for a sample :—" By the second (eviction) an old widow named Her- raghty, her son Hugh and his wife, who was weak and ill after a confinement, and eight children were rendered homeless. After the police had left the place the mother and baby, a month old, were found lying on a few sacks in the shelter of a gable of the house. The poor woman was pale and emaciated and wept bitterly ; toe ladies remained behind for a time to give her comfort, and Sir John Swinburn, who was deeply moved by the scene, declared that if he had perpetrated one-tenth of that cruelty on his estate in Northumberland he would have been strung up to his own doors by his tenants, and the country would have said • Serve him right.'"
BY L GORDON BYLANDS, B.A. (Continued.) But even more strongly can I recommend a some- what more imporant work, which Mr. Rylands pub- lished in 1847; a little book of 118 pages, entitled,
"'The Pulpit and the People; or, an Inquiry into
,he Cause of the Present Failure of -Christian
Agency." The object of this work was to show. the superiority of individual exertion over that of ,a

special class of paid agents. The author begins by pointing out that "Christian agency viewed in rela- tion to the spiritual necessities of mankind, is, at the present time, a lamentable failure" and contrasts ' the remarkable success and rapid growth of the Christian Church in its early days with its stagna- tion and declining influence now. The cause of this great contrast he considers to lie in the fact that the spread of Christianity in early ' times depended almost entirely upon individual effort. He points out that the Apostles only differed from ordinary men in their zeal and ability, that they formed no special class set apart and consecrated for the service of their God, but that any individual was at liberty to preach the Gospel and make con- verts, and obtain the honourable title of Apostle by common consent, by proving himself worthy of it. He proves that Paul held no rank in the Church such as is held by .a. Bishop now; that, in fact, no such hierarchy as the present existed, but that in every separate town-where a church had been formed, a president and other officers were chosen by the votes of the membersoawing obedience only to those , by whom they had been elected. There was th us no

distinct order of preachers, but every man who felt that he had something profitable to say was at liberty to say it. Mr. Rylands shows how efficacious this system was, and, points out how greatly the distinction between clergy and laity which appeared first in the time of Tertullian—paralysed the energies of the Church. The evil results of this distinction he maintains to be these : That the spread of religion has ceased to he a disinterested labour of love, and has become a trade; that elo- quent preachers no longer preach to those who most want preaching to, but regard their abilities as the means by which they may win honours and emolu- ments; that hundreds of inefficient men, having as a duty to deliver two sermons weekly, utter the most wearisome common-places upon the most trivial subjects; that sermons have, to a large extent, become a mere "routine of sacred words ;' that mere doctrial views are elevated into a greater , importance that practical godliness ; that the gospel is preached to the rich, who crowd to listen to a preacher of distinction because he is "fashionable," and remain unconverted because, Pharisee-like, they believe they need no conversation; but that to the poor the gospel is not preached, because they can- not afford a suit of Sunday Clothes, nor to pay the rent of a pew; that many of the "noblest efforts, springing from the spirit of Christ's teaching, for the social and religious elevation of mankind, have had to struggle at the onset against the attacks of reverend ' opponents, and have had to overcome the indifference af religious men whose energies were withered by sectarian frigidity and priestly domination '." that, however closely a man conform to the precepts of Christ, yet if he refuses submission to the dogmas " of the Church," he is perse- cuted and anathematized as an infidel; and that, in con- sequence of all these things, the Church of the present day, in spite of (perhaps partly because of) its enormous revenue of more than ten millions per annum, is losing ground, whereas the primitive Church, poor though it was, advanced with gigantic strides. Well would it be for the Church if it would pay heed to such arguments ' and exhortations as those contained in Mr. Rylands' book; but now, at the end of 40 years, every word which Mr. Rylands wrote is still fully applicable. It is very much to be feared that all such exhortations are as words spoken to the winds. The arguments of those who utter them are based upon an assumption which is false, and that assumption is, that the Church, as a body, desires, alone and disinterestedly, the moral elevation of the people. It.is sad to be obliged to think that this is not so. What would grieve the hearts of the Bishops and Church dignataries far more than the bestiality of the multitude, would be the loss of prestige and influence in- volved in the severance of Church and State; and, though the founder of their religion was poor, and a man of the people, they would bitterly resist the proposal to employ for the common good any portion of those millions of pounds of which they wax fat and live luxuriously. The young man to whom Jesus said, "it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven," went away aorrow- ing ; and quite as poignant would be the mental anguish of is modern Bishop could Jesus now address him in the same words. But Mr. Rylands was too much a man of action to give himself up entirely to a literary career; and, hav- ing commenced at an early age to take part in political strife, and an active interest in the public institutions of his native town, he presently found that the claims of private business and a public career left no time for literary pursuits. At the ago of 21 he was already well know in Warrington as a public speaker, when he joined the Reform party of the borough in the attempt to oust Mr. Blackburn, the Protectionist member. Between the years 1841 and.lB4B he actively assisted the efforts of the Anti-Corn Law League by many public speeches, delivered at Warrington and other towns, in favour of free trade in corn. He was present, as one of the depu- tises from Warrington, as the great banquets and public meetings held during the week commencing January 30 and ending February 3, 1843, in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, at which- nearly all the leading Leaguers were present, and not long after became one of the vice- presidents of the League. During the same time Mr. Rylands was becoming one of the leading men in WatrringtAm. He actively assisted In procuring the incorporation of the borough, which took place in 1848, and was elected a town co.unclllor in o year. He at once began to 'apply to municipal matters the sound commonsense and great business ability which were his by nature, and which had been increased by the training undergone In connection with the development of the firm of Rylands Bros. His judgment and powers of argument soon secured for him an ascendency in the Town Council, by which he was, after a short time, elected Alderman. The subject of education was one in which Mr. Rylands had always taken much interest; while quite a youth he been chiefly instrumental in founding a British school, which is now a flourishing institution, under the name of the People's College. He believed that much Injustice was done to Nonconformists by the system of sectarian education which prevailed In schools, and which often prevented Nonconformists and others from sending their children to the best school through the fear that their religious convictions would be tampered with. oUnder the influence of this feeling he eagerly united with .a number of Lancashire Imen, who contemplated forming an association for the purpose of promoting secular edu- cation. On the 25th of August, 1847, a meeting of these men was held at the Mechanics' Institution, Cooper Street, Manchester, at which the following resolutions were passed On the motion of Mr. Samuel Lucas, of Manchester seconded by Mr. Peter Rylands, of Warrington, It was resolved— " That this meeting do now constitute itself an Asso- ciation, to be (Ailed The .Lancashire Public School Association, for Promoting the Establishment of a General System of Secular Education in the County ed Lancaster." On the motion of Mr. Thos. Ballantyne, of Manche- tar; seconded by Mr. Hugh Mason, of Ashton-under- Lyne, It was resolved— " That the principles enunciated in the pamphlet now laid before the meeting,be adopted as those of the Asso- ciation ; that the plazacontained in the pamphlet be also adopted, with a view to its introduction to the House of Commons in the shape of a Bill; and that the efforts of the Association be directed to procure aniexpressioa of public opinion in this country in its favour. A Provi- sional Committee was appointed, of which Mr. Rylands was a member, and on which were also nominated Mr. .Jacob Bright, Mr. James Heywood, M.P. (North Lan- Cashire), Mr. Hugh Mason, afterwards M.P. for Ashton- under-Lyne, Mr. William Rathbone, Mr. John Rylands (Mr. Peter Ryland's eldest brether), and Mr. J. G. McMinnies (Mr. Peter Bylandta.brother-in-law, and after- wards M.P. for Warrington). The Association became very active. The Provisional Committee met frequently at Manchester, and public meetings were arranged in various parts of the county, as well as in Manchester, at nearly all of which meetings Mr.. Rylands was one of the principal speakers. The life of the Association was a short and rather stormy one; much opposition was met with, chiefly, of course, on the part of members of the Established- Church, but to some extent even on the part of Dissenters, and, as is usual in public controversies, the designs of the Associa- tion were shamefully misrepresented. The members were declared to be opposed to all religion, and were called " Godless educationists," "advocates of a lifeless utilitarianism," and many otheriard navies, employed, it is to be presumed, to conceal the weakness of the adversaries' case; but in spite of bitter opposition in influential quarters the Association made way. In 1850 it was reconstructed on a wider basis under the title of the "National Public Schools Association," and had gained the active support of Many leading man, among whom were Richard Cobden, M.P., Rt. Hon. T. Milner Gibson, M.P., Alexander Henry, M.P., President of the Association Sir Elkanah Armitage, R. N. Philips, and Sails Schwabe. The Association did not, however, live long in its new form; but although it failed in the sense' that it did not then succeed in securing the objects for which it was formed, yet its many public meetings and the discussions to which they gave rise, must have done much to enlighten people on the subject, and prepare the way for the legislation which has since taken place in the direction advocated by the Association. (To be continued.)

We have received from Messrs. Cassell and Co., volume five of what is modestly called" An attempt towards the history of English Literature, by Henry Morley, L.L.D., emeritus Professor of English lan- guage in the University College, London." We have before had occasion to sleek in terms of the high- est praise of this monumental work; and every volume that is issued adds to the sense of its impor- tance. The book to hand brings the record down to the 14th century, and necessarily deals largely with the literary work and career of John Wyelif, the reformer; and Chaucer, the poet. Nonconform- ists will find much to interest them in this record of Wyclit's work. He was ahead of the times in many respects; and, it is worthy of note that one of the doctrines which he taught was the imperishability of matter. Referring to the relation between the Church and the Bible, Pro- fessor Morley says Except translations of the Gospels and of other parts of Script are made before the Conquest, and of versions of the Psalter, there were no translations of the Bible into English earlier than those known as John Wyclit's." Wyclif died on the 31st December, 1384; and, forty years after his death, by way of reward for his services, "his bones were taken from his grave at Lutterworth in obedience to the decree of the Synod of Constance, to be scattered far away from holy ground. They were taken and their ashes were thrown into the little river of Lutterworth the swift. So speeds the plough I" Of Geoffery Chaucer we are reminded that "no English met equalled him, who had preceded him, or lived in his day." It is a matter of course, therefore, that the author of this work on English writers should devote no small time and space to the father of English poetry. He tells us all that is to be known of the "Canterbury Tales" and other works, and concludes by saying—" So shrewd, so simple of cheer, genial and joyous, he was, rich in true humour, and wit unattainable by triflers, we have seen how small a part of the great poet was the sprinkling at the form of jest now obsolete. England herself ' shall have become obsolete when the source of her strength in that spirit which gave life to the works of Chaucer has passed out of date." It should be added that the volume is provided with a most copious index,' and that the next issue, which will be shortly ready, will cover "from Chaucer to Caxton, including the rest of the literature of the 14th century." "Manual training in Education" is the title of the last volume which has reached us in the Cc ntem porary Science series, published by Mr. Walter Scott. It is from the pen of Professor C. M. Wood ward,of Harvard University, . United States; and may be said to be the best text book and the highest authority upon the subject. The writer is gratified with the great progress which manual training has made not only in America, but in England; and I refers to the distinguished services of such men as Sir George Whitworth, Mr. William Mather, M.P., Sir ; Phillip Magnus, Sir Henry Roscoe, and Sir Lyon Playfair. The various'chapters treat of the defective nature of the traditional curriculum and the primary grades: the scope and content of manual training; exercises in joinery; • wood carving ; wood turning and wood moulding; work 1 on the anvil and forge; bench and machine tool work of metals, with a record of the fruits of manual training in education, and its: relatioe to bocky and mind. It will be seen that the whole field is well covered. The work is ' appropriately illustrated, and is likely to be of the ! highest service to promoters of technical education. We have in the Camelot Series "Essays of Elia by • Charles Lamb." This shilling volume, which, it is a ; matter of course to say, will be a source to those who • possess themselves of it of unfailing delight, is accom- panied by a biographical sketch by Mr. Ernest Rhys. It ; is too late in the day to begin criticism, or describe , Charles Lamb's qualities as a writer, but all who are r familiar with him will agree with Hazlett in saying— , "No one describes the manners of the last generation so well as Mr. Lamb, with so fine and yet so formal an 5 air, with such vivid obscurity, such picturesque quaint- ness, such smiling pathos." . Amongst "Great Writers," also published by Mr. I Scott, we have the "Life of Arthur Schopenhauer." As it is from the pen of Professor W. Wallis, it is a matter ' of course to say that the work is well and carefully written. The German philosopher's personality was a , striking ozae. His writings, like those of Swift, are full of force, with a touch now and then of down-right ; rudeness, hut they are perhaps, none the less interesting I on that account. Schopenhauer takes high rank in Ger- many as a philosopher and metaphysician, and it is well • that English readers should be made acquainted, in this accessible form, with the work which he accomplished. "He went for a Soldier" is the title of a novel by John Strange Winter, which is issued by Messrs. F. V. White and Co., as " Winter's Annual." Like all this 1 writer's works, it is eminently readable, and shows up ;the best side of the soldier's character. It is, perhaps, too much like other stories from the same pen ; but it Is so diverting that the sameness is lost sight of in the interest in the characters. From Messrs. Griffith, Farren, and Co.,we have" The Silver Sickle "—a series of stories by Mr. F. Frankfort Moore. They are all brightly written ; the characters are clesrly portrayed, and the plots well worked out. There are no less than 65 illustrations of the stories ; and they are all cleverly executed. The Silver Sickle is altogether so good that it is sure to be largely in de- mand. The November number of "The Magazine of Art," forms the first part of a new volume. It is printed on new paper which has been specially prepared for obtain- ing the highest artistic result from wood engravings, and it is due to Messrs. Cassell and Co. to say that, re- markably successful as they have been before , the new departure Is a distinct improvement. The frontispiece is a splendid etching of" Fate Mergana," by Mr. G. F. Watts, R.A. "Warwick Castle and its treasures" by J. M. Gray is profusely illustrated, and other illustrated articles are "The English School of miniature art ; " "The modern schools of painting and sculpture ;" "A great painter of cats ;" and "The Salting collection of oriental porcelain." People who have not hitherto patronised the" Magazine of Art "cannot do better than commence with the November number. The current number of "The Cabinet Portrait Gallery" Ii adorned with portraits and sketches of Sir Charles Russell, Q.C.' M.P., Madame Nordica, and Sir Algernon Borthwick. The highest praise we can give this issue is to say that the sketches and 'portraits ars in every reepeob equal to their predecessors. "The Wooing of Chrystabel "and " Woman-like," are continued in the November number of Cassell's Magazine. There are two complete sterjes, and a series of illustrated miscellaneous papers, including Waterlow Park the Garden in November; Art of Cameo Cutting; What to Wear; the Gatherer, Sac. "The Quiver" has for its frontispiece a most charming picture in colour with the title of " A Daughter of Sympathy." There is a full supply, as usual, of stories and sketches, and other Sun- day and general reading. The serial stories of "Little Folks" are " The Secret of the Silver Lake," and- "The Wilful Way." The current number more than holds its own in the vigour and brightness of its stories, sketches, and illustrations. Cassell's Illustrated Almanack for 1891, although published at sixpence only, is crowded with illustrations, and information which is of a most valuable kind far referenee purposes. Amongst the portaits should be mentioned an admirable likeness; of the late poet Brown- ing. Amongst the latest issues of the firm are part lof "Natural History," edited by Dr. P.M. Duncan, F.R.S., and part 1 of the "History of Modern Europe," by Mr. C. A. Fyffe, M.A., vice-president of the Royal Historical society. Both issues are profusely illustrated, and in i each case the first number s accompanied with a capital presentation plate. We have also to hand from Messrs. Cassell, the current issues ef " Illustrated Shakespeare," "Don, Gallery," "Familiar Wild Flowers," "British Battles on Sea and Land," "The Sea," "Science for all," and "The World of Adventure." "Hood's comic Annual "for 1891, published by Messrs. Dalsiel Bros., is like its predecessors in being a store- house of good things. The stories and sketches are for the most part by eminent writers, and the illustrations are alike humorous and clever. The current issue of the "Manchester Quarterly," is more than usually strong, and includes papers on Mr. Meredith's novels, John Leech, Matthew Arnold as a poet, Sacs and "a story sf a picture" by John Mortimer. We have also received from Mr. John Heywood an in- vestigation by Mr. J. S. Wilson into "The Creation story and Nebular theory," by Mr. W. E. Gladstone. Mr. Wilson's criticism is of a trenchant character, and he pets a large number of "posers "to Mr. Gladstone. An- other issue from the same firm is a series of three lectures •by the 'Bishop of Manchester an "Christ and his sur- roundings." Following as they do, upon other popular ilectures of a similar class, they are sure to be well re- ceived, as Dr. Moorhouse has always something thought- ful to say. "The Ladies' Treasury" preserves its place as an ex- cellent household magazine of literature, education, and fashion. The current number contains illustrated papers of "the Needles, Isle of Wight," the "Fashion of other days," notes on dressmaking, millisery &c., and there are, besides, articles on cookery, household management, literary notices, &c. Mrs. Leach's "Family Dress Magazine," and Mrs. Leach's "Fancy Work Basket," published, as they are, at twopence each, meet the wants of a large number of readers who cannot afford the high-price periodicals.

THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVANUS COBB, JR.
CHAPTER IV. THE CHALLENGE.

In the afternoon Runic retired to his shop, where he went at work upon a gun which had been ordered some days before. As yet he had said nothing to Paul concerning the affair of the day before since his return from the Kremlin. He asked him now, however, if any one had called. " Only the monk," returned Paul, without seem- ing to consider that there was anything very import- ant in the visit.

. , "Do you mean the black monk—Valdimir ?' asked the young man, starting. "Yes, my master. He called here about the middle of the forenoon. He wanted one of the small daggers with the pearl haft." "And did you let him have one ?" "Certainly. He paid me four ducats for it, and would have paid more had I been willing to take it."

"And did he make any conversation ?" "Yes. He asked me why the Count Damonoff came here yesterday.' "Ha—How did he know of their visit ?'' "He was waiting at the inn for a sledge when he overheard the Count and his companion conversing upon the subject." And did he ask you any questions touching the particulars ?" " Yes—many." "And how answered you ?" "I told him the whole story, from beginning to end. I found that lie knew something of their pur- pose from what he accidently overheard, and rather than have him go away full of surmises, I told him all."

"Of the message, too ?" "Yes, my master. I told him all that happened, from the showing of the paper which the Duke had drawn up, to the departure of the angry man." " And what did the monk say?" Rtuic asked, very earnestly. " Why—he said he knew the Count, and that he was a proud, reckless fellow, and worth but little to society. That was all. He did not seem to care much about it anyway; only he said he should have done just as you did, and that every law of justice would bear you out. He had more curiosity than interest, though lam sure all his sympathies are with you."
" Very well," returned Runic. "It can matter but little what the monk thinks about it, though I would rather have him know the truth if he must know anything, for I would not be misunder- stood."

" He understands it all now, my master; and I trust you are not offended at the liberty I took in telling him." "Not at all, Paul—not at all." Here the conversation dropped, and the work was resumed in silence. It was past three o'clock when Ruric's mother came and informed him that a gentle- man, in the house, would speak with him. " Is it Stephen Urzen ?" asked the youth. His mother said it was. "Then bid him come out here." , Claudia retired, and in a few moments more the gentleman made his appearance. " Ruric Navel," he said, bowing very stiffly and haughtily, "I bring a message from the Count Damonoff." "Very well, sir," returned the gun-maker proudly, "I am ready to receive it." Thereupon Urzen drew a sealed not from his pocket, and handed it to Ruric, who took it and broke the. seal. He opened it, and read as follows: "Runic NEVEL.—An insult of the most aggra- vating nature has for the time leveled all distinc- tions of caste between us. Your blood alone can wash out the stain. I would not murder you out- right, and in no other way but this can I reach you. My friend, the bearer of this, will make all arrange- ments. If you dare not meet me say so, that all may kncw who is the coward.
" DAmoNoFF."

When Runic had read the missive he crushed it in his hand, and gazed its bearer some moments in the face without speaking. " Will you answer" asked Urzen. He spoke more softly than before for he saw something in the gun- maker's face which he dared not provoke. " Are you acquainted with Mario Orsa, a lieuten- ant of the guard ?"
" Yes, know pim well.' "Then let me refer you to him, He will make al necessary arrangements, and I shall hold mysel bound by his plans. I trust that is satisfactory.' "Yes, air."

"Then you and I need have no more to say." "Only on one point," said LTrzen, with some little show of confusion. "You are the challenged party, and you will have the choice of weapons. The Count has not mentioned this—mind you he has not; but I, as his friend, deem it no more than right to speak of it--I trust-you will choose a gentleman's weapon. In the use of the pistol, or the gun, he is not versed."

"While you imagine I am," said Runic with a con- temptuous curl of the lip; for he knew that the man was lying. He could see by the fellow's very looks that Damanoff had commissioned him to broach this matter.
"Of oourso you are, returned Urzen. "And the Count is most exoellently versed in the U, of the sword, is he not ?" _
"Ho is accounted a fair swordsman."

"Aye—so I thought. Bat it matters not to me. The thought had not entered my mind before, save that I supposed swords would be the only weapons thought of. However, Ora will settle it with you. I have given him no directions at all, save to serve me as he thinks proper, and to act upon the under- standing that if I had given offence to the Count, I woald do the same again under provocation. You understand now i"

" I t:o, sir," returned Urzen in a choking, tone. "Then wait a moment, and I will give you a mes- sage to Oren." Thus speaking Runic went to his desk, and upon the bottom of the missive he had received from the Count he wrote:

"DIJAD. Ardturo—l send this to you by the same hand that bore it to me, and you are hereby em- powered to act for me as you may deem proper. I shall be governed strictly by your arrangements. " Rintic." Having written this he showed it to lirzen, and asked him if he would bear it to the lieutenant. An affirmative reply was given, and then simply folding the note in the opposite way from the original fold, the gun-maker superscribed it anew to the lieuten- ant, and handed it to his visitor. I.Trzen took it, and with a stiff bow, but without speaking, he turned and left the place. That evening, about eight o'clock, a sledge drove up to Rune's door, and Alaric Orsa entered the house. He called the youth aside, and informed him that the arrangements had all been made. Damonoff is in a hurry," he said, "and we have appointed the meeting at ten o'clock to-morrow forenoon. It will take place at the bend of the river Just beyond the Viska "And the weapons?" asked Runic. "Swords," returned Orsa. "The Count will bring his own, and he gives you the privilege of selecting such an one as you choose." "I thank you, Alaric, for your kindness thus far, and you may rest assured that I shall be prompt." "Suppose I call here in the morning for you?' suggested the visitor. "I should be pleased to have you do so." "I will, then. I shall be along in good season with my sledge, and we will both reach the ground , together." Thus it was arranged, and then Om took his , leave.

When Ruric returfted to his seat by the fireplace he noticed that his mother watched him narrowly, and with more than ordinary interest. lie had once made up his mind that he would say nothing to his mother about the affair until it was over; but as the time was set, and the hour drew nigh, his mind wavered. When it was over where might he be ! But he was cut short in his reflections by the voice of his parent.

" RUric," she said, and her voice trembled while she spoke, "you will pardon me for prying into your affairs, but I cannot hide from myself that something of more than usual moment is the matter with you. Why are these men calling to and fro? And why are you so thoughtful and moody? You know a mother's feelings—and you will pardon a mother's anxiety." "Surely, my mother," the youth returned, gazing up for a moment, and then letting his eyes droop again. At length he resumed—" I had made up my mind to tell you all ere you spoke." There was something deep and significant in Rune's tone, and his mother quickly caught the spark..
-" What is it? "she tremblingly uttered, moving ber chair nearer to her child's side.

"Listen," the young man said; and thereupon he detailed his circumstances attending the visit of the Count Damonoff to his shop. Then he told of his own visit to Rosalind, and its result; and then of, the visit of Stephen Urzen. "And now, my mother," he added, without wait— ing for any reply, "you know it all. You see how am situated. Remember, our nation has reached. , its present point by successful war. The soul or the nation is built upon military honor, and sinoe our noble Emperor has opened the way of advance- ment of the lowest of his subjects who are brave and true, the coward is lookeU upon with disgust upon all hands. Yet, my mother, I would have yot• Speak." For some moments Claudia Nevel was silent. But at length she said, while a tear glistened in her eye:

" I have given one loved being up to my coun- try's good. Russia took my husband from me, and, I can ill afford now to lose my son. Yet, rather than one stain should rest upon his name I would see him dead before me. Oh, Runic, you know whether dishonour would rest upon you were you to refuse his challenge."

" I will speak plainly, my dear mother," returned' the youth in a tremulous tone, for his parent's kind- ness had moved him. "In my soul I should feel per- fectly justified in refusing this meeting, for no principle of real honour is at stake. But were Ito back out now trom this, I should never meet another generous look in Moscow. Every one would point the finger of scorn towards me, and the word cosard would ring always in my ears. It may be a false state of things—l feel that it really is so ; but how can I help it ? It is the curse of all great military epochs. Battle alone makes heroes, and so all must measure their horror by the force of their arms. The Count carries even now upon his brow the mark of my blow, and all will say lie has a right to demand satisfaction; though I know that he pro yoked the quarrel on purpose. I cannot refuse him on the ground of station, for he is above me in that. I must meet him."

" Then," said the mother, in a low, calm tone, but with much effort, " you shall not feel that your mother would thwart your design. If your own good judgment says go—then go. If they bring your body to me in the stern grasp of death, I shall pray for the soul that has gone, and shall hope to meet you in the home of the redeemed. If you come back to me alive I shall thank God that you are spared! but alas! the joy will be clouded with the thought of blood upon your hands, and the knowledge that my joy is another's grief." " No, no, my mother," cried Rune, quickly and earnestly. "I will not have a fellow-being's blood upon my hand if I can avoid it. Only to save my own life will I take his. He has done all this him- self—all—all. The quarrel was his own, and the first blow was his. The challenge is his, and now is not the responsibility his also ?" "It is my son, so far as he alone is concerned, if you have a responsibility it must be to your own soul. But tell me—has not the Emperor made some new law touching this practice of duelling ?" " Yee —but only the challenger is responsible. The party challenged is held free from blame in the epee of the law." "Then I shall interpose no more objections," said the mother. lie tried to speak hopetully, but she could not hide the fearful sadness of her heart. "Could fervent prayer avert the blow it should not fall • but I can only pray as one without power." Along time after this was passed in silence. Both the mother and son seemed to have something upon their mild! w:lich they wished to say, but dared not. But the former at length overcame her raki,,- tance.

"Rune, my son," she said, keeping back the tears that struggled for utterance in their silent speech, is there any little word you would leave ?—any matter of moment—" " No, no," the boy answered, speaking calmly by effort. "1 am yours, and all is yonrs. But I shall not fall." " Ah—be not too confident, my son. Let no such assurance lead you to forget your God. I have heard of this Count. It was he who slew Rutger ; and Momjako, too, he slew in the duel. He is an expert swordsman, and surely means to kill you if he can." "I am aware of that my mother. But do you not know that we are all prone to overlook our own powers when wondering upon the feats of others! I may be pardoned for assuring you that the only man who has ever yet overcome the Count at the sword-play was one of my own scholars. While in Spain I practised with some of the best swordsmen in the kingdom. But listen: I will send one word. For yourself I can tell you nothing which you do not know; but you may see Rosalind. If you do, tell her—but you know my soul. You can toll her as you please. But I shall not fall." It was now late, and ere long Ruric kissed his mother, and then retired to his bed. And the widow was left alone. With her eyes she followed the retreating form of her beloved son, and when he was gone from her sight she bowed her head and sobbed aloud. When she reached her humble couch she knelt by the side thereof, and poured forth he pent-up soul to God. Whoa her head had pressed the pillow she tried to hope—she tried to fasten one hope in her mind; but she looked only in the night. Not one ray of light reached her struggling soul. She opened her eyes of piro- MiSe in vain—she looked into a gloom so utter that out of its depths loomed only the blackness of Despair. Sleep on, Runic. But oh, could'st thou know bow thy fond mother's heart is racked, there'd be no sleep for thee! _
(To be coettisued.)

div.head: "IN DARKEST AFRICA."
div.p: "IN DARKEST AFRICA."
SHOCKING CUARGE3 AGAINST THE LATE MAJOR. BARTTELOT.

The "Star" says :—Mr. Bonny corroborates every statement which Mr. Stanley made about ,Major Pantelot's barbarous conduct, and adds to the charges. More ghastly and brutal acts were never committed by any African savage. One ,is tempted to think that the tropical climate must have pro- duced mental aberration in the ' Major before he could have sunk so low.
Bonny's main charges, for which he gives chapter and Terse, are that—
1. Barttelot attempted to poison Tippoo Tibb's chief man. 2. He fastened his teeth in a native woman's face. 3. He showed his teeth and grinned before the natives like a fiend.
4. lie prodded the natives with a steel-pointed staff.
5. Ile killed the clever native boy Soudy by kick- ing him. . _ _ _

6. Ile wanted to shoot John Henry, the mission boy, and then had him flogged to death. "This scene," says Mr. Bonny, "was the most horrible I ever saw. Mortification set in, the man's flesh fell off in pieces to the ground, and his body swelled to twice its ordinary size. Within twenty-four hours John Henry died." 7. He sent his steel-prod into the body of Sanga thirty times, and then beat his brains out. This is the catalogue of damnable atrocities which Mr. Bonny says were committed by an English officer! The Turks in Armenia, the Bashi Bazouks in Bulgaria, never committed more horrible outrages than these.

Mr. Troup admits that Major Barttelot committed certain acts of cruelty, against which he protested, , but Mr. Herbert Ward says that he neve/ saw any- thing in the Major's conduct derogatory to him as an officer. But it should be noticed that both Troup and Ward seemed to entertain a certain enmity to- wards Stanley, and they are more inclined to con- demn his conduct than say anything against Bartte- lot. It is no answer to say that Stanley would have, or perhaps has, committed brutal acts himself. If

these gentlemen know more about the very darkest spot "in darkest Africa they should speak out. As if Major Barttelot's reported cruelties were not euought to make every honest Englishman loathe this much vaunted expedition, there comes the other harrowing story that Jameson paid natives to eat a native girl before his eyes. The evidence of this act also looks conclusive. Jameson

told Bonny, and showed him the sketches he made of the inhuman deed. A Christian interpreter cor- roborates it by a sworn statement. The sketches were seen by Mr. Troup and others. Mrs. Jameson is, therefore, wrong in saying that the charges are entirely founded on the interpreter's statement. Mr. Ryder Haggard, who knew Jameson, says, "a more gentle, kindly, good hearted gentleman I never met," and would tell anyone who said he was an eye witness of the horrors that he lied. Mrs. Jameson may be able to clear her husband, but it looks black for him at present. In face of all these stories of horrible and ghastly barbarities we can- not blame the Paris " D6bats " for saying that they " seriously interfere with the Biblical varnish with which pious England likes to cover her most selfish enterprises." , The letter in which Sir William Mackinnon and his colleagues this morning protest against the iusinua- , tion that the Emin Relief Committee were inspired by any thought .a filthy lucre is an edifying and ingenuous document. But there is one rather im- portant omission in it. It does not notice the some- what important fact that nearly the whole of the committee were more or less directly interested in the exploitation of Emin's province. Just look at 1 a few of the names which Sir William Mackinnon kindly gives mi.:- 1. Sir W. Mackinnon, East India merchant; pro- moter and director of the British East Africa Com- pany ; director of the Congo Railway Company, and of the Suez Canal Company. 2. Mr. W. Burdett-Coutts, director British Bast ' Africa Company. 3. Sir John Kirk, ditto, ditto. 4. Sir Lewis Pelly, ditto, ditto. 5. Sir F. de Winton, ditto, ditto. 6. Mr. Alex. L. Bruce, ditto, ditto. 7. Mr. George S. Mackenzie, ditto, ditto. 8. Mr. James F. Hutton (now deceased), director of the African Mills Company and the Royal Niger Company. 9. Mr. Peter Denny, director of the two lines of steamships directly interested in trade in this direction. It is very impressive to see ,all this boardroom- full of philanthropists laying their hands on their breasts to-day and declaring that they never were "in the slightest degree actuated by any thought of personal advantages, whether of fame, riches, or ivory." But it would be rather more to the purpose if they would give a categorical denial to the state- ment, published and repeated in a dozen quarters, that the first business of Stanley when he had found Emin,was to propose, on behalf of the British Africa Company that Emin should enter the service of that company and practically hand over his province to them. It is much better.in these eases to let the world know the facts. It can then judge for itself about the motives.

And (tf.n.) that was after all a little ela.use in the contract about Emin's ivory. A mere trifling pro- viso, of coarse, but just enough to secure that if any ivory was found the Egyptian Governtnant should ,not grab it all. The most disinterested philanthrop- ist is entitled to a share in any commercial profit that may result from hie humane efforts. liven a

Star man can't deny that. The "Pall Mall," by the way, has got Stanley on the hip. On 21 Aug., 1889, he wrote denying Assad Farran's statements, which included the awful story of Jameson's sketching.a girl who was .being murdered in order that she might be eaten. He said that the statements were " ineonceiveable .non- sense " and "sensational canards." Now he repeats and adopts for himself the very worst of those atoties which he had previously denied; and to-day welearn that he met Assad Farran at Cairo, and took down his sworn statements—the statements he had previously denied—which impressed him ao much that he could not but believe tliem.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY -AT THE MANSION
div.p: LORD SALISBURY -AT THE MANSION

HOUSE. The Lord Mayor's banquet was held on Monday night. at the Guildhall, London, when there were among others present, Lord Salisbury, the Lord Chancellor, the Chan. cellor of the Exchequer, Lord George Hamilton. M.l - Stanhope, and Mr. Ritehie. Responding to the toast a "Her Majesty's Government," Lord Salisbury said be. had on previous occasions in that hall prophesied peaos in Europe, and he could not do otherwise at this time- All the omens seemed to point for peace, at least for the- next twelve months. One of these omens was the fact that the heir of the Emperor of Russia wasabout to visit India as the guest of her Majesty. With regard.to Africafl matters, he had no doubt that so far as Italy was con- cerned there would be a speedy and successful Wee to' • negotiations now proceeding. Ile was sorry to soyhe could not make the same announcement respentirg Portugal, but there was no danger of any sinister com- plications. With regard to Free Trade, it was our dull' to conserve, unify, and strengthen the Empire, because it was to the trade carried on within the Empire of the Queen that we looked for the vital force of the commerce of this country. The conflict we had to fight was still a conflict of tariffs. In regard to questions of capital and labour, one of the delusions at present existing was that by an extension of the criminal law they would promote ' general prosperity. He held that if we were to have an Eight Hours' Bill preventing men from exercising their strength and industry, we must be prepared for the natural result, namely, that they would go to other coun- tries where there was no such delusion.

div.head: TRAGEDY IN MANCHESTER..
div.p: TRAGEDY IN MANCHESTER..

ALLEGED MURDER OF A BROTHER. The residents of Ancoats were aroused on Monday Morning to a pitch of intense excitement by a report that another tragedy had been enacted. Inquiries sub- sequently elicited the fact that shortly before ten o'clock on Monday morning two brothers, named Matthew and William Hayes, who live with their widowed mother at 15, Grime-street, Bradford-street, Ancoats, quarrelled. As far as can be gleaned by the police up to the present time, both men were under the influence of drink. Mrs. Hayes was upstairs and heard the dispute going on. She, however, took no particular notice until her son William came to the bottom of the stairs and exclaimed" Be has done it." Mrs. Hayes at once rushed down, and wag horrified to see the young man lying on the floor with his throat cut from ear to ear. The woman at once gave an alarm, and medical aid was called in. Doctors Quicke and Winchester attended, but despite all their endeavours the unfortunate man died directly afterwards. Matthew in the meantime had left the house, but was captured after the lapse of a short time by Sergeant Bates and Police Constable Parker (C Division). He was taken to the Canal-street Police Station, where the inspector ill charge, Mr. Steel, found him in such a drunken con- dition that he decided not to formally charge him with the crime. _

On Tuesday morning, Matthew Hayes, a man who worked as a knocker-up, thirty-seven years of age, living in Grime-street, Ancoats, was charged at the Manchester County Police Court, with the murder of his younger brother, William Hayes, by cutting his throat during a drunken quarrel. The prisoner, who appeared to have got over his drunken fit, seemed to acutely feel his Pos''' Lion. Evidence was given by the police to the effect that they received information of the prisoner having cut his brother's throat. When arrested shortly afterwards, ho said in answer to the charge, "I have nothing to say ; I would sooner die now." He was much distressed. No further evidence was taken, he being remanded until Friday. The mother, who was in court, sobbed bitterly during the hearing.
