div.p: • WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. aLDBRMAN FRANCOMB RE-BLECTED MAYOR. A meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held on Monday at noon for the purpose of electing -a Mayor for the ensuing year,and transacting other business which comes before the first meeting of the natmicipal year. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided and there were also present, Aldermen Harrison. Wright, Sutton, Chandley, Davies, Burgess,Holines ; Councillors Shaw-Green, Cannell, Taylor, Voisey, GreenalL Bolton, Dixon, Flood, Ilepherd, Muir, Jenkins, Heaton, Hutchinson, Ash- ton, 11. Roberts, Browne, F. A. Roberts, Pierpoint, Blackhurst, Beaman, Walker, Garner, Fleming, R. T. Fairclough ; Messrs. Whittle (town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), Longdin (borough surveyor), Madeley (librarian), Fairhurst (rate collector). There was a large attendance of the public, and amongst those present ,we noticed Mr. H. Greeuall, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Mri' J. Fairelough, Mr. P. Davies, Mr. J. Walker, Mr. C. J. Holmes, Mr. VT. Roberts, &c. TILE NSW COUNCILLORS. The MAYOR announced that each of the councillors •elected on the Ist November had subscribed the declara- tion required by law. THE ELECTION OF MAYOR.—THE COUNCIL IN A DILEMMA. The Mayon having announced that the first business -Was the election of his successor, Councillor VOISEY said the election of Mayor that day would, because of a variety of circumstancel, be at- tended with unusual interest. They were aware that on the occasion of the last election there was one name which was particularly mentioned as likely to be accept- able to that Council and the people outside—the name of Mr. F. Monks, a gentleman well known in the town, of considerable influence, and well suited in every respect to fill the position of Mayor. It was felt on this occasion by those members of the Council who acted with him (Councillor Voisey) that they were in duty bound before proceeding any further with the selection of Mayor to see whether or not it was the case that Mr. Monks would now be willing to accept the position. He had himself taken an active part in getting at Mr. Monks, who, as they were aware, was at present in America, and by the help of Mr. Monk's son they did manage to reach Mr. Monks. A very plain and simple question was sent to him—would he he willing to accept the Mayoralty if that position was offered to him. They had only to wait a few hours, and the message had been sent by telegraph, for a reply which was " Decline the Mayoralty." That at once got rid of the opinion expressed by many people that Mr. Monks would be a suitable person. There was another gentleman in town whom many people would like to place in the position of Mayor—he referred to Mr. Robert Davies. (Hear, hear). They were all agreed, he thought, that if Mr. Davies could have been influenced to take that position they could not have got a better gentleman in the town. He and two or three others ap- proached Mr. Davies to see whether he would take the position. Mr. Davies admitted that it was an honour to be asked to take such a position, and he felt that he would like to take it, but after some consideration his conclusion was that he could not in justice to his part- ners and his clients, and with some proper regard for I himself, throw up his close connection with the office and take the position. That, therefore, settled the matter so far as Mr. Robert Davies was concerned. A good deal had been said about party politics and party feeling, but, naturally, as long as they were divided into two parties they would look amongst their own party for the Mayor. It was afterwards de- cided, before the elections, to offer the position to Mr. James Fairclough if he were disposed to take it, but the matter was left in abeyance till after the elections. Mr. Fairclough, as they knew, was defeated, but it was still decided to offer him the Mayoralty, and, after.consider- able influence had been exercised, he consented to accept the position. It was then thought the matter was fairly settled, but Mr. Fairclough seems to have got into con- sultation with some members of his family, and more particularly with his medical attendant, who told him that if he did not wish to jeopardise his health he must not take the position, and the result was that a message was sent that he could not take the position. There the matter rested so far as outsiders were concerned. For his (Councillor Voisey's) own pact he had always had the opinion that they did not start that question quite fairly. It had been the custom in the past to invite the Mayor to stand a second and even a third time, and he thought the reason why the present mayor was not approached directly and asked if he would not take the position a second time, was simply that first one said and then another said, till it went right round the table that the Mayor was not inclined to take the Office again. He (Councillor Voisey) was, how- ever, going to put it to him if he would take that posi- tion again, and, if so he would propose that Alderman Francomb be elected' Mayor for the ensuing year. He was a suitable man to take that position, he had done his work well and shown himself a man of considerable ability ; he was a man of position, a man of good pre- sence, and, being a man of means, he could give the time. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON said that on occasions of that sort there were sometimes two or three Richmonds in the field, but he hoped that they were in a position that morning to present simply one Richmond, one who was well known to them all, one who had done them good service, and, therefore, he hoped they would be able to proceed in the even tenour of their way without moles- tation and without interruption. As the gentleman was so well known to them all, they need not waste many words or minutes over his induction into the effice, and if it were not for the majesty of custom, they might dis- pose of the whole business in the one well known line of Pope, translated from the Odyssey— " Welcome the coming, speed the parting guest." (Hear, hear and laughter.) Having referred to the loyalty of the Warrington Corporation and people, which is proverbial and indisputable, Alderman Harrison said that if there was one more gratifying sight than another for the people of Warrington, it was to see their Mayor at all times looking happy and radiant, and on all public occasions to see him canonised, as it were, in the municipal purple, with the beautiful badge and chain which must be taken tc indicate the moral worth of the wearer as well as the symbol of the exalted, ancient, and honourable office of which, in the words of the poet, "Age cannot wither nor custom stale its infinite variety." (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Maxon said that five minutts before coming into the room he had not the slighest idea that he was going to be proposed a second time. He could very ill afford the time, and he should be very much pleased to see some other gentleman take his position. (Hoar, hear.) He was very sure they would believe him when he said he had not sought to be elected, and had no wish to be elected a second time. He believed the office of Mayor ought to be handed round from year to year so that each roan might have a chance. (Hear, hear.) Ile had been in the Council ten years and he had never denied that he should like to he the Mayor some day. He had now had the honour of being Mayor, he had done his best and he should be very much pleased if he could throw off those robes. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Councillor DIXON proposed that Councillor Voisey be made the Mayor. (Applause.) He thought Councillor Voisey would till the office as well as anyone there. ' 4Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said he should very muchlike to be able to second that proposition. Councillor VOISEY said it must of course be extremely gratifying to anybody to be nominated to such a posi- tion, but those who him and his business relations must I knew that he could not possibly take the office. He really could not under the circumstance of his business bake the position, not that he should not like it if the circumstances were more favourable. Councillor H. ROSEIITS said he liked the Mayor's speech that morning as well as anything he had beard him say in that Council Chamber. It had been manly, straightfor- ward, and honest,but hewas rather surprised at the other speeches they had just been favoured with. The gentle- men who came there that morning were undoubtedly in a serious difficulty. They had exhausted the whole list of probable and possible candidates, and now they came to the Mayor to ask him to be a step-gap Mayor for a second year. (Fleas', hear.) They had had three weeks in which to carry out the ordinary custom of asking the re- tiring Mayor, to again accept the position, and Alderman Franomb was the first MaTor who had not had that com- mon courtesy allotted to him. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Mayor would value those speeches at their honest worth. If the Mayor respected himself he would decline the office. (Hear, hear, and applause from the specta- tors.) Cnuncillor Rol:l'gs : It has been offered to him. Alderman Strrrox said Councillor Roberts was speak- • ing off the book and did not know anything about it. He had hiniself asked the Mayor on several occasions • whether he would allow himself to be put in nomination again and he had distinctly said no. All the members of the Conservative party had put the same question but the Mayor had always said "No." It was, therefore, out of respect to that decision of the Mayor that they did not press him. It was only on account of the unfortun- nate circumstance as to Mr. James Fairclough, which came suddenly upon them, that they had no alternative but to come forward and ask the Mayor to reconsider his decision and allow himself to be put in nomination for a second year. Alderman CrIANDLEY said that after Mr. Fairclough had unfortunately been advised by his medical man that it would not be wise for him to undertake that office, • they did not see any more likely man than the present Mayor. With regard to Councillor Roberts' remarks, it was a dirty bird that fouled its own nest, and he re- gretted that Councillor Roberts should be guilty of any such remarks. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he should like to know who was the dirty bird, and whose the nest that Alder- man Chandley referred to. (Hear, hear, and interrup-
tion.) - Alderman HARRISON : We cannot have these discus-
sions. Alderman DAVIES said it struck him that they would get on much better if that was put to the vote. (Hear, hear.) 1t would be much better if that Gouracil was not

dragged at the tail of politics, and he would appeal to both parties to pass the vote unanimously. (Hear, hear.) That being done, he should turn with equal propriety to his Conservative friends, and desire them to be unani- mous likewise in the vote tor a Liberal Mayor. Let them sink politics, for goodness sake, for he felt satisfied that the interests of the town were being sacrificed at the tail of politics. He appealed first to the Liberals to let that vote be unanimous, and afterwards he would ask their Conservative friends to let their vote be unani- mous for the Alderman. (Hear, hear.). Alderman BURGESS asked his friends in the Council, if there were any there, to elect the Mayor unanimously, so that when the time came for them to propose a Mayor on another complexion they should have a right to expect the same success. (hear, hear.) Councillor Prarr supported the remarks of Alderman Burgess and other members of the Council, that the honour should be offered to the Mayorunanirnously, and the Mayor would surely then bow to the wish of the , Council and consent to stand. (Hear, hear.) The proposal was then put to the meeting, and Alder- , man Francomb was unanimouslyelected Mayor. The MAYOR, in returning thanks, said the past year had been a very hard one, not only for himself but for a great many round that table. They had a consider- able amount of business to do in London, and they had attended, he was going to say hundreds of meetings in that Council Chamber which were not recorded in their favour, but which all meant a lot 'of hard work, and a great deal of interest for the town of Warrington. He had received every kindness through the year both from his Conservative and Liberal friends. He had never once to come there without having a quorum, and had never attended a single committee meeting where there was not sufficient members. (Hear, hear.) Of course they had got on or two noisy members, and two or three bad-tempered ones—(laughter)—but in their cooler moments they were not so bad. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He had never once been set at defiance, although only a new man and a young man for the posi- tion. He had no doubt that every gentleman would do his best to support him through the coming year. (Hear, hear.) It was sometimes said the wife wore the breeches —(laughter)—and he did not know what he was going to say when he got home. (Laughter.) His wife had done her utmost to help hini,a,nd although his work had some- times kept him out rather late at nights still there was no grumbling. The Mayoralty had of course to be blamed. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The MAYOR then made the usual declarations. THE ELECTION OF ALDERMAN. The MAYOR said the next business was the election of an alderman to supply the place of Mr. John Crosfield. Voting papers were on the table which should be filled up and then handed to him. After the voting papers had been filled up and handed in, the MAYOR announced that the voting had been as follows : For Councillor Platt there voted the Mayor, Aldermen Sutton, Harrison, Wright, Chandley, Davies, Burgess, and Holmes ; Councillors Fleming Blackhurst, Muir, Walker, Henry Roberts, Ashton,Garner, R. T. Fairclough, Pierpoint, Browne, F. A. Roberts, Hepherd, Flood, Jenkins, Dixon, Greene', Beaman, Voisey, Shaw-Green, and Cannell-28. For Councillor Ashton there voted Councillor Heaton, Taylor Hutchinson, and Bolton-4 The 'MAYOR declared that Councillor Platt had been duly elected an alderman. (Applause.) Alderman PLATT thanked the Council heartily for the almost unanimous vote which they had given that day. , His thanks were more especially due to his friend, for he must call him friend, Alderman Davies, who proposed I him at the meeting on Friday night. When he was first elected to that Council fourteen years ago Alderman , Davies was the first to welcome him there. (Hear, hear.) He (Alderman Platt) hoped that the gracious action on the part of the Conservative party must lead to a great extent to the great exclusion of party politics from the Council. (Applause.) TIM DEPUTY-MAYOR AND MAYOR'S CHAPLAIN. The MAYOR said he appointed Alderman Sutton to be Deputy-Mayor and the Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) to be Mayor's chaplain. THE MEETINGS. On the motion of the MAYOR the usual resolutions as to the fixing of quarterly and monthly meetings of the Council and the adoption of Standing Orders were passed. "THE TRADE AND THE WATCH COMMITTEE.— COUNCILLOR BOLTON OBJECTED TO. The MAYOR moved that the following members form the Watch Committee :—The Mayor, Aldermen Chand- ley, Harrison and Sutton; Councillors Bolton, Cannell, Greenall, Platt and Tinsley. There was still one vacancy on the Committee. Councillor BOLTON proposed that Councillor Pierpoint be a member of the Committee. Alderman WRIGHT seconded. Aldermen BURGESS said that eight out of the ten mem- bers resided outside the borough, and he moved that I Councillor Voisey should be a member. He referred to the condition of Sankey-st. on Sunday evenings which he said was not creditable to the Corporation, and for the purpose of having a gentleman on the Committee who resided near the snot he moved that Councillor Voisey should be a member. Councillor DIXON seconded this proposal. He said he was also requested by some voters in the ward he repre- sented to say that Alderman Harrison during the past year had shown a very great deal of favour in supporting the Chief Constable in the case of the sergeant who had been discharged. What they asked for was that there should be justice and not friendship. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PIERPOINT said he resigned the position on the Watch Committee for the simple reason that he resided out of the town, and that it was far better somebody should be appointed in his place who was more in the town. Councillor Voisey would make a very excellent member, but he should just like to remind their friends on the opposite side— Alderman Suwon (interrupting) : There is no opposite side. Councillor PIERPOINT said he would give Alderman ' Sutton an opportunity to speak afterwards. He did not want to raise the reg rag of party politics over that appointment..but if they looked at the composition of the Committee they would find there were nine Tories on it and one Liberal, and now they were going to put on Councillor Voisey another Conservative. If they would allow him the priv\elege af nominating somebody to succeed him, he t bought a very fit and proper person to be a member of the Committee was Councillor Beaman. (Hear, hear.) Alderman PLATT supported the nomination of Councillor Beaman, and he pointed out that the working- men of the borough were not directly represented on that Committee. Alderman WRIGHT said he should be glad to propose Councillor Fleming to be a member of the Committee. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SUTTON seconded this nomination. It struck him as Very odd that their friend Mr. Pierpoint. —(Councillor Pierpoint : "Councilor Pierpoint, please" and laughter)—should always remind them that they ought not to show :the red rag of politics and yet be always telling them they were appointing politics, and that there were so many Conservatives on the Com- mittee. (Laughter.) It seemed to him that Councillor Pierpoint had got nothing else in his head but the ques- tion of politics from beginning to end, but if he wanted to hoodwink them in that sort of a fashion he was very much mistaken. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He agreed with Alderman Burgess that they ought to appoint on that Committee, and on every committee, members who were able to attend. Councillor F. A. Ronnurs said that in order to meet ' the desire to have men on the committee who lived in the town would it not be as well to revise the committee and take off one or two of those men who live so far out of the town. (Hear, hear.? They would remember that twelve months ago they had a rather warm discussion and a vote on the matter whether Councillor Bolton re- mained on the Committee, and he thought that Coun- cillor Bolton ought now ;to graciously give place to Mr. Voisey. (Hear. hear.) Councillor BOLTON : I won't. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS would not affect the com- position of the Committee at all and he suggested that Councillor Bolton might give way. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON said he might as well dispel that Illusion at once. He did not intend to retire •, in fact he should be a member of that Committee as long as the Council would leave him on. (Laughter). Councillor VOISEY said he had no desire to displace any member of that Committee. Councillor Fleming would be very willing to let his own name be withdrawn. Councillor BEAMAN said it was advisable that the com- position of the Watch Committee should be altered, and 'as it seemed to be desired that members of the Com- mittee should live contiguous to Sankey-st., and other streets that were much complained of on Sunday even- ings he would propose the names of Alderman Burgess and even- ings, and Voisey. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said he had been in Sankey-st. on several Sunday nights, and he had not seen any bad behaviour, i except n the case of a few children. It was then agreed to add Councillor Fleming's name to the Watch Committee. Councillor BOLTON (as Councillor Pierpoint was rising to speak) : No politics, now. Councillor PIERPOINT said he would not have any poli- tics nor any personalities. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Twelve months ago he very plainly stated his views with reference to Councillor Bolton remaining a member of i the Watch Committee, and he was beaten n the Council. At their caucus meeting last Friday night,he again raised the question, and he was again beaten. He still held the opinion he did last November, and it was just as incum- bent upon him to now propose the resolution he proposed to move as it was twelve months ago. He should like to say that, personally, he had nothing at all to bring against Councillor Bolton, or against any member of the I trade to which he belonged. Some of the members of that trade took exception to remarks he had made at the caucus meeting on Friday, and he thought very unfairly twisted his words to suit their own purposes. They put opinions into his mouth he never intended to utter, and he wanted to say, that, so far as the licensed victuallers were concerned, there was no man in that room had a right to say a word against them so long as they conducted their business In a legetimate manner. (Hear, hear.) He must say he could not understand that great wish on the part of

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 15, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 15, 1890

the licensed victuallers to have a representative on the Watch Committee, because he believed that no respect- able licensed victualler need fear the police. (Hear, hear.) Unfortunately, there must be and were times when the police were hindered in the execution of their duty by the mere fact that Councillor Bolton was a mem- ber of the Committee. (Hear, hear.) He did not want to say one word that was too strong; he was going on the main principle that was accepted by most large towns with reference to their Watch Committee, that licensed victuallers or anybody directly or indirectly connected with the trade should not have a seat on the Committee. What had they found in Liverpool? An alderman of that borough, who was only lawyer to a firm of brewers, said he felt it his bounden duty in deference to public opinion expressed outside, to retire and no longer hold the position of a member of the Watch Committee. (Hear, hear.) That had taken place in, Liverpool, and he thought he was not unfair in bringing that matter before the Council that day. He had no wish to injure Councillor Bolton, nor any licensed victualler, but he believed it was his duty to bring that matter before them and again ask that Councillor Bolton be left off the Watch Committee. (Applause.) Councillor H. ROBERTS seconded the amendment pre- posed by Councillor PIERPOINT. Lb. might say at once that it was perfectly immaterial to them who was ap- pointed in the place of Ceuncillor Bolton. They did not care whether it was a Liberal or a Conservative; all they desired was that the Watch Committee should be above I suspicion. (Hear, hear.) At the present moment it was not in any particular good odour.. (Cries of "Question.") His election proved that. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He made the question of the Watch Committee a leading matter and the result was that he got the biggest majority they were likely to have in Warrington for a good while, and if they liked he dare resign his seat (Alderman SUTTON: I wish you would.) and fight them in any ward in the town on that question, and beat them, if they kept their party politics out of it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was told in the Council Chamber last year when he was proposeN for membership of the Watch Committee that he was not eligible because he held certain opinions, and because being a teetotaller he was a prejudiced and biassed man. He was not going to admit the wisdom of such an opinion as that ; he thought it was as illogical as it could possibly be, but he put it to them as logical men, if his position as a teetotaller was one that compromised and made him disqualified to be appointed on the Watch Committee. What about the logicality of mem- bers of that Council at the same time pro- posing and supporting a man who was not only a brewer but a publican? It was a degrada- tion and an insult to the intelligence of that Corporation to attempt to prove that the two positions were the same. He had strong opinions and he expressed them strongly, and he should continue to do so. As long as he was sent there to fill a public trust he should fulfil it as honestly as he could. (Hear, hear.) It was well- known to at least half a dozen members of that Council that Councillor Bolton had said that his sole and entire object in forcing himself into a position on the Watch Committee was to keep the police off his own houses. That statement was made publicly last year. Councillor BOLTON asked if this was a fair accusation to make against a member. It was not gentlemanly conduct, and he denied that he had ever used the words. The Mayon said it was quite fair debate and Councillor Bolton would have a chance to reply directly. Councillor ROBERTS could only say that Councillor Bolton had told Councillosr Pierpoint, and had told other members who were present in that room that his object in forcing himself upon the Watch Committee was to look after his own interests as a brewer and publican in War- rington. In the face of that were they going to degrade themselves that morning by appointing a man who had told them avowedly what his despicable object was. The Watch Committee ought to be above suspicion and he claimed from them as honest and honourable men that they should throw Councillor Bolton off the Com- mittee and face it from personal feeling and interest se that it might serve the ratepayers faithfully and well.j (Applause from the spectators.) Councillor FLOOD supported the proposal to leave Councillor Bolton off the Watch Committee. Two years ago, lie said, he rose in his place in that Council for the express purpose of opposing Councillor Bolton in the positien he held on the Watch Committee, and he repeated that recent events in connection with Councillor Bolton's own business would still further Incline men ,who were disposed to deal justly,to take him off the Watch Committee. He had no hesitation in say- ing that those events spoke very loudly against the con- duct of Councillor Bolton inasmuch as they tainted the action of the police with suspicion. (Oh, oh.) He re- peated that Councillor Bolton's presence on the Watch Committee deterred further proceedings being taken which might have been taken had he not been on the Committee. Councillor Bonron : I don't know what you mean. , Councillor FLOOD : You may not know, but the rest of the Committee may know. If they adopted a poll that day in Warrington the action of Councillor Bolton would be denounced. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Robert's elec- tion was a test question on certain actions of the Watch Committee which were not in touch with public opinion in Warrington. (Hear. hear.) The MAYOR : Councillor Bolton, do you wish to say anything more? Councillor BOLTON said he was waiting to see if there were any more mud slingers. The Liberals wanted to be social dictators, and if they had their own way they would be emperors. (Laughter.) They attacked that Committee under the guise of public morality, and they said he could not do his duty because he was mixed up with the trade he was in. They singled him out, although there were other members on the Committee besides him-

self. One person had said that he (Councillor Bolton) had told him that he was on the Watch Committee for the interests of himself and for the benefit oFhis own houses, but that individual had never told a bigger false- hood in his life. Perhaps Councillor Pierpoint believed that he (Councillor 13D1ton) had said something of that sort, and he would not say that Councillor Plerpoint said what he did not believe. (Laughter.) Councillor F. A. BOBAIITS : In the interests of the licensed victuallers is what you told me. iouncillor BOLTON said there was another construction put upon it. He would not dispute that he stood there a representative of "the trade" upon which they had been throwing mud, and which had through him been maligned. (" No, no.") Well every speaker had been doing it so far. They told him they had nothing against him personally, but it was all because he was a brewer. (" No, no,") He left the matter to the Council, but he objected to being attacked by what he called the tag-rag .1 of the Liberal party. (Laughter and applause.) A vote was then taken on the amendment proposed by Councillor Pierpoint that Councillor Bolton should be left off the Witch Committee with the following result For: Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, and Platt, and Coun- cillors H. Roberts, Pierpoint, Shaw-Green,F. A. Roberts, Beaman, Flood, Walker, Blackhurst, Brown, Dixon and Fleming-15. Agerixst : The Mayor Aldermen Sutton, Harrison, Wright, Chandley, and Davies ;. Councillor R. T. Fair- dough, Taylor, Hutchinson, Cannel!, Muir, Ashton, Hepherd, Jenkins, Bolton, Heaton, and Gretna!! The amendment was therefore lost and the committee • was constituted as proposed with the addition of Coun- cillor Fleming.

FINANCE COMMITTSH. On the motion of Aldermen Holmes, seconded by Councillor Shaw Green, the Finance Committee was appointed as follows :—The Mayor: Alderman Holmes ; Councillors Fleming, Green, Greenall, Hepherd, Jenkins, Pierpoint, Tinsley, Voisey, and Walker. STREHT IMPROTHItIENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTER. Alderman PLATY moved that the following form the above-named Committee :—The Mayor. Aldermen Sut- ton, Wright, and Platt; Councillors Blackhurst, Browne, Muir, Pierpoint, and H. Roberts. He left off the name of Councillor Bolton as there were ten members without Councillor BLACKHURST seconded. Alderman SUTTON referred to the name of Councillor Bolton being left off, and The MAYOR said if they took his name off and left on the name of Councillor Bolton they would then have ten members. Councillor BOLTON: He does not want that. Alderman WRIGHT said they had distinctly understood on Friday night that Councillor Bolton should be a mem- ber of the Committee, and he did not see why his name should not be considered as well as any other name. Alderman PLATT was quite willing to fall in with the suggestion of the Mayor. The Committee was then approved with Councillor Bolton's name on, the Mayor being an ex-officio member.

SANITARY COMMITTEE. Alderman BURGESS moved that the Sanitary Com- mittee be as follows :—Aldermen Burgess, Sutton, and Wright ; Councillors Beaman, Browne, Flood, Hepherd, H. Roberts, Voisey, and Walker. Councillor DIXON said he had fully expected that the list would have been overhauled. They had had the intercepting depots put down by the committee and the nuisance arising therefrom was so serious that those who resided in Fairfield Ward made the most fearful corn- ' plaints against both the depots. He entered his protest against the composition of the committee. The proposal was agreed to. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. Alderman Devins moved that the committee be formed as follows :—Aldermen Davies, and Wright ; Councillors Ashton, Beaman, Fairclough, Flood, Heaton,',Hutchinson, Muir, and Taylor. Councillor H. Itormars explained that his action on Friday night when the Committee was selected had been somewhat misunderstood. He had no personal feeling, and for the present he did not wish to press the matter I any further. I The Committee was then approved.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COVAIITTEE. This Committee was formed as follows on the motion of Councillor Fleming, viz. :—Alderman Chandley ; Councillors Beaman, Blackhurst, Dixon, Fleming, Flood, Garner, Green, Heaton, Muir and Taylor.

- MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTER. On the motion of Councillor Roberts the following Committee was appointed :—Aldertnen Davies, Harrison, and Sutton ; Councillors Browne, Flood, Green, Jenkins, Muir, Pierpoint, Platt, Henry Roberts, and Voisey ; and the following non-Members of the Council,viz. :—Messrs. Robert Davies, T. G. Rylands, Wm. Owen, James Pater- son, Robert Pierpoint, J. E. Worsley, Linnceus Greening, F. W. Monks, John Peers, F. Monks, and J. F. Dutton. CEMETERY COMMITTER. The following Cemetery Committee was appointed, on the motion of Alderman Harrison, viz. :—Alderman Harrison; Councillors Ashton, Fleming, Flood, Heaton, Hutchinson, Jenkins, Muir, Taylor, and Garner. TOWN RILL, PARE, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. Appointed, on the motion of the Mayor, as follows The Mayor; Aldermen Chaadley, Harrison, Sutton, and Wright; Councillors Bolton, Cannell, Heaton, Jenkins, and Muir. MARKETS COMMITTEE. Appointed, on the motion of Councillor Greening, as fellows :—Councillors Ashton, Blackhurst, Browne, Gar- ner, Green, Greenall, Hepherd, 13utchinson, Taylor, and Tinsley. GAS COMMITTEE. Appointed, on the motion of Alderman Holmes, as

follows :—Aldermen Chandley, Davies,Harrisor4Ablmo,. and Wright; Councillors Fairclough, Hepherc4 1,, A, Roberts, Tinsley, and,Walker. RIVER COMYGI'TEE. Appointed, on the motion of Alderman Davies, as follows :—Aldermen Burgess, Davies, Sutton, Francomb ; Councillors Fairclough, Heaton, Platt, H. Roberts, F. A., Roberts, Taylor. FIRE ENGINR COMMITTEE. This Committee was formed as follows :—The Mayor; Councillors Ashton,,Cannell, Heaton, Hepherd, Hutchin- son, Jenkins, Mtair, Platt, andlaylor: WARIER COMMITTEE. The following members were proposed as a Water Committee,. viz. :—The Mayor ; Aldermen Burgess, Davies, Harrison, Sutton, Wright ;• Councillors Bolton, Fleming, Green, Greenall, Ilepherd, Jenkins, Hy, Roberts, Voisey, and Walker. Alderman CuAimuv suggested that the Committee should be smaller. The Water Company, he said, managed their business with only three directors. Councillor H. ROERRTS offered to withdraw from the Committee. Alderman Iluxuess thought it would be better to adjourn the list in order that it might be revised. Councillor H. Roselyn suggested that the number of aldermen on the Committee should be reduced. It was agreed that the appointment of the Committee should be deferred. TRE RENEWS PURPOSES COMMITTEE. The Mayon moved, and it was agreed that the Mayor, Denuty-Mayor, every member of the Council who has , held the office of Mayor, and the Chairman and Deputy- Chairman of the several Committees (being members of the Council) be appointed for the ensuing year "The General Purposes Committee." TEE RETURNING ormcsns. The MAvox moved the appointment of the return- ing officers as follows:—Town Hall Ward, Alderman Davies ; Whitecross Ward, Alderman Platt ; Bewsey Ward, Alderman Holmes ; Orford Ward, Alderman Har- rison ; St. John's Ward, Alderman Sutton ; Fairfield Ward, Alderman Wright ; Howley Ward, Alderman Francomb ; St. Austin's Ward,Alderman Burgess; Latch- ford Ward, Alderman Chandley. TIM RESIGNATION OF COUNCILLOR MONIES. r The MAYOR mentioned that Councillor Monks had now paid the is. neonh resigning his pcsition as a member of the Town Council, and there was now a vacancy on the Council. 'TER MAYOR AT mirttca. The MAYOR also announced that he intended to keep to the good old custom of attending the Parish Church on Sunday morning, and he invited as many as possible , of the members of the Corporation to accompany him.

A list of the attendances made by members of the Warrington Town Council at Council and Com- mittee meetings from the 9th November, 1889, to 28th October, 1890, has been issued. We give the number of Council and Committee meetings attended , by each member. The Mayor attended 16 Council' meetings, and 111 committee meetings; Alderman Bur- gess, 14 and 60 respectively; Alderman Chandley, 5 and 30 •, Alderman Crosfield, 3 and 5 ; Alderman Davies, 9 and 55; Alderman Harrison, 15 and 152; Alderman Holmes, 14 and 100; Alderman Sutton, 14 and 84 ; Alderman Wright, 13 and 101. Councillor Ashton, 12 and 68 ; Councillor Beaman, 6 and 19; Councillor Black- hurst, 10 and 79 ; Councillor Bolton, 15 and 86 ; Coun- cillor Cannell, 13 and 36 ; Councillor James Fairclough, 11 and 74 ; Councillor R. T. Fairclough, 15 and 48 ; Councillor Fleming 15 and 125 • Councillor Flood, 16 , and 71 ; Councillor: 'Garner, 11 and 47 ; Councillor Green, nand 129 ; Councillor Greenall, 9 and 68 ; Councillor Heaton, 12 and 43; Councillor Hepherd, 14 and 62 ; Councillor Hutchinson, la and 64 ' • 'Councillor Jenkins, 12 and 50 •, Councillor Marsh ,8 and 54 ; CounCibr MOnkS, 13 and 21 ; Co.:10.110r Muiri 14 ata 5 councillor Percival, 11 and 51 ; CoUncillor Pierpoint, 15 and 46 ; Councillor Platt, 9 and 50 ; Councillor Henry' Roberts 10 and 41 ; Councillor Frank A. Roberts, 4 and 10 ; Coun- cillor Taylor, 12 and 87 ; Councillor Tinsley, 14 and 34 ; Councillor Voisey, 13 and 33. It should be explained that the opportunities for put- ting in attendances were much more numerous in some cases than in others, as some of the members of the Council are on more committees than other members. We may explain, too, that Mr. Hepherd was elected in November 22nd, 1889, and Mr. . Beaman the 25th April, 1890, while Mr. Marsh resigned on the sth August.

div.head: WE:ECK OF A BRITISH
div.p: WE:ECK OF A BRITISH
CRUISER.
SUPPOSED LOSS OF 173 LIVES.

THREE OF THE CREW SAVED. MADRID, WEDNBSDAY.—An official telegram from Coruna announces that the British cruiser Serpent has been wrecked off Cape Buoy, near the village of Cama- rinason the north-west coast of Spain. The telegram adds that there were 176 personsou board, of whom only threeavere saved, while the bodies of three ladies have been washed ashore. The Governor of Coruna has in- structed the authorities at Cumarinas to render every assistance. 10.45 vac —The three sailorswho were saved from the Serpent swam ashore at Camarinas, which is a small port seventy kilometres south of Coruna. They express the belief that the rest of the crew were drowned, but accor- ding to thelatest information only four dead bodies have been washed ashore. There is no telegraph station at ; Camarinas. Much consternation was created at Portsmouth, on. Wednesday evening, by a report that H.M.S. Serpent has been lost at sea. Scores of applications for intelligence were made at Portsmouth Dockyard, but the officials were unable to, furnish any information on the

subject. Her Majesty's ship Serpent, was a new ship built and launched at Devonport, and was a handsome vessel of 1,700 tons and 4,500-horse power. This was her first voyage. She was a cruiser of the third class, and was commissioned at Devonport on 24th of June last for ser- vice on the West Coast of Africa, to relieve the Archer onthat station. She would have left England soon after that date, but in her trial trips considerable difficalty was experienced with her machinery, and she was detained for some time in consequence of several mishaps. She left Plymouth on Saturday last after the gale had sub- sided which caused so much damage along our coasts, and was under orders to call at Grand Canary, St. Vin- cent, and Sierra' Leone, en route for Accra. The Serpent was understood to be an excellent sea-boat, and the news of her loss has caused great excitement in the three towns of Plymouth, Stonhouse, and Devonport, where the families of many of the crew reside. A painful scene was witnessed in Plymouth on Wed- nesday evening. The loss of the Serpent, together with the statement that all hands had perished, was placarded in the window of one of the newspaper offices, and ths wife of a warrant officer Gn board the Serpent read the announcement as she was passing the window. The shock was so great that with a loud scream she fell faint- ing on the pavement, and some time elapsed before oho recovered consciousness. She was afterwards removed to her home in a cab. The Serpent had a complement of 150 officers and men. 1 The earlier unofficial information which alone was ob- tained in London indicated that the disaster occurred in the open seas after the cruiser had passed Madeira •, but on comparison of the distance and the time at which the Serpent left Devonport on Saturday afternoonit became evident that this version could not be accepted as even [ approximately correct. It was true that the Serpent in i the ordinary course of her voyage to the West Coast of Africa would have been first reported from Madeira • but in answer to private telegraphic enquiries addressed to that place it is stated that nothing has been seen or heard of the vessel. This is now unhappily explained by the fact that the wreck probably took place on Tuesday night on a remote part of the Spanish coast. Camarinas. near which town the Serpent went on the rocks, is situated at the mouth of the river of the same name, almost within the shadow of Cape Tosto. It is about twenty miles north of Cape Finisterre, and between fifty and sixty miles from Corunna, which is the nearest important town on the coast, and the delay in the receipt of the news is doubtless due to the fact that the only communication between the two places is by means of mountain roads. A Plymouth Correspondent telegraphs : The news came to hand while the Patti concert was in progress, and , was at once announced to the Duke of Edinburgh, who was present. The Duke at once sent his equerry to the office of a local paper f.:l' further information, and was much relieved to learn that at tne time it was supposed that the men had been taken off. Subsequently, how- ever, the more disastrous features were confirmed, and his Royal Highness forthwith left the hall. The inform- ation was not generally understood by the audience. During the evening the newspaper offices were besieged by the distressed wives and children beseeching infor- mation, and most distressing scenes occurred, the unfor- tunate people bursting into tears. The father of one of the crew stated, that his son .always spoke of the unseaworthiness of the ship and had told him that they were not very comfortable with the captain. In fact his son stated that during the mobilis- ation it was remarked in the service that they were going to get two men-of-war to stay her up to prevent her from ' sinking. He had also heard that she had run out of coal, and had to be towed about the Bay of Biscay. Another man said the Serpent was very small for the work and there was hardly room in her to swing a cat round. A seaman of H.M.S. Anson, who also gave his name, but wished it to be reserved for the time, said he had a brother who was a stoker on board the Serpent. He had heard men generally give the Serpent a very bad name. The workmen in the dockyard described the Serpent as "a brute." She always broke down on her steam trials from the time she was built until she left Plymouth. The Serpent, according to the official Navy List, has six guns, and is described as a twin-screw cruiser of the third-class. She was built at Devonport Dockyard and completed in 1888. The complement is 176 officers and men, and the displacement 1,770 tons • total indicated horse power 4,500 ; extreme draught 14'ft. 6in. ; length 225 ft. • beam 36ft. She was engined by Messrs. Harland and Wolff at Belfast, and her total cost was £121,000. As to her armour-plate the official description says she had an unprotected steel hull and her armament consisted of six-inch 5-ton B.L. guns, eight quick-firing guns, two machine guns, and one light gun. Her speed was 18 knots an hour. Her coal endurance is given as 475 tons stowage, and with that stowed she could have steamed 7,000 miles. The Serpent took part in the Naval Manceuvres of 1889, under Admiral Sir George 'Tryon, K.C.8., and this year she waj one of the units of C fleet which assembled at Torquay, under Vice-Admiral Sir Michael Culme Seymour. She was commanded by 'Com- mander Harry L. Ross. The other officers were—Lieu- tenant Guy A. J. Greville, Navigating-LieutePant Peter N. Richards, Lieutenant Torquill Macleod, Staff-Surgeon W. ' M. Rae, Paymaster James W. Dixon, Chief-EngineerJohn J. Robins, Assistant-Engineer William P. - Edwards, Assistant-Engineer Frederick V. Head, Torpedo-Gunner ,Frank Halsgrove, and Boatswain John Dwyer. LATER DETAILS. Mstap-Df THURSDAY, 12.45 r.re.—A few further par- ticulars have ien received regarding the wreck of the Serpent. The threc sailors who are, it appears, the sole survivors have susta-tni.'ll severe injuries, having been hurled against the rocks as fh" swam ashore. They will be brought as soon as possible to Corunna, where , they will be well cared for. Orders beVe PC'Ca sent by the Spanish Government that the authoritie3 ihe re are , to do all in their power for the shipwrecked sailors. A private telegram received here reports that when the ' Serpent struck on the reef off Cape Huey she had already sustained some damage, having encountered a heavy gale during her voyage from England. The shock of her striking was such that the ship went down in a few moments. An effort was made to launch the ship's boats, but there was no time before she foundered to get a boat clear of the vessel. The catastrophe occurred to- wards midnight. The waves washed up a quantity of wreckage on the shore, and a party of Carabineers have been despatched to the coast to keep guard over every- thing that is thrown up by the sea and prevent property being carried away by the people of the neighbourhood. Isamu), THURSDAY, 3 P.M.—The naval commandant of the maritime province of Corunna has telegraphed as follows to the Minister of Marine "The maritime authority at Camarinas informs me that the British crusier Serpent, from Brest, ,bound for Africa, has been wrecked on a rocky headland called Punta Buey. Three sailors were saved. Ido not know the fate of the remainder of the crew, but it cannot fail to be a sad one, for the place where the vessel went ashore is very dangerous: The waves continue to cast up bodies on the beach, and several have already been recovered." An able naval officer attached to the Admiralty has stated that he knows the place where the wreck occurred well. He said it was difficult to explain the cause of the wreck, but he thought that there might have been a fog, and that the look-out men on the Serpent could- not see the light in Cape Villano lighthouse. Another possible explanatien, added the officer, was that the compasses of the British man-of-War had been disturbed by contiguity to the vase masses of iron on the coast. Several wrecks attributed to that cause had occurred on the north-western shores of Spain, and it was extraordi- nary what an influence the enormous quantity of iron in some of the Galician mountains exercised on the needles of ships' compasses. _ THE CAUSE OF THE CATASTROPHE. The "Daily News" says :—The coast is known to be a dangerous one ; and it is impossible to conjecture the cause which brought the -Serpent near it. The guesses of various naval experts tend, however, to confirm the anticipation we expressed that " some unusual circum- stances—something against which courage was power- less and good. searnanship useless—has occurred." An , accident to the steering apparatus making the ship un- manageable is one theory; another, and perhaps a more likely one, is an aberration of the compass, caused by the nearness of the vast masses of iron in the Galician mountains. This is the explanation suggested by an ex- perienced officer of the Spanish Admiralty. Admiral Sir George Elliot has expressed the opinion that the engines may have broken down, and that the vessel drifted ashore on the strong current which the Gulf Stream pours against the coast of Spain, and which is always - during westerly winds. _-___......._

div.head: COERCION SENTENCES QUASHED.
div.p: COERCION SENTENCES QUASHED.

At Tipperary Quarter Sessions on Tuesday, County Court Judge Anderson reversed the decision of two resi- dent magistrates sentencing John Ryan and fohn Dwyer, the former to six months' and the latter to three months' imprisonment under the Coercion Act on a charge of taking part in a conspiracy to advise persons not to buy cattle from a boycotted farmer named Hogan.

div.head: CANAL BOAT CHILDREN OF RUNCORN.
div.p: THE CANAL BOAT CHILDREN OF RUNCORN.

In a blue book recently issued, relating to the year 1889, 11. M. Chief Inspector, under the Canal Boats Act, thus refers to Runcorn :—At Runcorn. which is a great centre for canal boat traffic, there are a large number of boats registered; indeed, more than at any other place. The Clerk to the School Board had taken great interest in the work of educating the boat children, but the difficulty of securing attendances were very great ; the parents pleading that they are obliged to take their child- ren with them on the boats, and in the face of their plea the Board did not feel itself justified in con- stantly persecuting the parents with police court summonses and fines, and, in fact, the magistrates are equally reluctant to grant convictions. 'What the Runcorn School Board does is to see that the children's names are on the school rolls, and to insist that attendances shall be made whenever the boats_ are lying there. The average number of attendances made by this class of children is three or four per week, which under all the circumstances a think, must be very gratifying. Cases of utter neglect and of defiance are punished. During thcs year 1889 there were 104 parents brought before the Attendance 'Committee, and 52 (exactly the one half) of these were afterwards taken before the magistrates and fined. - -

Butt Lord Stuasartav sees a bogie which him more than, the prospect of a war of tariff 3,, and that is the destruction of trade which may COMt,. of an Mght Hours Bill. He was always a preacher of the gospel of Ruin; but it is not always from the same quarter that ruin is to be especte4l. When it was proposedo to pant the. franchise. to the working-classes/ ha foresaw the ruin of the country in the shifting of the balance of power; and in later days it has ,been preakted that the sun of England's, glory would set as soon as Home Rule was granted to 'lreland. Now he harps on another string ;it is the agitation for shorter hours of labour which threatens to drive trade from the couatry, and leaves Es all idle and helpless. But the Tory leader has so often proved a false prophet that people don't mind much what he says; they have come to look upon it as his way of trying to keep back reforms of all kinds as long as he possibly can. We are a long way as yet from adopting a universal Eight Hours Bill, for the working classes are not agreed that it would be good for them. The subject was before the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, at the annual dinner at Earlestown on Saturday, and one of their chief spokesmen was emphatic in declaring that the question of shorter hours was one which they could and should settle without the aid of Parliament. The issue is a great one, and it has reached the stage of discussion and examination; but it is not ripe for legislation. A Case has, we think, been made out for miners, who work underground, and run great risks; but it is just possible that even as to them the eight hours system will be generally adopted without appealing to the legislature. It is cheering to see that the
scareal

miners of Belgium are bestirring themselves in the same direction. We have great hopes of labour successfully asserting itself when it moves solidly as between one country and another. Humanity would be the gainer if the eight hours plan Caine in force throughout the world; but we are still a long way from the realisation of this day dream. There is no need, however, to despair, or to suppose that the battle will be so fought out in England as to drive trade from the country. John Bull is alto- gether too slow for that. He will move a step at a time, and he will feel his way at each step. The end of it all will certainly be shorter hours of labour; but it does not follow that the hours will be ruinously short, or that the restriction will be enforced 141 Act of Parliament.

"The Trade., IT has been an unwritten law which and has been observed by the majority of The Police' the Town Councils of the Kingdom, that people who are interested in the drink traffic should not have seats upon Watch Committees. It is a regulation founded upon common sense and wide experience, and, wherever itis broken,it is a discredit to the Corporation that breaks it. Public opinion has been strongly expressed in Liverpool, because the chairman of the Watch Committee, though not in "the trade" himself, was the legal adviser to a firm of brewers; and in deference to that opinion Alderman HUGHES has, like a citizen who has a reputation to maintain, resigned the im- portant post which he held. Liverpool is, there- fore, free from reproach in this particular respect; but Warrington has not thus purged itself; it IS setting public opinion at defiance. Exception nag taken at the first meeting of the new Town Coun- cil, on Monday, to Councillor BOLTON being again placed upon the Watch Committee. Councillor BOLTON is not only a brewer, but he is the owner of ;several licensed houses in the town; and, he is .theref ore, in the position of being the one Town 'Councillor who above all others ought not t;o have )a special voice-in the control of the police. What ,if a policeman in course of his rounds shoultt find he law being broken at one of the houses owned by Councillor BOLTON? Does anybody suppose teat he will not think once, twice, and even thrice before laying arAnformation which may prejudice hZin in the eyes of a person who stands in the Wei' tin of being one-of his masters? Will he not be tempted to consider whether it would not be better for • him to wink at the offence rather than risk dmuaging his chances of advancement in the mat- terof promotion and pay? It is obvious to all who ore not "blind as never bat was blind" that the presence on the 'Watch Committee of a eom- powati of brewer, license holder, and Watcher,is- General to "the trade" is more or less of an. in- timidittion to every member of the force—from the Chiet Constable downwards. If Councillor Borrelf had any true sense of decency he would refuse to' occup7,4 such an anamolou.s and objectionable position. What would be thought of a magistrate who sat in a case in which he was personally in- terestlad P The law haa so guarded the public- in licensing matters that,. if a magistrate happens to be a shareholder only in a Railway CompanY ; which holds licenses for railway stations, he is for- bidden, under a heavy, penalty, from sitting as a licensing.magistrate. But his interest in any case' that right have to be considered is extremely remote as compared. with the interest Councilke BoLrovniay have in sitting in judgment upon Watch, Committee cagPs. There is this, too, to be borne in. mind, that,. while the proceedings of the licensing, jostices are conducted in open court; . those ot the Watch Committee are conducted with closed doers; and they-are not even reported to the Town Council. It isclear then. that mischief may be doriaagain and again, and the public be, no wiser. Uwe are to-have a Star Chamber, we /riot • at leazt :have some t assurance that those ,:ipho are members of it,: are not acting as judge and jurytwhen they. ought to be in the positicmoi culprits.. As the matter stands,. an outrage has been ccasueitted upon. common fairness; and it significant that, while the, whole of the Tory mom- bers of the Council voted fen putting a brewer upon the Watch Commiee, *hens was not one of those who could bring himself teeay &single word in, its favour: They were evidently, ashamed of the tzans- action,,but they had.responded, to the party whip. and allowed their 'ward forparty to over-ride.their regardlor. justice. By a ,conspiracy of silence and a. narrovw.majority of:three„they have succeeded. for a time in repeating thepeopetration of an iniquity. But it ,is only far atinme they have succeeded ; their majority is melting,:away,. and it will disap- pear altogether, if they do not mend their ways. The Watch Committoe. is distrusted amongst otheri- reasons. fell the, harsh treatment to, which Police-Sergeant .Shaw was, subjected; it is under a cloud, and it wiltrenana under a cloud so, long as there are members. upon it who are concerned for the interests-opt the. publican rather than the interests of the public:. Let there be fair plaY; that is all that, the inhabitants ask for;; and we have faith in them, that, in due course,. they will lice that they/get fair Play.

Brunner Tgz, member for the Iforthwich , at Division of Cheshire fully recog- Runcorn. nises.the duty which he owes to his constituentlin giving, year by year, some account f, the doings of Parliament, and his views- !upon the topics,of the day. He has already ad— dressed several meetings, and, on Wednesday even- ing, he addressed his Runcorn and Halton consti- tuents. Judging from the way in which he pet- forms his. Parliamentary duties, and. the hold ho has acquired ,upon the electors as an advance.4l politician, there is no likelihood of his being suc- cessfully opposed at the next election. That there will be opposition of some kind may be taken,for granted; for,, as Mr. BRUNNER remarked, where ever there is plenty of money, a candidate isisurs to be. found, at the last moment. He referresli to a statement in "The Brewing Trade Gazette" to the effect that the Eccles election would have been won by the Tories, if there had been a Brewers' Committee with a thous an 4 pounds te, spend. What this means may be gathered ftoan the further statement that "there arc* plenty of ways to spend money without com- ing within the reach of the Corrupt Practices Act." Forewarned, how.-ever,is to be forearmed ; the Brewers' Committees will be watched at the next election. Mr. Barigniza is not disturbed, for he proceeded, on Wednesday, to re-affirm his belief in the necessity for Local Option as a means of remedying the evils of the drink traffic, and deal- ing fairly with the people who are most concerned. There was no desire on the part of Liberals to ruin the brewing trade, but there was a desire that the inhabitants of a town or district should have a voice in determining how many licensed houses they would have in their midst. Touching UP' on Home Rule and the imprisonment of Irish Nationalists, Mr. BRUNNER made a strong point of the inconsistency and iniustice of the present Government. A demand had been made by the Swiss Government for the extradition of Louis Castioni, who was eharged with murder in con- nection with the late rising Ticino bnt Eng-.

sh judges had this week decided that the crime was a political one, and that he could not be sur- rendered. Whilst the case was pending, Castioni had been well-lodged and well fed ; treated, in fact, with consideration as a political prisoner. What a contrast in law, and in the application of the law, to the barbarity of treatment of Irish offen- ders! They, too, are political prisoners, but because they are British subjects, and their crimes are no crimes at all in the eyes of their country- men, they are treated as if they were the vilest of malefactors. But a day of reckoning is approach- ing for this wholesale practice of hypocrisy and brutality; and we may be sure that the electors of the United Kingdom will not forget the object lesson which they have this week witnessed in the release of CASTIONI. Mr. BRUNNER referred to other matters of interest, commenting at some length upon the McKinley Tariff Act, and the way in which it was converting the people of the United States to the doctrine of Free Trade. He concluded with an appeal to the electors not to sell their birthright for a mess of pottage; to watch their own interests; and to stand by the oppressed in Ireland and in every other part of the world.
"TOUCH AND GO."
" E.B."—The correct designation is Thelwall, not " Thelwell."

It is stated that a Yankee inventor has hit on a ' method of using the clouds as an advertising medium ; but perhaps it is only another castle in the air. It is appalling to think of the heavens declaring the glory, not of their Maker, but of somebody's soap.

The late gales have wrecked a considerable num- ber of vessels, and there has been great loss of life. No less than 24 life boats were at work, and it is some comfort to know that they were the means of saving as many as 96 lives. All honour to the Institution, and to the gallant fellows who man the boats !

General Boulanger has issued another mani- festo, as if it had not already been made manifest what sort of a man he is. He says he made a mis- take in relying upon the Conservatives, and trust- ing to their good faith. And the Conservatives say ditto as to him; and they are both right. Ergo : let the people of France trust neither Boulanger nor his backers.

The British Government seem to be taking cre- dit for the successful attack upon Witu ; but is it creditable ? These people were supposed to be under British protection ; and it ought to have been left to the Germans to take action, seeing that it was a German subject who had been killed. African natives may not have much perception, but they have sufficient to reflect that it is a queer sort of protection which results in the destruction of their villages.

Another life has been sacrificed because of the dangerous road along the towing path between Runcorn and Weston Point. Two men walked into the canal in one night, but at different points, and one was drowned. The Coroner remarked that the verdict should really be that the death was -caused through having no proper roads. There is something or somebody sadly at fault. How many lives must be sacrificed before there is a pro- per road?

People who are watching every phase of the eight hours movement will be interested in learn- ing, on the authority of the " Review of Reviews" that—" One very curious case recently occurred in the North of England, where an arbitrator, who had given the workmen the Eight Hours Day, was' waited upon by them shortly after, and asked to withdraw his award and compel their employers to establish the nine hours." Their objection to the eight-hours day was that there was no sign of its being accompanied with nine-hours pay.

Bit by bit we are getting at the truth as to the doings of Stanley's Rear Column. If what is told of the atrocities of the late Major Barttelot proves to be wholly, or even half true, the natives were justified in putting him to death. The details are sickening, and it is charitable to hope that the leader of the Rear Column had gone out of his mind. He certainly behaved like a madman. There has been a good deal said of the glory of the expedition; but all the talk now is of its shame.

What of our civilisation, and its refining and Christianizing influences? The words are a hide- ous mockery in face of the barbarities of the whites when amongst the blacks. It would seem that when the " civilised man" reverts to his savage state he is a demon incarnate. Emerson tells of a traveller who said to him :—" I have seen human nature in all its forms ; it is everywhere the same ; but the wilder it is the more virtuous." Can this be true? And, if it be true, whither are we going?

"In these Democratic days, concealment of the truth has become a fine art, and the War Office is organised upon a system which works out with =failing regularity one result and only one—entire impunity and irresponsibility for everybody con- cerned." This is the language not of a Liberal organ ; but of the "Times." Is it possible that the old weather-cock perceives that the Govern- ment are played out, and is it getting itself ready to tarn round?

The visit of the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes cannot have other than a stimulating effect. He is alive and earnest from head to foot, and, if he does now and again say what seems a hard thing, what then? Hard things need to be said to rouse people who have become soft and flabby. There is, as he says, too much prudence and policy, and too little of aggressive grappling with evil. It is not good for man to have too much pudding; it makes him for- get at times that there is such a thing as principle and that it is worth fighting for.

The floodingof the Ship Canal has beenthe ab- sorbing topic of the week in this part of the coun- try ; but the excitement, like the water, is subsid- ing. It was assumed too readily at first that a number of lives had been lost, and it is sad enough to know that at least one man was drowned. The engineers see no great difficulty in pumping out what remains of the flood, after the subsidence; but it must take several weeks, and meantime a large number of workers will have nothing to do. They deserve every sympathy, encouragement, and help.
LIR HOME IRON TRADE.

Notwithstanding adverse influences a high Bank rate and Stock Exchange panics—it cannot be said that the English iron market has changed sen- sibly. There is still a steady, if moderate, trade, prices being fairly well maintained, the reductions which have been made being chiefly attributable to the causes mentioned. The demand for steel shows no abatement, and ruling prices are in consequence well adhered to. Shipbuilders continue active, and although the placing of fresh orders is not general, in one or two instances good bookings have been made. Engineers have a respectable amount of work in hand, and a good many of them are very busy.—" Iron."

HYDROPHOBIA IN CHESHIRE. A case of rabies is reported by the Northwich police from Lostock Graham, near Northwich. It appears that Mr. Buckley, of the Black Greyhound Inn, Lostock Graham, had a pet dog, a cross-bred animal, principally of the pug type, which some three or four weeks ago appeared to be unwell. He called in a veterinary surgeon, Mr. Eastwood, of Northwich,who examined the animal,and,suspecting rabies, advised that the dog should be isolated. This was done, and the dog died soon afterwards • but unfortunately before its death it bit Mr. Buckley. In order to ascertain whether there was any dan- ger from the bite, a portion of the animal was sent to M. Pasteur, and a reply just received from Paris states that the dog undoubtedly was suffering from rabies. Mr. Buckley is accordingly advised to leave for Paris immediately for treatment. The muzzling order in Cheshire was only discontinued a couple of weeks ago.

THE REV. LILFORD WILLIAMS, OF RUNCORN. The pastor of St. John's Presbyterian Chapel has passed the synodical examination of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodists. There were 48 candidates and Mr. Williams is seventh on the list in order of merit. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankeir-st.. Warrington.—Advt. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN. Wm. Walsh, ropemaker, of Duke-st., was found dead in bed on Tuesday. The deceassd who was 52 years of age, had been suffering from bronchitis for some time past and the coroner decided that an inquest was un- necessary. ALLEGED THEFT AT RUNCORN. Alfred Cosgrove, a stranger, was remanded by the Runcorn magistrates on Wednesday, on a charge of stealing a coat the property of Joseph Lythgoe, of Gilbert-st., on the 10th inst. The coat was missed and afterwards found pledged at Mr. Imison's, and the pri- soner was arrested on suspicion. STOVES (Petroleum).—Garland, lamp dealer, Warrington. and Earlestown.—Advt. ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE CLASS, RUNCORN. A preliminary meeting of this class was held in Trinity School, on Wednesday evening • when 30 students gave in their names. Dr. McDougall', who will again fill the position of lecturer, gave a resume of the work of last year, and narrated instances showing the valuable assist- ance rendered by several members since that time. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adet. A RUNCORN SCHOONER WRECKED. . The Schooner Margaret, from Runcorn to Belfast. laden with a cargo of bricks and tiles, was discovered early on Tuesday morning to be in distress, during a severe gale which prevailed over the north of the Isle of Man. The crew of three men were rescued by the life- boat, Two Sisters ; but the schooner lies under water in a heavy sea, and is reported to be breaking up. This course was agreed to. The Clerk, in answer to Mr. Poole, said several students had joined the science and art classes in consequence of the alteration of of the fee at the last meeting. div.head: ACCIDENT AT FARNWORTH.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT FARNWORTH.

An accident occurred at Farnworth about noon on Thursday to a man named Richard Southern, residing at 12, Chathsworth-street, Edge Hill, Liverpool, and - em- ployed by Mr. Lee, contractor, of Liverpool. Southern was repairing the roof of Farnworth Parish Church, when he slipped off the scaffold erected for the purpose, and fell to the ground, a distance of about 20 feet, sus- taining serious injuries to his head and fracturing his left leg in two places below the knee. H now lies at Widnes Accident Hospital in a serious condition. NAUTILUS GRATES.—SoIe agent, Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. SUDDN DEATH AT WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest on the body of a child nine weeks old, the son of Win. Reid, 3, -Thorpe-st., Widnes, who was found dead in bed on Sunday morning. The evidence showed that the parents went to bed sober on Saturday night, and at 3 a.m., the mother gave the child a drink. At twenty past seven the child was dead and there was froth on the nose and mouth. Its life was insured in the Prudential, but it was not in benefit. A verdict of " Accidental death from suffocation" was returned. RUNCORN MODEL YACHT CLUB.

The last race of the season took place on Saturday, when the flag of the club was competed for. The course sailed over was in the Weaver Canal at Rock Savage,and the race was run in four heats. In the first heat Mr. F. Bibby's Murial beat Mr. W. Hoxworth's Willie, and in the seccnd heat Mr. Bibby was again successful his Olive beating Mr. Hoxworth's Joey. Murial also beat Mr. W. Cooper's Annie in the third heat. In the final a good race between Murial and Joey, resulted in a victory for Mr. Hoxworth's yatch, which was awarded the flag. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The ordinary meeting of this Committee was held in the Town Hall. Widnes, on Wednesday afternoon, pre- sided over by Mr. S. Robinson. The members present were—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. D. J. Brookes, F. H. rank- hurst, J. T. Allen (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian). The Librarian reported that during the month of October 4,727 books had been issued, being a daily average of 175, an increase of 466 in the lending department, and an increase of 13 in the reference department. Me atten- dances at the library were 13,560, giving a daily avar- age of 502, a decrease of nine compared with the same period of last year. SONS OF TEMPERANCE. At the usual meeting of the above order, on Saturday, there was a discussion on the "United Kingdom Al- liance." The subject was introduced by Mr. Thomas Heesorn, who gave an interesting sketch of the proceed- ings at the recent annual meeting of the Alliance in Manchester. Mr. lleesom spoke strongly in favour of temperance and local reformers making the direct veto a vital issue at elections, and refusing to support any candidate irrespective of creed or party, who declined to support temperance legislation. There was an interesting discussion in which the following members took part— Messrs. Cooke, J. Johnson' Edward Key, Jeseph Parker, and D. Bisbrown. Mr. James Johnson occupied the chair.
A BATCH OF THIEVES AT W JONES.

At Widnes Police Court, ou Monday,Thomas Wassalley and Patrick Fleming, tramps, were convicted of stealing an article of clothing from the drapery shop of Mr. Tebbutt, Ann-st., West. Fleming, against whom previous convictions wero recorded ,was sent to gaol for six weeks, and Wassally was sentenced to a month's imprison- ment.—Three boys named John McCormick, Wm. Glynn, and Andrew McCann were charged with having stolen four codfish and a basket the property of Catherine Delaney. a fish hawker, from Liverpool.—The charge against Glynn was withdrawn and he was called as a witness. He said he was employed to wheel a barrow and look after the fish on Thursday, when the prisoner came and took the basket of fish into Mrs. McCann's house. The boys were each ordered to receive six , strokes with the birch rod, and Mrs. Margaret McCann was sent to goal for a month for receiving the stolen goods, the magistrates saying she was convinced she had sent her son to steal.—Mary Kiley of Marsh-st., and Martin Farragher, of Parr-st. were committed for trial on a charge of stealing £lO irom the pocket of George Harrison, a soap boiler, under circumstances already reported.

div.head: ADULTERATED COFFEE AT RUNCOEN.
div.p: ADULTERATED COFFEE AT RUNCOEN.

On Monday, at Runcorn Police Court, Walter Collier, grocer, Church-st., was summoned lor selling half a lb. of coffee, which was not of the nature, substance, and quality . demanded.—Mr. Roger Hind, inspector of weights and measures, &c., deposed to purchasing the coffee from the defendant's assistant, and the analyist had certified that it contained 20 per cent, of chicory.— In cross-examination witness said he had not been in- spector very long, and therefore could not have had great experience. He asked for shilling coffee. The de- fendant said if witness knew anything about coffee he must have known that it could not be sold pure for that price, as there was no coffee in the market at a less price than is. 3id. a lb. The inspector had full value for his money.—lnspector Hind said the assistant wentupstairs to find the coffee and mixed it with chicory in the ellen. —F. W. Williams, assistant, said the inspector asked for shilling coffee, and when he had supplied him he asked if it were the best. Witness replied " No. I shall mix it for you at a ls."—Mr. Hind denied that the assistant told him it was a mixture.—The defendant said the cus- tom of the shop was to supply the coffee and the chicory separate. It was not sold to the inspectors prejudice be- cause they were giving him Is. for Is. A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs LI 2s. 3d. was imposed.

div.head: FELONIES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FELONIES AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, James Buxton, aged 11 years was charged with having an the 27th ult. stolen a shawl worth 10s. the property of Emmeline Ellis, wife of James Ellis of Norfolk-st. Mrs. Ellis said the prisoner was her nephew and had lived with her for seven years. On the date named he took the shawl from behind the door and pledged it at Mr. Marshes' pawnshop. He had previously stoled 2s. from her. She had sent him to his father at Glossop but he had run away. The father said he could do no good with the boy. He had obtained half time employment for him, but as soon as he had got money he ran away and was found in a Workhouse. The Bench said the prisoner had embarked on a bad career and ordered him three strokes with the birch rod, his father afterwards to take charge of him. Walter Wilson was charged with having stolen a silver watch and chain the property of Wm. Jones of Cawdor- St. The prosecutor said on Sunday night, prisoner knocked at the window and when the door was opened he walked into the house. He declined to leave and was was put out, but in the struggle he took prosecutor's watch and chain and then ran away. The prisoner was afterwards apprehended by P.C. Benfield. The prisoner now said he was in drifik at the time and was very sorry for what he had done. He was ordered to pay 30s. or go to gaol for a month. THREE AT A BIRTH. On Tuesday morning, a woman named Shields, wife of a telephone labourer, living at 12, Iledgis's- yard, North-end, Croyden, gave birth to three boys, all of whom are doing well. An application will be made for the Queen's bounty. - - -

James Cottingham, to the—Hon. and Rev. C. F. Cross, son of Lord Cross, at present curate at New Brighton.
