NORTH COUNTRYMEN'S GATHERING. The Tyne and Wear-siders, resident in and about St. Helens and Earlestown, held their second annual gathering at the Railway Hotel, St. Helens, on Saturday night, when about sixty sat down to a substantial dinner. On the removal of the cloth Mr. Frank Cunningham was voted to the chair, and Mr. J. G. Wolfe to the vice-chair. The evening was spent in a pleasant manner, toasts being honoured, and appropriate songs given.

_ FATAL COLLIERY EXPLOSION. James Twist, aged twenty-seven, of Barton-st., was on the 4th inst. at work in tile No. 11 pit, be- longing to the St. Helens Collieries Company, when an explosion of gas occurred, and lie was so badly burned about the head, face, and body, that he suc- cumbed to his injuries in the Cottage Hospital, on Wednesday last. It appears that the deceased was engaged in repairing one of the roads, and was us- ing a naked light. He came across a quantity of gas, which caused the explosion.

EMPIRE THEATRE OF VARIETIES. This place of amusement continues to be well patronized, and this week the programme is of a most attractive nature, there being no less than twelve" turns." Mr. Bob Martin's cat, which per- forms a parachute descent a is Baldwin each even- ing is very much appreciated. The "star " un- doubtedly is Arthur Corney, and the D'Ostas give a wonderful "second sight" entert&nment. The Voltynes exhibit their skill as gymnasts, and, though their performances are exceedingly difficult, they acquit themselves in a most satisfactory man- ner, and frequently call forth the plaudits of the audience. The other artistes are all familiar, the list including Maud Fern, Lizzie Paine, Fred Izant, Will Bell, and Fiske and Muldoon, all of whom are well up in their respective parts. The brothers Echo are a source of great merriment in their burlesque of " Slavin and McAuliffe ; and, taken all round, the bill provided is a capital one, and is suitably varied. Tim LETTERS OF THE LATE MR. PETER RYLANDS. The London Correspondent of the "Birmingham Daily Post " says :—Considerable comment has within the past fortnight been aroused in political circles here by the publication of " The correspon- dence and speeches of. Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P.," edited by his son ; and there are increasing signs, that something more tanginle than comment may follow. Apart from any question of good taste, a legal point is involved which neither author nor publisher appears to have considered. The first volume consists of letters, mainly from people still ltving, concerning many of which it is simply im- possible to believe that permission to print was given. But it was ruled in the historic case Pope v. Curl], brought by the poet against a publisher, that the property in letters remains in the writer, and does not pass to the receiver ; and this was affirmed only a few years since in an action brought by the present Lord Lytton against the executrix of his mother, who had contemplated issuing some letters written by the first lord to his wife.
A MAIL CART hISAPPEARANCR AT ST. HELENS.

An extraordinary occurrence was reported to the postal authorities at St. Helens, last night week. On the arrival of the male cart from Rainhill with letters and parcels for despatch on to Liverpool and Manchester, the driver reported that when nearing St. Helens he discovered that a mail hamper of par- cels had disappeared from his van. The hamper, which was one of the ordinary kind used for parcels post purposes, was placed on the top of the mail cart behind the driver. The latter, on arriving in Prescot-road, missed the hamper for the first time. The road from Rainhill to St. Helens passes between the high walls of the old and new departments of Rainhill Asylum, and thence through Thatto Heath and St. Ann's district. The loss naturally occa- sioned some anxiety, and the matter was, at once reported to the police authorities. The mail cart arrived at St. Helens at the usual time. about 9.15, and after leaving a portion of the mails at St. Helens, the driver proceeded, in accordance with his usual duty, to Prescot, with additional mails for Liverpool and Manchester to be conveyed by the mail coach. It was subsequently ascertained that the missing hamper was afterwards found in the road near the Black Horse Inn, close to Rainhill Asylum, and the finder was a young man named Robinson, a nephew of the driver of the mail cart. The hamper was transferred to the mail cart, and it was carried on to Prescot in the usual manner, without suffering any delay. Rant WATICR SEP.aavron.—Agent, J. S. Garland, Iron. monger, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATCRDAY, NOVEMI
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATCRDAY, NOVEMI

of alkali works for the district complaining of the nuis- ance arising from the emission of sulphuretted hydrogen from local chemical works. The Committee thought the emission was not reduced to the extent that it might be. —Mr. Hayes said the nuisance caused was dangerous to health, if net to life and knight to he stopped. In his opinion they ought to apply to the Local Government Board in addition to the alkali inspector. The nuisance had been going on for a long time, and many people were afraid when they went to bed that they might not wake in the morning--Mr. Wright said the Health Committee had complained to a num- ber of manufacturers with regard to the gases. Dr. O'Keeffe said the sulphuretted hydrogen usually found its way out at night, and it seemed as though, when the owners and managers had left for the time being, those in charge did not take so much care to prevent the emi- sion of gas from the works. The gases were of such a deadly character, that too much care could not be used, and they would do well to call the attention of the Local Government Board to the matter.—lt was resolved to call the attention af the Alkali inspector and of the Local Government Board to the nuisances.

div.head: ROAD TO WESTON POINT. ANOTHER VICTIM,
div.p: THE ROAD TO WESTON POINT. ANOTHER VICTIM,

The Coroner, Mr. J. E. Worsley, on Tuesday, held an inquest at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, on the body of William Williams, a Ship Canal navvy, who was drowned in the Runcorn and Weston Canal, on Saturday night. The evidence showed that the deceased and a companion went to Runcorn early on Saturday evening, and at 7 o'clock the deceased commenced to walk home alone. He was quite sob,er. About 8 o'clock Mr. Okell, the postmaster, was waL king along the towing path of the canal wiTn he heard a splash. The night was very dark and wet, and he could not see distinctly, but he thought he ohs erved a man's hat on the water, and having ob- tained a stake from an adjoining hedge he tried to reach the drowning man but failed. He informed P.C. Flamers] ey of what he had seen and that officer dragged the canal and removed the body about 10 p.m.—The Coroner sa id he had commented upon this kind of case on numerous occasions but his comments seemed to have no effect. As long as the road from Runcorn to Weston Point was along the towing path of the canal, human life would be sacrifled and he should have to hold in- quests in the future as in the past. All the jury could do was to return a verdict of found drowned ; but it should really be death was caused by having no proper road.—A verdict of "Found drowned" was recorded. A juryman said another man fell into the canal on Satur- day night but a passer by fortunately rescued him.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday at the Town Hall. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Mr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. B. Brown, J. Midwood, F. Hayes, S. Sadler. J. Houghton, F. Liddell, I). Wright, T. Cook, H. Timmins, J. Taylor, J. T. Allen (clerk), Sinclair (surveyor), Carr (engineer), Dickson (inspector).

div.head: WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: THE WATER SUPPLY.

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee con- tamed the report of the Engineer who stated that there was a large increase in the consumption of water, the average daily consumption during the last four weeks had been 2,716,356 gallons, and an increasing quantity of water was still being delivered. The sum of £ll5 would be required for wages each week from the next month. The months accounts amounted to over £1,600. THE FLOOD AT THE OAS worms. Mr. Brown,in moving the adoption of the minutes,said in consequence of the storm on Thursday and Friday, the gas works were flooded, and the town was plunged in darkness for four nights. No doubt the Committee and Mr. Carr had been much blamed in the matter, but it was a circumstance over which they had not the slightest control, and no man could do more than Mr. Carr had done. He never left the works from Friday morning until Sunday night and there were members of the Board who would bear him out in saying that on Sunday Mr. Carr was more dead than alive. He worked with Intel igent energy ;in the endeavour to keep the town supplied with gas. The water commenced to rise about 8 a.m. on Friday. They thought on Saturday that it would be arranged so that the town would not be in dark- ness at night and that on Sunday the supply would have ready, but the water came in again and rose to a con- siderable height. On Monday it was found that in con- sequence of the wet, many of the retorts were out of order, and they could not get them to work as well as they should have done. Consequently there was not the expected supply on Monday. It would be patent to them that the result would be a serious loss to the Gas Committee. Some damage had been done to the gas holder, and, adding damage to plant and stores, the total loss was set down at £B5O. There was no doubt they would have gas that night.—The Chairman said the ex- planation was quite satisfactory. • HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.—THE GAS NUISANCE. The minutes of the Health Committee contained the report of the medical officer, who stated that during October there had been 113 births and 68 deaths, includ- ing 27 children under one year, and 19 betw2en one and five years. There had been 17 deaths from zyinotic disease. Ninety-eight cases of infectious disease had been notified. The nuisance inspector reported that there had not been so many complaints in regard to the prevalence of sulphuretted hydrogen as in the previous month.—Mr. Wright moved the adoption of the minutes, and proposed that the Clerk write to the chief inspector

div.head: TIIE CHARTER OF INCORPORATION:
div.p: TIIE CHARTER OF INCORPORATION:

The General Purposes Committee reported that a house to house convass had been made with regard to the ques- tion of incorporation, and the result was as follows: Total number of houses visited, 5,102 ; deduct empty houses, 64 ; deduct houses of persons not in, 2,188 ; total number of houses where opinion has been ascer- tained 2,850. Of this number 696, or 2442 per cent. were neutral ; 159, or 5.58 per cent. were against the proposal ; and 1,995 or 70 percent., were in favour of it. The ratable value of the house property was £54,415 55., of works £50,137 Sc., of railways and canals E 24,143. of land £2,133 153., of public buildings, gas and water mains, offices, warehouses, coalyards, £8,510 10s. ; making a total of £139,339 15s. The ratable value of the property represented by the signa- tures in favour of and against incorporation .was—in favour of, £23,323 ss. ; against £2,264. The Committee suggested that a charter should be applied for in accor- dance with the minutes of the last Board meeting. Mr. Midwood moved the confirmation of the minutes and remarked that the canvass did not include the whole of the ratepayers but only those who were householders. He did not know why the ordinary ratepayers had not been asked, and lie thought that they should all have been requested to vote.—Mr. Liddle said he had never been asked and he knew a great many manufacturers who had not. The opinion of the principle ratepayers had not been obtained.—The Clerk pointed out that before a Municipal Act could be obtained it was necessary to " obtain the opinion of the inhabitant householders of the district." That did not include the iatepayers living outside the district. He understood that now he was to proceed in the usual way to report to the General Purposes Committee. The question of the division of wards would have to be considered and other work done before a charter could be applied for.—lt was resolved that the necessary steps be taken to obtain a charter of incorporation.

div.head: , --- UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: , --- UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

The fourth lecture of the seires of lecturers on the Problems of Wealth and Industry was delivered on Thursday evening, by Mr. H. Llewellyn Smith, B.A. B.SC The subject for the evenings consideration was Rent, Interest, Profit, and Wages. Assuming, I said the lecturer, that every man was pursuing his own interest and making use of all opportunities that presented themselves to him of increasing his share in the wealth that was produced, the question was how much under these circumstances could each exact. Dealing first with rent, the lecturer defined the landlords share as recompense for allowing the land to be used for production, while rent for a house was rather to be considered interest on capital ex- pended in building the house. Rent was a surplus charge ; it was the measure of the efficiency of the land as an instrument in the making of wealth, and it was the result and not the cause of the price of corn. If the price of corn were 355. per quarter, that the farmer could just afford to pay £lOO for the rent, it was not because he had to pay £lOO tor rent that corn was sold at 355. per quarter. If the whole of the landlords were to make the tenants a present of the land, the price of the produce would not be affected. The price of corn in England was ruled by the wheatfields of America, which by modern science, was more closely con- nected by railroads and steamers with England, than in the old days was London and Scotland. Rents were affected by the price of the products, but the price was not affected by the rent. Rent was not an item in the cost of production, and the result of remitting rent would not be to cheapen the necessaries of life. Passing on to the consideration of interest, the lecturer said interest was the amount paid for the use of capital, and it was fixed by competition of two sets of people, those who had capital, and people who had not got capital, but who wished to engage in productive enterprise. Interest depended upon the supply and demand of capital, and after the interest upon capital was paid, the rest of the product went to labour, and the question was how was it divided between employer and employed. The amount paid to actual labour itself was verging on the threshold of the wages question the most unsettled of problems in the distribution of wealth. The amount of wages which a labourer would receive would de- pend upon two things—the total amount of the pro- duce of labour and the mode in which that produce I was divided. The employer was one who by his business skill and resource set the industrial machine in motion and brought capital and labour together in the right proportion to pay interest on one and wages for the other. The charge of the employer for his services might be large, but it was a great truth that they could not pay too highly for real business of power, and they could not pay too little for real business, in capacity The huge risks of commercial speculation the lecturer described, as gambling. The wages of labour moved be- tween two limits, the level to which they actually arrive, depended upon a variety of circumstances affecting the power to make an advantageous or a disadvantageous bargain; but he should devote the whole of next lecture to the wages question, and passed on to describe the differences of wages in different industries.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.

That Ihe transformation of Widnes into a corpor- ate borough with Mayor Aldermen and Conncillors is now only a mere question of time, as the Local Board, at their meeting on Tuesday, unanimously resolved to apply for the necessary charter. That the flooding of the Gas Works caused great inconvenience to the people of Widnes, but the dis- pensers of candles and paraffin oil must have rea- lised a little through the trementhusly augumented trade in those articles of illumination. That Mr. Carr, the engineer, deserved all the encomium passed upon him for the energetic and intelligent manner in which he coped with the flood, and afterwards repaired the disastrous results of the inundation. That the Cheshire County Council have adoptep the Technical Instruction Act, and intend to spend their grant of £13,000 from the liquor tax to for- warding such instruction. That Runcorn Commissioners,acting on the initia- tive of Mr. E. W. Humphreys, have asked the Coun- cil to set aside Runcorn's proportion of the grant, and as Mr. P. Speakman is a member of the County Committee which has the subject in hand, our in- terests in this matter may be considered safe. That, although the Commissioners have applied for this grant, they have not yet adopted the Tech- nical Instruction Act, but there can be no doubt, that as intelligent men, wishing to advance the status of their town, they will do so after due con- sideration. That Mr. Pritchard touched upon a real want, when he mentioned a middle class school, and it would be a boon to the town if his idea could be carried out. That in the manual on "Education in Cheshire" written by Air. J. T. Brunner, and Mr. T. F. Ellis, M.P., the following reference is made to the educational facilities of Runcorn :—Not long ago a suggestion was made by one of the writers that a Home Reading Union should be established in Run- corn. This suggestion very quickly led to the establishment of two courses of Oxford University Extension Lectures. They have been most success- ful. Their success re-acted on the public library, whose Committee reported.—" But what is more gratifying still is the influence of the lectures on the reading of the general public using the Library, by creating a taste for a higher class of literature, as is shown by the fact that in the classes containing books on the lectures, viz., philosophy, science and art, his- tory, biography, and miscellaneous literature, the number of issues was 5,196, being an increase of 808 over last year." (A note is added that the issue of novels had decreased). This year an evening school has been most successfully started. Science and art classes are also held for the first time. Not satis- fied with all this, the Runcorn people have now established a class in technicological chemistry, as applied to local industries, in connection with the City and Guilds of London Institute, while the School Board has before it a motion to petition the Improvement Commissioners to adopt and levy a rate under the Technical Instruction Act of 1889. Does not such a community thoroughly deserve its full share of the liquor money from the County Council."

div.head: DRST REPOBLIC IN THE WORLD.
div.p: THE DRST REPOBLIC IN THE WORLD.

(Applause.) Our Government was that in the whole world which answered quickest to the will of the people. Let only the will of the people be unmistakeably manifested and any Government that opposed it would go in a week. (Applause.) That was not to be said of any country in the world. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Brunner referred to the case of Louis Castiogni, who was accused of murder in Switzerland, which was decided in the High Court of Justice, on the previous day. It was argued that the crime was a political one, arid three English judges de- cided that it was so, and that Castiogni must not be given up to the Swiss Government, but remain under the British flag a freeman. Contrast this judgment with the treatment accorded to an Irish member of Parlia- ment. This Swiss was well fed, well lodged, and kindly cared for, although he was accused of murder. Mr. O'Brien—and all honour to him —was forcibly stripped, insulted, beaten, half starvocl—for to our shame belt said we half starved all our prisoners—and compelled to herd with the vilest of the vile ; and he was accused, not of murder, but of simply counselling tenants of Lady Kingston, at Mitchellstown, to hold to their homes for a few days. Justice Denman defined

div.head: POLITICAL CRIME
div.p: POLITICAL CRIME

as furthering a dispute between two parties in the State. He should like to ask in the name of common sense, what was Mr. O'Brien committed for but furthering. a dispute between two parties in the State, and he said shame upon us that we treated a Swiss better than we treated au Irishman. (Applause.) Few things had happened lately more interesting to men who made their living by manual labour than the wonderful revolution which has taken place in the United States. They knew I very well of the MC SINLEY TARIFF ACT. So far as the industries of that locality were concerned, the Bill had made no changes in the duties upon alkali, except a reduction upon an item of small importance—in the duty upon bi-carbonate of soda, and in the duty ' upon salt, so that this great change in the fiscal arrange- ments of the United States affected them and their neighbours to a very small extent and to that extent beneficially. But it had unluckily done an enormous amount of immediate injury—which he knew would not be lasting—to a good many English trades. Happily the Republican party, which passed the Bill, I had been utterly routed at the polls from one end of the ' country to the other, and the Democratic or Free Trade party had a majority of 150. (Applause). That was in a house whose total number was 363. All over the United States the tradesmen had been publishing lists in the newspapers showing the old price of articles and the in- creased price under the McKinley Tariff Act, and that had been an excellent object lesson for working-men in Free Trade, and they had taken full advantage of it. (Applause). Mr. Brunner showed how America by her Protectionist policy had thrown nine-tenths of the ship- ping trade of the whole world into the hands of the Eng- lish, and he illustrated how a similar policy operated dis- advantageously in France and Spain and other countries. He was in hopes that Old England was going to lead the way in the matter of Free Trade yet. (Applause.). We saw the Americans cosning to their senses, and one after another of our colonies and the foreign countries of Eu- rope would follow the example of the Democratic party in America. (Applause).—There was a great power for evil in money, and they had more than one illustration of it within the past few years. Now the Liberal party had opposed to them nearly all the money bags in the country,—(hear, hear)—and Ile wanted to warn them of what was coming at THE NEXT GENERAL ELECTION. The Liberal Unionists were money bags and nothing 1 else 'but money (bags—(laughter and applause)—and although Mr. Kniveton spoke very strongly in pro- phecied that they would not have a contest n North- wich Division, he did not think they would resist the temptation. Wherever there was plenty of money a candidate was sure to be found at the last moment. (Hear, hear.) They had not only the Liberal Unionists to face in this matter, they had got the brewers to face. On November 4th the "Brewery Trade Gazette" said that had there been a brewers' committee in Eccles, with a thousand pounds to spend, the election would not have gone the other way— (laughter) —and it was added "There are plenty of ways to spend money without coming within the reach of the Corrupt Practices Act." In the issue of last Saturday, the paper states Mr. Gladstone was trying to ruin the brewing trade—(ap- plause)—and advocated the formation of the nuclus of a league strong enough to influence sufficient votes to turn half the contests in the country. Mr. Brunner denied that the Liberal party desired to ruin the brewing trade, but they wanted to take the power of granting licenses out of the hands of the magistrates, and give it to the people whom it concerned. (Applause.) He wanted to go in for

„ LOCAL OPTION down to the lowest degree, and insist that no man should have a licensed house anywhere unless the neighbours permitted it. (Bear, hear.) There should be fair play on both sides. They could not sell a house next door to a public-house for as good a price as they could a house a few hundred y ards away. What right had the brewers to get an enormously increased value for their houses in conseqnence of licenses granted by magistrates, and after getting this increased value, reduce the value of the houses on either side ? (Hear, hear.) It was not that the Liberal party wanted to ruin the brewing trade ; but they wanted to put the power in the right hands, and permit the people to keep an abominable nuisance away if they wanted to. (Applause.) He was convinced that when the people of this country got this matter of licen- sing directly into their own hands they would, to para- phrase the words of the Bishop of Peierborough, ” keep England, not only free, but sober in the bargain." (Ap- plause.) In conclusion, Mr. Brunner paid a high com- pliment to Runcorn School Board, for their enterprise in establishing evening classes, and for asking the Commis- sioners to adopt the Technical Education Act, and at

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF THE NORTHWICH DIVISION.
div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF THE NORTHWICH DIVISION.
MR. JOSEPH VERDIN'S REPLY..

Mr. C. J. Hughes, Secretary of the Northwich Division Conservative Registration Association, has received the following letter : Thq Brockhurst, Northwich, Bth Nov., 1890. Dear Sir,—l am glad to hear that my letter to you of the 3rd inst. was in time to prevent any inconvenience to the members of the deputation that proposed to call upon me with reference to my becoming a candidate for the Northwich Division at the next election. Whilst I feel very grateful to my friends of both wings of the Unionist party, I cannot, as I have already stated, com- ply with their renewed request to enter upon a contest, which will certainly be of a very severe character. Whilst discharging my present duties it would be too great a strain upon my strength, and my health has not been as much benefited by a long holiday as I was hoping it would be. I have never contemplated being a political candidate; but it is to me a matter of regret to be obliged to decline the overtures of my friends, made with so much kindness and consideration, and had I consented to stand I feel I might have relied upon them doing all they could to ensure the success of the Union- ist cause in this Division, and which I believe will triumph at the next election. For many years it has been my privilege to work for the Constitutional narty, and I hope to have many opportunities of doing so again, and, at the next election especially, I, in common with every other Unionist in the division, will feel it to be an act of duty to our country to make a special effort to return as member for the Northwich Division one who will worthily represent the principles we are psoud to uphold.—l am, dear sir, yours faithfully, JOSEPH VERDINT. To C. J. Hughes,Esq., Northwich.

div.head: VENETIAN BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: VENETIAN BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.

With the object of raising funds to complete the Church of St. Miehael and All Angels, Runcorn, a four days' bazaar was commenced on Wednesday afternoon. The nave of the church was built some years ago to meet the religious requirements of Newton and Higher Runcorn, a district wl.ich had increased in population, and has since developed in a surprising manner. At that ti:ne a paucity of funds led to the postponement of the erection of the chancel and spire, but the congregation which weekly assemble in the edifice have assumed proportions which lead those in authority to believe that the time has arrived to com- plete the structure in all its handsome propor- tions. It is estimated that a thousand pounds will suffice to carry out the project, and towards that sum subscriptions have been promised or received to the amount of £3BO. The bazaar was or- ganised with a view to obtaining the balance, and the Public Hall had for the occasion been transformed intoja representation of St. Mark's Square, Venice; a drop scene placed at the far end of the room heightening the realism of the effect, and the Venetian character of the affair was sustained by the numerous fair stallholders, who were attired in the picturesque costumes of that sunny country. The stalls were burdened with a wealth and charming variety of material for sale that would not have disgraced even a "Venetian bazaar." Each stall was distinguished loy an appropriate quotation from the Merchant of Venice or the new opera the Gondoliers, and the com- plete list of stalls and attendants was as follows : Parish Church Stall :—Mrs. Meredith, Mrs. Abel, Miss Wood, assisted by Miss Dallewy. Miss Auckland, Miss Carrie Abel, Miss Fanny Abel. Girls' Friendly Society —Mrs. Holden. Mrs. Whittaker, Mrs. Marwood, Mrs. Jones, assisted by Miss Smith, Misses Beamer, Miss Jones. St. Michael's Stall :—Mrs. Lake, Misses Smith, Miss Ains- worth,'Mrs. Pownall,Mrs. Worrell, Miss Hill, Miss Bankes, Miss Moore, Mrs. Ridge. Flower Stall :—Mrs. Norman F. Martin, assisted by Miss Fletcher, Miss Elsie Garnett. General Stall :—Mrs. Joule, Mrs. Poole, Mrs. Roberts, Mrs. Crosby, assisted by Miss Johnson. Miss Mellor, Miss Richardson, Miss Savage. Toy Stall :—The Misses Cros- by, assisted by Miss Blanche Price, Miss Connie Price, Miss Ainscow. Refreshment Stall :—Mrs. Gorst, Mrs. Towns, Mrs. James Littler, Miss Statham, assisted by Miss Gorst, Miss Moss, Miss A. Towns, Miss G. Sutton, Miss Sergeant, Mr. W. Towns. The American stall in charge of Miss Statham was ably described as follows : " When you have nothing else to wear But cloth of gold and satins rare, For cloth of gold you cease to care, Up goes the price of shoddy." At the opening ceremony, there were present, besides the numerous stallholders,Lady Brooke, Lady Payne Gall- wey, Mrs. Wyatt, the Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. Dr. and Mrs. Preston, Rev. G. D. Wray, Rev. J. Holden, Rev. J. Jameson, Rev. G. H. Seeley. Rev. W. Kingston, Dr. IMacLennan, Mr. P. Speakman, C.C. Miss Speakman, Mr. T. Speakman, Mr. F. A. Lake, Mr. J. B. Holland, Mr. J. R. and Mrs. Frith, Mr. W. Whittaker, Mr. E. and Mrs. Imison, Mrs. Fielding, Mr. H. and Mrs. White, Mr. J. E. Meredith, Mrs. J. W. Lightburn, Miss Evans Capt. and Mrs. Abrams, Mr. P. Collins, Mr. J. J. Potter, I. Speakman. Mr. W. Shaw (missionary),Mr. A. Jordan, Mr. R. and Mrs. Rawlinson,Mr. J. Yates, &c.—ln introducing Lady Brooke to open the bazaar, Canon Wood expressed the pleasure he felt in her presence. The landed interest was often represented as being in some way at variance or to have different interests from the commercial and manufacturing interests, and they gladly recognised In her presence that day something which showed that there was not a very great gulf, at any rate, in this part of Cheshire, between the two classes. (Hear, hear.) For about three or four centuries the heads of the family of Brooke had been the lay rectors of the parish of Run- corn, until within the last two or three years, and Canon Wood related instances of the great and active interest they had taken in church work. He mentioned that the late Sir Richard Brooke, two or three days before his death, contributed a cheque for £lOO towards the build- ing of the church of St. Michael and All Angels, and he (the speaker) should never forget the kindness and cor- diality which Sir Richard evinced towards him when he first came te the parish. In having Lady Brooke that day they had just the person they would like to have amongst there, and no one could possibly receive a warmer welcome than she would receive. (Applause.) —Lady Brooke, who had a most cordial reception, said it was a source of great pleasure to be present to open that bazaar. She had to thank Mr. Wood for the many kind expressions he had used towards his family. As he had stated they had had a close connection with the town and neighbourhood for many hundreds of years. With regard to the bazaar, she hoped it would such a success as to enable them to finish the church. On behalf of Sir Richard Brooke, she had to express his regret that he could not be present on account of a previous appoint- ment, and to hand his contribution to the treasurer of the fund. Amid loud applause Lady Brooke then declared the bazzar open.—Mr. W. Whittaker proposed a cordial vote of thanks to Lady Brooke for her kindness in opening the bazaar.—Mr. T. Speakman seconded the motion on behalf of the congregation of St. Michael's Church, and he expressed the hope that the success which Lady Brooke wished for would be attained. (Applause.)— Lady Brooke briefly acknowledged the compli- ment, and business was then commenced. There were numerous attractions and entertainments for the amusement of visitors, and an official programme and guide was issued by the Committee. The programme was a capital example of the printer's art from the es- tablishment of Mr. G. Bellamy, and on the cover was a sketch of St. Michael's Church as it will be when completed, and a sketch of St. Mark's Square, Venice. A party of children, trained by Miss Stubbs, gave a most enjoyable entertainment, and later, a concert, arranged by Miss Isherwood, was given by Miss Isherwood, Miss Jones, Miss Taylor, Mrs. W. B. Kay, Messrs. Gates and , Wood. At a later period the " Wandering Gipsies" gave

their "world famed entertainment" to a large and ap- preciative audience, Mr. James Little officiating as con- ductor. There was also a nigger entertainment, given by dusky minstrels. The amount of the check contributed by Sir Richard Brooke was £2O. The bazaar was con- tinued on Thursday, when a good company assembled in the afternoon to witness Miss Barclay perform the opening ceremony. In introducing Miss Barclay, Canon Wood said for more than 40 years her father occupied the honourable, if anxious and difficult position, of vicar of Runcorn ; and, during that time, formed ties of close and strong interest between himself and parishioners, as well as between his family and parishioners, and if it were only as a proof that those ties were not broken nor forgotten, they should welcome Miss Barclay there. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The object of the bazaar was the completion of St. Michael's Church, and the loriginal resolution to build that church was taken, and very great efforts made to effect the object under the late Canon Barclay. That Miss Barclay should be there upon the platform while they were endeavouring to carry on the work of her father, was most suggestive, for it shadowed forth a truth never to be forgotten that one soweth and another reap- eth—that wile the individual workers change, the work of God goes on. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion he assured Miss Barclay that they appreciated and were grateful to her for her interest and work in the parish, and cordially welcomed her to open that bazaar. (Ap- plause.) Miss Barclay, who was loudly applauded, said she was sure they knew what interest she took in her old home and it was a great pleasure to come and help in any way for the completion of the church that her father began during his life time. (Applause.) She was much obliged to Canon Wood for the kind words he had spoken, and to the audience for the kind feelings they had shown towards her late father and his family. She had much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Ap- plause.) Miss Barclay at this point handed the Vicar a cheque for £25. Mr. E. Imison said he esteemed it a great privilege to be allowed to move a vote of thanks to Miss Barclay for her presence that day. They recognised by her presence that she had not forgotten her cld love, neither had she failed to remember the parish in which she so successfully laboured for so many years. (Ap- plause.) Mr. W. Mellor seconded the resolution with pleasure, and remarked that Miss Barclay had been a good friend to Runcorn in church matters. (Applause.) The motion was carried with enthusiasm, and the band in attendance played "Auld lang Syne." The sales then commenced. In the evening a variety of entertain- ments were provided, including concerts, wandering gipsies, troupe of niggers, &c., and were well patronised.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.

The weekly meeting of the above association was held on Wednesday evening, in the Wesleyan school. room, when Mr. J. W. Garnett read an interesting paper, entitled "Signboard History." The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Gandy, and after various items of business concerning theassociation had been disposed of, he briefly introduced Mr. Garnett. The essayist said that a signboard was either a name board or a symbol, and gave a brief history of their origin. Signboards could be divided into three great classes, 11e7aldic, Royal and Historical, and the devices on them were generally taken from one of these classes. lie gave the names of a great variety of signs, and illustrated some of them by sketches on the blackboard. At the close of the paper, a number of photographs of famous sign- boards were handed round. The paper was greatly enjoyed by the members present, and, at the close, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Garnett.

div.head: CHRIST/AN WORK IN THE ARMY IN EGYPT,
div.p: CHRIST/AN WORK IN THE ARMY IN EGYPT,

On Sunday evening, the Rev. William Jackson (Wesleyan missionary at Cairo) gave an address in the Wesleyan Chapel, Penketh, on Christian work in the army in Egypt. Mr. Jackson said that early in 1883 he arrived in England, after 14 years' service in the West Indies. Ile had not been in England a fortnight when he was offered an appointment as chaplain to the Grenadier Guards, then just about to start out to relieve the British troops in the Soudan. He immediately accepted the offer, and. in about a month was on board a transport on the way to Suakim. Immediately on arrival there, a place outside the town was set apart for the erection of chaplains' tents, and they were told to wait there till the tents arrived. They waited till dusk, but no tents had come, and then they realised that some mis-carriage of the order had occurred, and the tents must have gone to some other place. They immediately returned to Suakim, and were kindly taken on board by the captain of an Indian transport lying in the harbour. During the night, the place where the tents should have been erected was "rushed" by the enemy, and in all proba- bility, if the tents had reached their destination as or dered, all the chaplains would have been destroyed. He gave an interesting account of his experiences during the campaign, and described the manner is which the British did battle with their crafty and cunning Soudanese enemies. He also described the religious service which all the soldiers were required to attend, and said that during the whole of the campaign he made it his duty to see that every Wesleyan soldierin the regiment to which he was attached had the opportunity of attending divine service similar to the one to which we listen every Sunday at home. After the war in the Soudan was over, Mr. Jackson was appointed as chaplain to that part of the occupation army resident at Cairo. The address was a very interesting one and was atten- tively listened to by a large congregation.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

CRICKET CLEI.—ANNEAL MEETING. At the adjonrned annual meeting of the members o the Frodshazn Cricket Club, held, in the girl's school Church-st., on Tuesday evening, Mr. Ily. Reynolds (chairman), the following officers were appointed for the ensuing year :—President, Mr. A. H. Talbot; vice-pre- sidents, Messrs. Chas. Reynolds, James Reynolds, Henry Reynolds, Alfred Thomas, John Brundrit, H. Linaker, S. Woodhouse, G. F. Taylor, Wm. Hayes, and John Hig- son ; captain for the year, Mr. A. H. Talbot; sub-cap- tain, Rev. A. J. Jameson ; treasurer, Mr. J. B. Holland; auditor, Mr. A. W. Abernethy; secretary, Mr. H. G. Linaker ; Committee, Rev. G. H. Kingston, Messrs. R. G. Carpenter, Henry Reynolds, C. A. Talbot, and C. W. Abernethy. It was decided that the secreta.y should advertise for a professional. The Secretary reported that during the past season 28 matches were arranged, 27 of which were played and one—Eaton Park, on the Eaton Park ground, had to be abandoned on account of the weather ; 12 matches were won, 12 lost, and S drawn. CONCERT AT FROM:IAN!. ' The first concert of the season was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday evening, the room being well filled. The first piece was the quartet" 0 who will I o'er the downs," sung by the Misses Jones and Birkett, and Messrs. Morris and Birkett. "On the banks of Allan Water," was also given later' and the vocalists received a genuine and hearty re-callfor their charming vocalisation. "Alone on the Raft" and the other song which followed at the later period by Miss Simkin were nicely given. Miss P. Pryde contributed greatly to the pleasure of the audience by her skill and fine rendering of the solos (pianoforte), Chopin's "Polonaise," and Weber's "II Moto Cavatina." The pianoforte trio" Les Tolls Oiseaus," by Masters A., G., and T. Illige, evoked an encore for its effective performance. Mr. F. Groves receive an encore for his song " The Diver." A recita- tion by Miss Cecily Sands, entitled Inasmuch," was splendidly given. The humorous readings by the Vicar (Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A.) and Mr. James Reynolds, J.P. caused much merriment. Miss Spooner contributed the songs" The Gift" and" Jack and Gill," fairly well, as was also those by Mr. G. Pryde, " I am dreaming" and "Non I ver' ly." Miss Nellie Dunsford's pianoforte solo was rendered in a very creditable manner. The other items on the programme, consisted of comic songs and sketches, which were given by Mr. Johnson with accustomed ability.

div.head: LYIIII.
div.p: LYIIII.

Two BIND or HOPE MEF.TINOS.—Mr. Joseph Thorpe presided over the weekly meeting of the Wesleyan Band of Hope Society, held in the schoolroom on Monday even- ing. There was a moderate attendance. The same evening the inaugural meeting for the winter session in connection with the Congregational Band of Hope was also held. The Rev. Charles Clay was in the chair. Mr. Manning, of Thelvrall, delivered an address in advocacy of temperance, and a variety of songs, recitations, &c., were delivered by the members. There was an encourag- ing attendance. POACHING AT THELWALL.—At the Lymm Police COurt, on Saturday, before Mr. G. B. Dewhurst and Dr. Bra- bazon, Wm. Bowdon and George Smith, Ship Canal navvies, residing at Thel wall, were charged with poach- ing on land in the occupation of Mr. John Longshaw, at Tlielwall, on the 7th November. Bowden was further charged with assaulting a watchman named John Leigh. James Hankinson said that on Friday last he heard the bark of a dog proceeding from Mr. Longshaw's land. He went in that direction, and found the prisoners, each of whom had rabbits and nets in their possession. Leigh said that when he was assisting to take the prisoners to the Lymm Police Station Bowdon struck him. Each of the prisoners was fined 303. and costs fer poaching, and Bowdon an additional lOs . and costs for the assault.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
Is MARRIAOII A FAILURE?

According to the opinion of William Cotton, and his wife Ellen, who figured at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, the answer would appear to be in the affir- mative. William was charged with assaMtin,„,, his wife on Sunday midnight, and in her statement to the Bench complainant said on Sunday midnight, without any provocation, her husband "thumped" her in a scanda- lous manner. Cross-examined by Mr. Browne, who appeared fer the defendant, she said she had lived un- happily for two years, and her husband turned her eut night after night. Mr. Browne suggested to the Bench that the best course to adopt would be to grant a separa- tion order, and he would draw up an agreement be- tween the parties as to tiae allowance the defendant should give his wife. The magistrates agreed to this, and the case was adjourned in order that the defendant might have an opportunity of fulfilling, his promise con- -tamed in the agreement.

div.head: NBOLBOT OF CHILDREN.
div.p: NBOLBOT OF CHILDREN.

At the Warrington Borough Court on Saturday, Thos. Healey was charged on a warrant with unlawfully run- ning aws7 from his children, on the 26th ;September, and leaving them chargeable to the union. Mr. B. Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the union. The prisoner stated in his defence that his wife was solely to blame for the step he took. Whenever she had money she spent it on drink, and on many occasions he had ha.d to go out in a morning without having a bite, and after doing a whole day's work come home and find the house empty, the wife being out drinking. When he went away, his wife was apprehended for theft, for -which she got a month's imprisonment, and .he left the children in charge of a neighbour, promising to send money for their maintenance. The prisoner Was arrested at Stockton-on-Tees.—The case was adjourned for a fort- night to allow the prisoner to pay for the expense of tak- ing him to Warrington. Mr. Shearer did not press the case, because the prisoner's statement about his wife was correct, and he would lose his pension if he was sent to prison. The prisoner had his pension papers upon him. '

div.head: THHPT OP A COAT.
div.p: THHPT OP A COAT.

At the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, a man 'named Frederick Border,employed at the Castle Rubber Works, was charged with stealing a coat, value £2, the property of the book-keeper, Mr. Evans. Mr. Hunt said the complainant in this case was the book-keeper at the Castle Rubber Works, and resided at Penketh, and the defendant was a waterproof garment maker at the rub- ber works. It appeared that complainant went to his dinner about one o'clock on Monday, leaving his coat banging in the store room ; and, when he returned at two o'clock he missed it. He made inquiries, but no one on the premises knew anything about it, neither could it be found. Information was accordingly,given to the police, i and D.S. Monaghan took the matter n hand along with other constables. Defendant was suspected of the theft from the fact that he was not at his work on Monday, attd was seen outside the premises between one and two o'clock. He was sought for and on Monday afternoon he was found drinking in Walker's Vaults, Bridge-st., by Monaghan., and was taken into custody. At the Police Station, he admitted the theft, and said he had pawned the coat at Tunstall's, for 3s. 6d., giving the name of Fred Baker. of Mersey-st. Prisoner was committed to prison for 21 days' with hard labour.

div.head: SHOCIING CRIIELTY To AN Ass.
div.p: SHOCIING CRIIELTY To AN Ass.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Friday, a boy, aged 14 years, named Thomas Roberts, was charged with 'unlawfully ill-treating a donkey. Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, said last Friday morning, about twelve o'clock, he was passing up Market Place, , and, as he was turning into Mill-st., he met Roberts,who ' was driving a donkey, which was attached to a cart, and , he kept kicking the hind part of the donkey with his clogs, the heels of which were very sharp. He stopped' the lad, and said he had a good mind to thrash him for his conduct, and told him it was a shame that he should beat such an old donkey, for he knew that he was 20 years old. This was the fifth time witness had been caught,' thrashing the donkey.—Constable Bell said on the day in ciution he was in Market Place, and from what was said to him he proceeded to Cheapside. He there saw the donkey attached to a cart. The donkey was bleeding from a wound on the hind part. He asked thetoy what had caused the blood to flow, and he answered "I have done it, but lam sorry for it." Mr. Harrison, one of the magistrates, said he thought the defendants' conduct was dAibolical, and the only consideration he was entitled to ,was on account of his youth. It was a shame that the donkey should be entrusted to such a savage.—Defend- -ant was fined 10s. and costs 95., or in default 14 days imprisonment.

div.head: SON OP IRELAND IN TROUBLE.
div.p: A SON OP IRELAND IN TROUBLE.

A case which caused a great deal of amusement was heard at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, when Philip O'Brien was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Naylor-et., on the 4th inst. After Constable -Clough had given evidence in substantiation of the charge, he was the subject of severe eross-examination by the defendant. In the course of his defensive inter- rogatories defendant asked the officer how he became acquainted with his (defendant's) name. From the next door neighbour was the reply. " Which next door neigh- bour ? " was then asked, but Inspector James requested the constable not to answer the question.—The defen- dant said the officer had a right to answer the question, - and that Mr. James had no business to interfere; because he was not a lawyer. (Laughter.) Defendant continued that the charge was nothing but a trumped up thing against him simply because he was a political man; but he was not ashamed to say that he was proud of his party. He denied that he was ever disorderly, and he said P.C. Clough was not worthy to be in the force. Inspector James said the defendant had been up pre- viously for similar offences and he always said he was not guilty. The Mayor said the Bench had decided to remand the case for a week, So that the prisoner would have an opportunity of procuring witnesses to show that he was not drunk and disorderly.

div.head: OBTAINING GOODS BY FALSE PRETENCES.
div.p: OBTAINING GOODS BY FALSE PRETENCES.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, a young man of very respectable appearance, named Charles Johnson,was charged with unlaWfully obtaining by false pretences from the shop of Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephews, on Saturday night, one pair of men's lace-up- boots, value 10s. 6d. ; also with obtaining by false ipretences, two shirts, value 7e. 6d. on the sth inst., the !property of Mr. Wm. Peacock, Manchester House, Latch- It ord. In support of the first charge Thomas Smart :inntion behalf of Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephews, sta.ted that on Saturday night between eight and nine o'cloc IC the prisoner entered the shop and made a state- ment to the effect that Ashton's had sent him for a pair of boots. Witness asked was it Ashton's of Sankey-st. ; and prisoner s:lid "No, shton's of the Bridge Inn." After further questiong witness let defendant have a pair of number seven men? boots. Prisoner then walked out of the shop, and, finding that the prisoner had not been sent to purchase the boots by Ashton's, witness gave informa- tion to the police, and the prisoner was arrested.—ln the second case it appears the defendant went to Mr. Pea- cock's shop and asked for two shirts for his father. The prisoner was accordingly allowed to take two shirts on approbation, and he was not heard of again by com- plainant until the police informed him of the prisoner's arrest.—The father of the prisoner, in a statement to the Bench said he had been disgraced by his son's conduct, and he would like the magistrates to send him off with- out committing him to prison, for he had been in prison once. He (the father) had tried everything he could to snake his son better, and he had nearly ruined him; but, still, he had left a fatherly feeling.—Prisoner was com- mitted to goal for 14, days with hard labour. A QUEER WAY OF GOING HOME. A man named Michael Hardman, residing in Howley, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with having been found on the premises of Thomas Barnes of Froghall-lane at 12.15 a.m., on Sunday, he being there for an unlawful purpose, to wit,to commit a felony. The prosecutor stated that about eleven o'clock on Saturday night he was in bed and he heard a great noise, which he at first thought was caused by the shunt- ing operations on the railway. The noise, however, did not abate, but continued upwards of twenty minutes. He then went downstairs, and there found his wife, who had not retired for the night, in a very frightened condi- tion, and he asked what was the matter. His wife an- swered that someone was knocking at the back door and that she had heard the knocking for twenty minutes. Complainant then looked through thy window, and pre- sently the prisoner came up the yard and entered the kitchen and commenced swearing and conducting him- self in a scandalous manner. With assistance the pri- soner was ultimately given into custody at the police station.—ln answer to the magistrates the prisoner said he was drunk and he remembered nothing about the occurrence.—The Mayor said he could understand a man Rot knowing a lamp from his brother; but he could not understand a man not knowing his own house from that of another person.—Complainant said that he did not think the prisoner intended to rob his house.—The Mayor observed that perhaps the man had lost himself and wanted someone to take him home. He added that there was no charge against the prisoner for having been drunk, neither was a charge preferred against him for having been found on the premises for the purpose of committing a felony, and under these circumstances the ...defendant would be dismissed.

div.head: IRIS X DELEGATES IN NEW YORK. GREAT DEMONSTRATION.
div.p: THE IRIS X DELEGATES IN NEW YORK. GREAT DEMONSTRATION.

NEW YORK, TITESDAY.—A reception was given yester- day to the Irish delegates at the Metropolitan Opera House, at which Governor Hill presided. The building was crowded to its utmost capacity. The list of those present included Mr. Cleveland, Mr. Grant (Mayor of New York), Mr. Charles A. Dana,. Mr. Ewarts, General Sherman,Mr. Chancey Depew, Mr. John A. Coekerill, General Sickles, and hundreds of others. Mr. Hill, in presenting the delegates, said—l am here more by my presence than by words to testify to my interest in the cause so ably espoused by these gentlemen, whom we gladly welcome, and which calls forth the sympathy of Americans, hallowed by the blood of martyrs, and made sacred by the tears of millions.—Mr. Dillon was the first to reply, and in his speech said—l told you ten years ago that our policy was a fighting party, and that we pro- posed to attack the source of famine in Ireland.—Mr. O'Brien, who followed, said that they were asking for fighting funds, and that they proposed to fight until they had uprooted the system of mis-government. He also referred in eulogistic terms to the men of Tipperary.--Mr. ' O'Connor and Mr. Sullivan also addressed the meeting, which subsequently passed resolutions of sympathy with the Irish cause. Heavy subscriptions were received, the money taken at the doors amounting to 4,000 dollars, while that collected in the building reachsd the total, of 33,000 dollars.

div.head: GENERAL BOOTH'S SCHEME. OFFER BY MR. BANCROFT.
div.p: GENERAL BOOTH'S SCHEME. OFFER BY MR. BANCROFT.

Mr. Bancroft, the veteran actor, writes to the London papers :—I know nothing of General Booth's scheme in detail, but it seems to me to be so noble in its object that something real soon and surely should be done to aid it. I read that the large sum of £lOO,OOO will be necessary to ensure an effectual trial, and, without the smallest pretext to hang on to even the skirts of philanthropy, I beg to say that if ninety-nine other men will do the same for the cause I will give General Booth £l,OOO towards it.

STOCKTON HEATH V". W. SATE'S THAN (LATCHFORD).— This match was played at Stockton Heath on Saturday. The latter team being represented by a majority of the Thelwall Hornets and players out of several local clubs enabled Mr. Bate to place a very strong team on the field. Stockton Heath, losing the toss, kicked off. In the first half Stockton Heath had slightly the best of the game, Glover and Y. Berry having very hard lines in not scor- ing. At half-time the score stood Stockton Heath 2 minors, Latchford 1 minor. On changing ends play was of a very even character until shortly before the call of time, when the home team had the best of matters, Broady crossing the line. The kick at goal failed. This brought about time, and the score stood, after a very hard game, Stockton Heath E try and 4 minors, W. Bate's team 2 minors.

WARRINGTON RANGIRS 2ND, V. BOWDON RANGTIRS The above,teams met on the ground of the former, on Saturday last, and the home team losing the toss, kicked off against the wind. A poor return being made, the homesters at once attacked, minors falling in quick suc- cession. From some give-and-take play Ashurst obtained possession, and after a good dodgy run secured a clever try, Whitfield failing at goal. At half-time the score read Warrington 1 try 3 minors, Bowdon nil. Up,sia the re- start, the game contined in favour of the home team. Whitfield obtaining a try. The same player a few moments later again rushed over the line, but lost pos- session, and Bradbury being close at hand completed the try, which, Cook converted. The home team eventually retired victors by 1 goal 2 tries 6 minors, to Bowdon nil. WARRINGTON "A " T. MOSSLEY " A."—Witha miser- ably weakened team, the Warringtonians journeyed to Mossley, on Saturday, to play this fixture, and to make matters worse, could only muster 14 men until halftime, when Rowe made his appearance. Only a moderate number of spectators had assembled when Warrington started uphill, and against a stiffish breeze, play locating in the home quarters, until a dribble carried the leather well into the visitors' lines, Lally saving. Although a smart bit of play by Williams transferred the scene of warfare to more desirable quarters,, a rush by the Mossleyites enabled Taylor to score. Dropping out, a kick by Williams sent the oval towards his, opponents' quarters, the position being, further improved by the smartness of Massey. A miss kick,however„ completely I altered' matters, and although Daniels saved.grandly to midfield, the homesters maintained a strong attacking, position, and the result of capital passing between Lees, Pleirford, and Mellor enabled the latter to score, which Piekford improved. This reverse was a staggerer, but the visitors quickly renewed, and in no wise dis- heartened, played up with renewed vigour. The kickoff was charged, but the lost ground was as quickly gained, for-some pretty passing by Lally, Heesom, and' Massey, more than neutralized. Some effective forward play by Mblynenx, Creaghan, Russell, and Isherwood followed, and Lally enhanced matters by flooring Taylbr at his own2s. Mossley by a rush transferred to midfield, until', Lally (who was playing half) receiving from Williams ran grandly to near the line and passed, but only a,'l minor resulted. This was decidedly bard lines, but directly afterwards Isherwood, Davies,. Howarth, and Hackett headed a fine dribble, .only to see Lees clear ef- fectively. This was somewhat nullified by Jolley, and although a strong burst by Malyneaus took the oval to neutral territory, the ground was again lost, but Samp- son repeatedly saved in daring style,cy minor being even- tually conceded. Following the drop out, Russell, Creaghan, Hackett, and Davies headed &rush to the, Mossley lines, the last named securing a. try, which Isherwood almost converted. Succeeding this, Williams threw out to Jolley, who effected a strong run, bvt was' puiled up when looking dangerous, half time arriving with: Warrington 0-1-1, to 11111 iteaurning,. the• home. team were allowed to gain a footing in- side the visitors' quarters,, and. Warrington for- a lengthened period had an anxious time of it Gradually the ball was worked out of danger, and thas. game was waging at midfield when Davies made a very- tine run to the lines, and a minor was conceded. After. this the hornester attacked, but Sampson replied splen- didly to a rush, and then Massey directly afterwarde saved smartly from a similar rush. Alot of monotonous. scrimmaging ensued, but at length, Rowe got the• oval away, and Jolley effected a fine dribble right under the posts when some effective i tackling was done by Rowe.: , A couple of minors then followed n gulch succession. Subsequently a bit of tricky play by Danielk-was taken up by Russell, Molyneaux, Isherwood, and Davies„caus- ing the game to hover about midfield. Here Lally Tot 1 possession, and out-manceuvring the home custodian, ' gained a really magnificent try, under the posts, ar.'"r..h Davies converted. Afterwards Mellor tried to get away from a cross kick, but was floored splendidly by Massey, time arriving with the score at.WArringtoa,l4-4..t0 D 4-1. Warrington : Sampson, back;: Hankie Jolley, and Mastey, three-quarters; Williamson and Rowe,, half backs'', Lally, Heesom, Molyneux, Isherwood, Hackett, Howarth, Davies, Russell, and Creaghan,. forwards. MOssley : Lees, back; Mellor, PickfOnd, and Taylor, three-quarters; Lees and Ogden, half backs Lees, Andrew, Grea.by, Hibbs, Kenworth,,Dearnley Hbwarth, Bottomley, and Taylor, forwards.

WARRINGTON v. MOSBLEY. After an absence of a month, the Warringt.eztians made their re-appearance at. Wilderspool on Saturday, when they met Mossley. It will be remembered that owing to some vnisunderstaading the Mossleyites did not make their annual visit laet season., but the line exhibi- tions which had been displayed in previous years had not been fortwtten by Warrington enthusiasts,, hence the large attendance, which must haxe been, nearly 4,000. When the teams had arranged themslves,.it was seen that Warrington were a somewhat mixed lot in the for- , wards,sevoral of their prominent players being absent. A late start was made,Ashton setting the ball in motion by kicking oft towards the pavillion goal. Berry stayed thern return, and in the first minute Jiames Bate ought to have run in,, but unselfish passing gave Newby a chance foiling Brans in his attempt tusenre. Moseley defended,. and a. spell of forward play,, in which Ashton was the , shining light, was at length relieved by a spell of pass- ing by Mossley, the final essay being interrupted by Webster, who floored pointed before he could passthe half way flag. Smart work by the Bates and Barnes resulted in a miner, and a capital piece of dribbling by Yovey and a long kick by Evans wereresponsible for the last minor of the match. So fat the game had been of a dragging description, there being little or no combina- tion among the forwards, whilst the backs had been, comparativery speaking, idle. Ashton was to the fore ; with some excellent work in the line-outs and scrum- mages, and after another spell of forward play, the home backs got the oval working,. and James and John Bate cleverly worked the oval to Barnes, who dodged, and finally passed smartly to Evans, the result being is clever try, Webster failing at the place. Following tins Jack Bate almost dodged in from a pack near the line, but the first half ended in Warrington having the advantage of a try and two minors to their credit. On the restart, Warrington at the onset meant business and after three minutes' play, Thorniley started a short passing move- ment participated in by Ashton, Knowles, Lloyd, and Holmes, the last-named running in near the posts, Barnes this time placing a goal. The homesters still attacked, and Morrell was repeatedly called upon to save his charge. Newby, Walker, and Corscadden dribbled effectively, Boscow staying the rush, but the relief was but a faint one, for Barnes securing possession beyond the half way flag ran through the thick of his opponents, and one of the finest runs it has been our lot to witness resulted in

a try, the spectators cheering te, the echo at so grand a display. Evans took the kick and landed a goal, Thorniley charged the kick off, awl) Warrington still kept oa the improve, the forwards workingnow well together,. Eventually a sharp dribble by the Itosalpy men rushed the leather to the Warrington end, and Makin scored. This was their last chance, for Warrington, going right away from the restart, soon gained a 6oting in the Mossley quarters, and Webster having EV shot at goal James Bate was handy, and the threequarter having raced up and placed him on side, a try wa.. the result, Evans making a good attempt with the place kick. 1 Evans foiled a combined effort of Mossley to 'lnvade, and from a pack near the quarter flag, James Bate threw to Webster, and the latter soon being in his stride, the Mossley backs had little chance with himond a try under the posts was the result, Barnes placing a goal. From a pestart Barnes put in another of those runs which have been long associated with his name, but nothing came of it and Warrington finally won by three goals, two tries, two minors, to Mossley one try. Teams ;—Warrington: Boscow, back; Webster T. Barnes, and Evans, threequarters ; James Bate and Webster, Bate, half backs; Ashton (captain), Povey, Thornifey, Knowles, Berry, A. Barnes, Catterall, Lloyd, and Holmes, forwards. Mossley: Morrell, back; Newley, Laach,and Pointon, ihree-quarters ; Billings and Makin' half backs; Mayall, Jones, Walker, J. Corscaddon, A. Corscadden, Bowers, Cunningham, and Philips, forwards. Referee,. Mr. ffilliamson,Salford.
A MANCRESTER TRAIN WRECKED SEVEML PERSONS INJURED..

On Saturday night the Belfasbmight-boat tvain wth runs between Manchester and Fleetwood, ma the Lan- cashire and Y,.;vkshire Ilailwa7, met with a most disas- trous accident; the whole train, consisting of an engine and nine coaches, being utterly wrecked. The ancident occurred about a mile from Chorley station, in a deep cutting, which is about a third of a mile 'lung, ita steep sides being supported by a high and masse stow retain- ing wall aft. to 30ft. high. At the entrance of the cutt- ing the retaining wall is lower, and at this paint on Saturday night a tremenEOus fall of eutli took place sud- denly, some scores of tens covering and blocking both sets of rails. The landslip was caused by the recent heavy rain. The expros ran into the obstruction, and the whole train, consisting of an engine and nine carri- ages, left the rails. The line was p,ioughed up for a dis- tance of sixty yards, and all the carriages were smashed on tho off side by coming in contact with the retaining wall of the cuttirg. Strange to say the driver and stoker and two er three passengers appear to exhaust the list of injured persons whose cases aro at all serious. A misleading report was circulated on Monday that a man had had his legs amputated, the confusion probably • arising through a platelayer named Samuel Bolton, aged 60, who was in the breakdown gang on Sunday% receiv- ing snch injuries to his leg that amputation had to be performed. Bolton is making satisfactory progress.

FLOODING OF THE SHIP CANAL. LOSS OY LIFE, AND IMMMSE DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY. The heavy fall of rain whieh took pace on Tharsday and Friday of last weekled to a disaster of the most stupendous descripel,en on the Ship Canal. The large rainfall swelled the volume of the river Mersey to stich a degree that en Friday great anxiety was felt lest the waters from the river should burst into, the canal at diffeerent point e be- tween Rixton Leys,.neir Lymm, and Ebllins Green, where the river and the canal cutting' are closely contiguous. These fears were, unfortunately, mere than realised, in spite of the fact that men were hurriedly drafted teeoughout Friday to the (index; gered points, and great efforts were made to pre, vent a collapse of the river banks. fleadually water began to trickle into the cutting, and aa night approached the stream increased in ferce des—' pite all efforts to cheek it, About midnight the. banks of the river gave way, and an immenseeolume of water, which is described as rushing into the cut- ting with se " head "of about eight to ten feet, swept everything before it, travelling in the direc- tion of Warrington with al noise that carried terror to all who heard it. Temporary bridges and other btructures were broken up, like matchwood and carried away with the °mush, and trams, locottne-e Cities, steam navvies, steanecrenes, and stock of ;all kinds were submerged. The noise of the advancing water as it rushed along the. canal towards Lateh- ford is described as terrific, and to be compared' tb nothing so much as the roar of cannons or succes- sive peals of thunder. The water rushed along submerging everything in its eoursa until it reached Stockton Heath, a distance of several miles from where it first entered the meek but at Stockton, Heath its course was stopped by the nneut portion, over which the Northwlch and Warrington road passes The appearance of the canal on Saturday morning pre- sented a wonderful contrast to that otthe previous day. Instead of large numbers of workmen and a great quantity of valuable plant being empleyee in the work of excavation and completion,the great cutting was filled, in some parts almost to the top with water. The aver- age depth of the water was said to be not less than 20 or 30 feet, and at some points-such as Latchford locks the depth was probably not less than 50 'feet. On the sur- face of the water was floating all kinds of wreckage and ' at some places the upper pees of some of the submerged plant could be seen. Early on Saturday the most startling fee-moues as to the loss of Wettest had taken pike were current in Warring- ton, and it was said that many workmen on the canal were missing, and these had, it was presumed, been caught in tee rush of water and drowned. But as time went on most of these men turned up, and there. is now reason to believe that only onaman was drowned. This small list of fatalities is due to the fact thalethe flooding of the canaltook place at night when few :nem were in the cutting ; had it been otherwise there •aan be little doubt that there would have been a deplorable loss of life.

The waterin its course washed ,away a portl'on of the soil under the main line of the London and .North- Western Railway near Latchford station, and as, soon as this was discovered it became necessary o. stop the traffic. At this spot there is a tunnel, which connects the canal with,the Stockton Heath section, and it was here where tlls danger to the lineoccurred. o?l,Baturday morning the down lino was put into use, all traffic pas- sing over it. In the meantime, all possible-haste was made to pre7elst the disaster assuming still greater pro- portions, and about a hundred men were set 1 to work banking the line up with ballast. It was also found necessary to close a portion of the Knutsford road, vehi- cular traffic being diverted by way of Grapp2nhall-lane. A wooden bridge connecting Wash-lane with the Grap- . penhall side we also closed to vehicular traffics. On Sun- day the side of' the railway line was still unsafe for traffic, and trains going to Manchester were backed at Latch- ford station znd sent forward by the other line to 'Mel - wall, where the original course is resumed. Tfains ex- Manchester fcr,Warrington and Liverpool change lines at Thelwail, and are put on the right line at Liitchford, after having passed the dangero:ss spot. Dining that day a special engine was several times run from War- rington to the part of the canal with substantial refresh- ments for the navvies. Mr. J. ilaorrison, stationmaster at :Latchford, was continuously in charge of the train, and also superintended the shunting+ arraincemmts.

On Friday crening when it was seen that there was a danger of flooding, four men on the locomothe engine Lancaster went into the locks to try to get out cranes, waggons, workmen's tools, or anything they could lay their hands to: Half-way down the incline there is a pair of points: The heavy rains had washed sand into the points, andl blocked them so they could not work. Consequently the front wheels of the Lancaster left the metalS. As flrey men were engaged putting the-engine . on to the metals again a man passed along the bottom of the canal cairying a bag of spies. He called to the xnen "Show us a light, mate," the night be'mg, dark. ; A moment or cm later the men hoard him shouting for ' help, and saw him being carried past them,and knocked to and fro amongst the timber carried down la7,the first wave of the fi*Kl,, which had burst- through the,Thel wall Island. This, was the first sign of their immediate 'danger. It wos.utterly impossible for them to, reach their unfortunate comrade,who wasbeing hurled towards the heading. - -The men with the engine shoutoelte the others working-at the heading to clear out, and these, nine in numher: effected their esrapes in a marvellous ! manner. And not a moment too soon, for witha noise like a terrific peal of thunder, the huge wave was upon them. The-other four men scrazahled up to the top of the embankment with great difficulty, anclt in five minutes thess. engine, the Lancaster, was surmorged, although it was standing half:-way up tl-e incline. A more miraculous escape was impossible. A gentleman living in thevicinity of the canal thus describes the rush of the water :--" We iseard a rce&likeithunder upoa, thunder, and clap upon clap. It was a frightful noise,.but we did not know what had caused it until the next morning. The noise,was ter- rific, and it is a mercy tha t only one life was lostr. Strange • to say, all' these accidents on, the canal have occurred dur- ing the night. The slip at Warburton was at night, and also the•ilood during the spring, and now, a.i midnight, the most serious accident of all has occurred. OFFICIAL STATEMENT.

The, official report of the disaster, issued by the Ship Canal Company, is as follows :—" The great storm on Thursday breached the embankments of Sow Brook, which is temporarily carried across the ship canal near Latchford, and filled the cutting at Rixton. It carried 1 away part of the bank by which Lasksy-lane is carried 1 over the canal, also. temporary,and in its course down the cutting destroyed the two shots which carry the `brooks at Latchford, Morris Brook, and boundary Brook, over the cutting. A heading has by arrangement with the London and North-Western Railway Company been driven under their Warrington and Stockport branch, and the water has naturally found its way through this tunnel. As a measure of protection the railway author- ities have found it advisable to work one of the two lines only. No damage has been done to the permanent works. The temporary works will be immediately re- newed, and the cutting pumped out, both of which operations will be accomplished in a short time. Un- fortunately, a number of men, while engaged in attempt- ing to remedy some of the damage caused, where placed in a very dangerous position, and one of them lost his life by drowning."

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
ASSOCIATION.

The League games on Saturday were productive of wonderfully even football. Of the six played three were drawn and two others, decided by one goal only. The meeting of the Rovers and Everton at Blackburn was patronised by something like 12,000 spectators, but it cannot be said play was of the highest class. There were absentees on both + sides. Victory finally rested with the Rovers by two goals to one, and they had the best of the game on the whole. Everton are not fulfilling the promise of the early days af this season, this being their third successive disaster.

There was a hard battle at Deep:We, where neither the North End nor Notts could score's solitary goal. The defence of both sides was very safe and reliable. The Preston front rank had been changed`,.MTenna, the ex- soldier, and Gallocher havieg beew reinstated, and the alterations were an improvement. Wolverhampton Wanderers defeated the Bolton Wanderers by a goal to none, and thus won their way to the top of the League, with Everton second. The present positions ef tho clubs are. however, somewhat misleading, zerno having run through more fixture 3 than others:

Accrington msde light of Derby County,.who are now at the bottom of tt e League table, and likely to remain there on present form. Burnley proved themselves equal to Aston Villa, the large number of four,goals being put through by each side. West Bromwich Albion were away at Sunderland, the game resulting in a draw.

Tommy Atkins is becoming a devoted football player. Last year the Gordon Highlanders carried 'off the Irish Cup, and there is now a trophy exclusivelpfer soldiers, which was won by another set of Highlanders—the 93rd. Football must be bred in Scotchmen. The 47th Loyal North Lancashire Regiment has formed a club at Enniskillen, and is doing very well, whilst the let Battalion of the Sherwood Foresters now have a club, and the results of their matches are so far roniarkably good.
