THE REV:.
G. S. REANEY'S
EXTLANATION A .ND DEFRNCE.

" Why,l Leff Cosprogahonalism ?" is the title, of an apologia by theße.v. George Sale Roaney, assis- tant curate St. Mary's, Riverhead,. Kent, and formerly., Congregational minister of Wycliffe Church, Warrington. Commenting onythe work the. " Manchester. Guardian" says :—" IL cannot be more thawfour,years ago since the 7rpsent writer heard the.author of this lively little book.say in. his eager, impetuous way, "Sign the Articles ?: I never r signed one filmy life; and as for signing thirty-nine, I shouldnever dream of it." Nevertheless the thing has beentlone, and: now we have the- apologia of the Rev. G.2;tlteaney before us as a curate, in the Estab- lished ChUrcb. The book will be widely read, and it deserves reading,. for it is a frank. and 'manly exposition of a change which most men would shrink friom making after reaching middle life. It is full of allusions to well-known persons living and, working amongst us, and some of_these allusions ere perhaps needlessly sharp and satirical; but Mr. Reaney states plainly in his preface that his q,uarrel has been,with &system rather than, with men, and on the whole he- keeps fairly within those lines. Theraare five chapters in the book„together with a note on the recent meetings of the Congregational Uaiou at Swansea. Of these five chapters only one is devoted te the merits of the church he has joined 7,3,1 l the restof the book being taken, up with an exposure—lL suctt it be— d the errors of the Church he has lett behind. Reaney'Atells a delightful story of his. boyhood which shows that he has-always been the impressible. Iteaney whom we know.

"Mpschoolmester was a deacon of the chapel. He was a really good man ; fervent marrows, and a little vain- He took gpeat care of his hair„ancthad it curled twice a.we,ek by-the barber. Somenmes this imteresthig operation took place in a little office in the schoolroom, much to our delight. One week there canteatraxelling the- atre to the town and I went to it. One boy told the dear old gentleman, and he gave us an awfrl discourse upon the • simot going to the theatre.' I wont very sect in the face, whietemingled shame and anger. Suddenly he paused, andflooking sternly at me, said, 'l!' hear that you went to the theatre last night ? ' I said,. 'Yes, sir I did with my father.' There was a solemn silence, and then, in naostsavero tones and evidently with, real anxiety, he said, f. Would • you like to die at the Theatre ?' I replied ima , momenbou a hot passion, ITO •. woold you like to die having your hair curled?'" Thshiok is full of quaint reminiscences of this kind, but we nrmst turn to more serious topics. Mr. Reaney did not remain with the ' Weslevans.. During a revival service he was baptised by immersion, "under a good deal of; pressure," and soon ' we find him a young Baptist minister at Falmouth and at Taunton alarming his flock hphisliberal views,which led him n in 1863 to accept a "call "-to Warrington„'where he became "a very decided Dissenter, a strong Liberationist, a vigorous Radical, and a hard- ! working pastor—a good all-reaud Congregationalist.' , The next three chapters, "Congregationalism : What isit ? Hew it Works, and Why I left it," are those which are most likely to arouse hostile criticism, and it will behest, perhaps, to leave them to be read in their entirety by those who are speaially interested in the questions which they raise. Clearly, then. Mr. Reaney was wise to leave a sinking skip.- but whither should he turn? It was the Church' of England that had always had, as he confesses and as most of us knew, "a kind of fascination " for him. " The Church of England," he says, "has drawn me back into her fold by the powerful attraction of her parochial system, by her nationality,by her catholicity, by her historical continuity, and by her 'primitive Scriptural teaching and practice." Well, we will not quarrel with his decision •, he can find all these things in the Church of England doubtless, though he will, if he moves about, find a good deal more besides, 1 and not all of it so much to his taste. But with all his vagaries, Mr. Reaney is a man whom everyone who, knows him likes, and all,will wish him rest and happiness.i in the fold to which he has in a certain sense, as he claims, "returned." Readers of his defence of his change will wish he had left some things unsaid. Pro- bably he will share that feeling himself before mueh time has elapsed. Meanwhile, everyone should read this racy chapter of autobiography, which is as interestingi and as amusing as anything of the kind that haa ap- peared for some time.

The death is announced, after a very brief illness of Mr. W. Rogers, J.P., of Coppull Grange, near Wigan. Mr. Rogers was Mayor of Wigan during 1888. By the collapse of a building in the course of construc- tion at Prague on Monday five persons were killed and a number of others injured.

div.p: IT!
REASONS FOR NON-CONFORMITY.

willeEe. v. J. Yonge preached an excellent sermon in jelliTe Congregational Church, on Sunday night, "utile above subject. In his discourse he said : 'l'lle occasion appears to have come for a formal Lite•ternent of the reasons of our existence as Dissen- 're from the Established Church of this country. A recent event, having peculiar interest to our „.._NPeeial community, because of past association, has o,l'erl to give new importance to our fundamental t,',, gelastical polity and position. We are, •in a es'illier, Challenged to assert and explain our ideas ;sd beliefs concerning the Christian Church. We I,"`Le. have no reason to evade the challenge of these 1 47641 circumstances. It is due to ourselves that, 1 strantich as a former leader in this community has "*t°unced the opinion of his past days, we should l• 4,ttillind ourselves oi the reasonableness of those ' Ctlions which he now seeks to subvert; and it is „_tle to those outside our own borders that we should ,-;lesert our reasons and let it be understood that n the detection of a once able exponent of them neither destroyed their foundations nor die- • our confidence in their maintenance. • • Yet, we have no desire to obtrude our Non-con- ,,W. It is not perfectly congenial to us to use the es ~"'‘ of Christian worship for the purpose of ecclesiasti- ssSuscussion. The reproach, recently thrown at us in a i,'Nazine article,th at Congregational Churches and Minis- isrt Only 'prosper in proportion to the constancy and stjLerness of their attacks upon the State Church, is 13' unwarranted. It certainly has no founds- in fact, as regards ourselves. So far as tnt • naemory serves, this is the first occasion in a lisatrY of 14 years in this pulpit in which a se"`43' discourse has been devoted to any exposition 42i.00-conformist opinions. It is not quite clear, in- s Tass that this policy of silence has been altogether wise. 14 '.6 is a Non-conformist Church, built, frequented, and t,Vorted by persons who decline to conform to the Es- Ishrnent. There can be no impropriety, therefore, 1 o.etinses there may be obvious expediency, in setting the principles which have produced and upheld the • Ctence of the community. At the outset, let me a. 13' lay down this fact about Non-conformity ; it is •sp"setially and fundamentally a matter of the highest tt; most definite religious principle. Although it is not ts,".„egh for a Non-conformist to be such because he was into it, still there is this to be said,a Non-conformist Ess_oo need to be ashamed of his ecclesiastical ancestry. I"e9 sheds a fadeless lustre around the fathers and 4clers of English Non-conformity. Neither have Non- ,r tor m ist bodies in this country anything to be ashamed t,' bet everything to justify their course, and everything kt'sake them satisfied with the position they hold. We le -Non-conformists because s-- 4,s,Ye dissent from the. principle of any State , il7lishment of Religion. so: We dissent from the particular church which is established in these realms. its, Our dissent arises first of all from our convic- mat matters of faith and worship are matters of tossseaence ; matters between man and God; and there- hot matters in which any human authority has any Zlt to interfere. Governments have no qualifications 11:4'4%.rer to touch or decide spiritual matters. Neither s,j,,a civil government any right or any fitness where- ss,7 to make selection of anyone Christian community, ▪ elevate it to a position of superiority,even supremacy, ttj other such communities. Our dissent is esson- st ,7 religious. It is not caused by any jealousy eit;flo dominant 'church. It is caused by our con- that a national establishment of religion is Cnthorised by the word ,of God, and antagonistic to best interests of religion. We believe, moreover,even more strongly that if the Lord Jesus Christ had ORned the alliance of his church on earth with the civil este', he would have given definite instructions to that and he would himself have taken the first steps .'"oure it. Se far from this being his intention, he is 41bed to us as having put away from his mind, as a table satanic temptation, the very idea of any com- pENsin,g and entangling alliance with the kingdoms of ~World and the glory of them. as."se don't question or deny for a moment the good that 114tr-Piscopal Church has done and is doing to the nation. to 1, We believe that her usefulness is in no sense owing 4,447 favoured political position, but in spite of it. She osjc'ete good, because Christ's spirit is in her spiritual 11,7•,ssituency, even as that same spirit is in the spiritual 4.'"uft... hood. of believers everywhere, of every name. est; we are Non-conformists, because we dissent liealy from the particular church that has been estab- , !Zed by the State. We do net believe in the scriptural- Of episcopacy. We cannot find any warrant in the tt: Testament for the episcopal order, as it is seen in as.i Anglican and Roman communions. We find no I Ptural authority for the variegated hierarchy, bishop , archbishop priests, canons, prebends deans, arch- -5 and countless other dignities,suchas we have in s,is,-erurch of England. All this, we say, is incongruous i " the simplicity that is in Christ " ; and with the I 5i4.71 of the early Christian communities, which were assiNY brotherhoods of disciples,having each its own pre- • ' Sider or bishop, and also its serving deacons,with, esOte as can be ascertained, no other church 4 _P,3 whatever. But our Non-conformity to the • "Pal church has far deeper and stronger brecs still. That church, I suppose, stands or falls isl,''er prayer book. We cannot conform to that es Ii - Not that we should all of us object to some form ki,,t4irgy, for occasional and modified use in public wor- qs Many of us would be glad of it, and it might be osue" greatly helpful to the general devotion of our Extetles. Not again, that we question the truth, or tcs'ley, or appropriateness of many of the prayers con- In the prayer book. On the contrary, we should ajalNly admit that it would be impossiole to find, and ,517411 t to frame, a manual of prayer more generally 4,3 Noted to express the desires of devout hearts. But, 4,'?litting all this, we cannot consent to accept the book ply 1,..t.i,5, or as it is commonly used in the services of the ls_ . We don't believe in the exclusive use of forms ts ~4Yer in public worship. We consider free prayer Assii at once the duty and privilege of Christian people. a 7", Inost assuredly, we do not believe ia a good deal of loctrine enshrined in the book ; and we dissent from Isir, if not all, of the ritual it prescribes. We do not iskeee, again, in baptismal regeneration ; nor in God- t„, enta in baptism; nor in the power of a Christian perlieter to absolve men from their sins; nor in the power sl' bishop to communicate the Holy Ghost to his fellow tsV Whom he ordains to the Christian ministry ; nor in s°-ealled real presence in the Lord's Supper; all doctrines, and assumptions, and conveyances of and authority are embodied in the doctrines and ss—,!.l of the book of common prayer. It might, how- be said by some—why not, for the sake of unity 474 brotherhood, for the sake of presenting to the world th:lere unbroken and compact front—why not join 04, , Episcopal Church and accept the prayer book as possible, declining only such portions as do not es'eb with your beliefs? The answer to such a sugges- ec is clear and straight. We cannot conform to any 41,tith with which we are not in cordial agree- IsS"lt ; or whose doctrines or pretensions we believe to 46.,`undamentally unscriptural, and opposed to "the Plicity that is in Christ." To accept a creed that we tot believe, to follow a ritual that we do not believe, tend upon a ministry which claims a power we do believe it to possess, would be dishonest and insin- %lts tow , a continual act of untruth. It is ever a duty we tsje to our conscience, and to God, and also to our ONe-naen, to manifestly repudiate what we believe to ssee, eoneous and untrue, and never so much so as in :',Zrers of faith and religion. These are matters in which Promise would be a sin. Finally, If asked to single the one feature in the Episcopal Church in this ssateY, which utterly and completely decides our firm "sTence to Non-conformity. unhesitatingly we lay our OekUpon its essential, and increasingly undisguised, 37`..d otalism. Very rapidly, with augmenting speed, by year, is the Church of England becoming the lech of the priesthood. There will soon be small essen- ,7s difference between the Anglican and the Roman Z'est. There is not much already in the outward ap- Orance of some of them. There is not much more in :!eir pretensions or their practices. I have not a single 7ctd to say in doubt or disparagement of the piety and 4heerity of the growing Ritualistic party, either clerical tlti lay, in the Church of England. It is unquestionable „..e.t some of the most spiritual and devout of her minis- re and members, those most devoted to the highest felfare of men, belong to this sacerdotal party. 1111 disposed, moreover, to the strong opinion that ;:ee believers in sacramental and sacerdotal doctrine S'"el rituaA are the truest and most faithful exponents of '4Q A P XI --octrine and ritual of the Prayer Book. They have i.„-sclost invulnerable defence behind the statements and Zbeecs therein contained. If the Episcopal Church is slyer to become soundly Protestant it will only be by the ts..'eision of its Prayer Book. It is a sacerdotal book sl-roughout,and can only be regarded otherwise by having issourse to unliteral interpretation and non-natural mean tags, words, and phrases. This determines and renders rnianent our Non-conformity. It becomes our duty, refere, to be steadfastly loyal to the only Priest; and ,s7solutely determine to have nothing to do with an flee of spiritual ministry that has always been a hind- to the Gospel. We will teach men that they p!'Ve the indefeasible right of personal access to the zeaveray Father; that they need no intercessor save e Great High Priest; that through Him, without any "itnan intervention whatever, they may obtain the for- roness of sins and that by faith in, and obedience to I irn they may grow up into a noble life, and be made ,I Meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in tight."
THE EXAMINER, SATUKDA V, NOVEMBER. 15,1890.

THE ROAD PAST THE GIBRALTAR COTTAGES. Sir,—From the report of the proceedings of the New- ton Commissioners as given in your issue of the Bth inst. I see there is a desire on their part to close the road past the above named cottages. Ido not know at what point they propose to stop the roadin question,but I presume it would be at the boundary of the Newton Township. Now, if that be the case, the residents there will be placed in a very awkward condition indeed. Suppose the road to be blocked at the point I have indicated, to getlfrom the cottages to a given point in Haydock which can now be reached in five minutes would then involve going at least one and a half miles to get to the same place. On the other hand if the road be blocked at the point where it leads into the road over the " Common" the result will be equally as bad when wanted to be approached from the Newton side. Further, though the beuses stand in the township of Newton, they would not accessible only by the road through Haydock. .1 Trusting that the road may not be allowed to be ynterfered with without further protest, and thanking you in anticipation for your insertion of this, I remain, ours truly,
PEDESTRIAN.

"LOCAL RATING " AND " LAW DISTRAINT." Sir,—Kindly permit me to inform your readers that on November 4th, the " Working-men's Home Union" (which now numbers nearly 30,000—members in London alone, and is rapidly extending to all the large towns of England and Wales), and on November 6th the " Tenant Tradesmen's National Union" unanimously passed the following resolution :—" That this meeting earnestly solicits the attention of the County Councils throughout England to the prevailing system of exempting unoccu- pied houses and shops from the payment of local rates, and respectfully urges that as such unlet property shares in the benefits arising from the rates for drainage, roads, bridges, lighting, cleansing, asylums, Police and School Board, at least one-half of the usual rates should be paid by the owners of such unoccupied property." And on November 4th, the" Working-men's Home 13nlon " also passed unanimously the following resolution i—" That this meeting records its earnest VOCess against the power for harassing and impoverlBhifig tihfortuile.6 'Tenants that exists in the present cruel law of distraint, and urges the early repeal of that law, and the substitu- tion of one which shall in a just and reasonable manner enable landlords to recover possession of their property from defaulting tenants." Of the two above-named organisations the "Tenant Tradesmen's Union" advocates fair rents and fixity of tenure for shopkeepers so long as agreed covenants are duly performed—also the exclusive right of the tenant to the value of the goodwill of the business which he alone, and not the landlord, has created or purchased ; as well as of permanent improvements made by him during his tenancy. The "Working-men's Union" strives for thorough sanitation and adequate arrangements for health, coin- fort, and decency in the dwellings of the toiling masses, and the reduction of rents to the same per centage on the value of the property as is paid by the tenants of middle class houses—namely, trom sto 6 per cent. Both Unions aim at arousing and supporting the legitimate action of local authorities, and at securing due propor- tionate representation of trade and labour in municipal Councils and in Parliament. There is no fee or payment whatever to join either of these unions. The working expenses are merely nominal, and can easily be met as occasion may require. Any number of membership forms and sanitary complaint forms will be forwarded, post free, on written applica- tion to meat International Coilege, Hampstead, London, or at 510, Mile End-rd., London, E.—Your obedient ser-

--- THE CASE OF EX-POLICE SERGEANT SIIAW. Sir,—Will you kindly grant me space in your columns for a few more facts with respect to my treatment and also to the treatment of other members of the Warrington Police Force. lam glad to be able to say that the last Letter I sent to you for publication, has not been answered or contradicted in any one particular, so that you wilt be able to judge whether I told the truth or not. I conlcude that silence on the matter is a plain proof that there was nothing that could be contradicted in it. During the time that the cloud was hanging over me, I was charged with working all the time that I was off duty on the sick list which, of course, I denied, and told 'them that they could not prove it to be so. The answer I got was—" Oh, yes, you have, you have been building a green-house in the yard." I said it was an untruth, and that I should like it proved, knowing full well that some one had been telling lies on purpose to injure me. That of itself is quite enough to show that some under- hand work was going on. The next thing that I was charged with was that I was in two Sick Societies, and I was receiving 12s. per week from one and 10s. per week from the other. That I denied and said was untrue. But if I had been in four, what difference did it make to any of them? I never asked any of them to pay my money for me. lam not in more than one Sick Society and that is the Independent Order of Reckabites, which I am not ashamed of anyone know- ing. If any other Sick Society has me on their books as a member, I hope they will publish it, and expose me and show the public whether I am fit to be believed, or the person who made the statement, as in my opinion, a man that is capable of telling Bea like that to injure a fellow- ' man is not a fit person to be in any police force, and I am sure would not stoop to tell a lie for any other purpose. When I first joined the force, I was as strong and healthy as any man need to be, but I am sorry to say that after I was made Sergeant my health was not what I should have liked it to be. Through the duties imposed upon me, I have had to turn out on a wet night and look after the men on my division, and, after getting thoroughly saturated with the rain, I have had to go into the office and commence writing ; sometimes for two or three hours in my wet clothes. If that is not enough to try any person and give them severe colds and illnesses. I dont know what is, no matter how strong their consti-

tutions are. The only wonder is that I have not got - rheumatism in my limbs through it. And then lam told ' that it is not fair to the other Sergeants and Inspectors. Now, I would not say a word about it if the other ser- geants had had their turns at the same work, but they had not. I had to do it all. That and that only is how I got all my colds ; and after ruining my constitution with their work, they pitchfork me out of the force to make room for another. To think that I as an Englishman ' would submit to be reduced for nothing! No, sir, I think rather too much of my reputation to be lowered in the scale like that. I would rather starve than submit to such cowardly treatment. My opinion of the affair is that it was done knowing full well that that was the only way to get me out of the force. Now, as to the treatment of other members of the force I think it is high time that some members of the Watch Committee made inquiries amongst the men to see whether they are satisfied with their lot. I consider that there are from eight to twelve men now on the force who are entitled to 295. per week; some of them should have had the rise years ago and others not quite so long. The only thing that I wonder at is that some of them have not left the force years since. When they see a man appointed and made first-class constable in twelve months time instead of at the end of two years, and then see the same man raised to 295. per week in three years instead of the end of five years, it is something I should think, to make them do their best to keep out of trouble, when they have been on eight or nine years and not got to that rate of pay yet. I should think that that of itself is enough to make them both careless and indifferent. I am mentioning this for I am very sure that if one or two members on the Watch Committee get to know,they will get the thing rectified as soon as possible. If there are • rates of pay put in the rules, I contend that they should be adhered to, or else discard all the rules at once and take no notice of any of them. I see from the report in the papers of Nov. Ist, that there have been three resignations, one voluntary, one through continued ill-health, and one compulsory. I should like to knew which of those three is meant for my case, as I consider that if the second one is mine it is radically wrong and misleading, as I consider that mine has been compulsion. Now, sir, I do not think that I shall trouble you again with any more letters on this subject unless there is an ! answer to this, as I fully intend to address the next letter 1 that I write on the subject to headquarters,tnat is to say, either to the Government Inspector or the Home Secre- tary. My mind is fully made up to have my case thoroughly gone into, if possible, by the proper authori- ties, and see whether I have been dealt fairly with. No doubt, when I have laid the whole matter before them, I shall have justice done, which up to now I have not had. One more matter before I close my letter is this—do you think a medical man would waste his valuable time M coming to visit me for three or four weeks together if there was nothing wrong with me? When I have mentioned being sick I have been sneered at as though I had been putting it: on and "foxing," which is not very nice. I will now close my remarks, and I hope that some gentleman on the Watch Committee will see my letter, and have the men who deserve their wages raising advanced at once, as a labourer is worthy of his hire at any trade or calling.—l am, sir, yours truly, EX-POLICE SERGEANT R. SHAW. 105, Manchester-rd., Warrington, Nov. sth, 1890. [This letter should have appeared in our last issue but was accidentally omitted. —Ed. Ex.]
TILE LOSS OF H.M.S. SERPENT.
LATEST PARTICULARS. THRILLING STORY OF THE SURVIVORS. THE DETAILS OF THE DISASTER. (Continned from Page 3.)

COItI7NNA, FRIDAY.—Owing to the fortunate circum- stance that a trader of Cainarinas was acquainted with English it has been possible to obtain some information from the three sailors saved. The story of the men them- selves was somewhat vague, all of them being in a weak state, from the effect of the injuries they sustained when swimming ashore. They state the Serpent was going full steam ahead, when suddenly she struck on the Buey Reef. She sank almost instantaneously. The three sailors themselves wera on the upper deck, and the violent shock caused by the ship striking hurled them ' into the sea. They were in the water for some hours battling with the huge seas which swept over the reefs and broke on the shore. They were repeatedly hurled against the rocks. They at last gained land in a very bruised and battered condition. One of them soon after being thrown into the water succeded in reaching a rock which rose above the level of the sea, and thought to have found a secure resting-place, but the tide rose very rapidly, and the poor fellow was washed off the rock, and had to swim for his lite. The three men seemed to have nothing to say as to what occurred on board their ship after she struck beyond the fact that there was great confusion, and no boat could be lowered as there was no time before the vessel went down. TWENTY-ONE BODIES WASHED ASHORE.

MADRID, FRIDAY, 3 A.M.—A. telegram from Corunna reports that up to the present twenty-one bodies have been washed ashore along the coast near Camarinas. All of the corpses are those of sailors ; none of the officers being among them. THE SURVIVCRS. _ .

The three survivors, according to latest advices were not in a condition to make the rough journey to Corunna, and they still remain under medical treat- ment at Carnarinas. It is understood that her Majesty's ship Lapwing, which has been ordered to the scene of the wreck, will take Gould, Burton, and Hotson, on board. The men will be technically under arrest, and they will be conveyed in nominal custody to Devonport, where they will be tried, in the absence of the surviving officers, for losing one of her Majesty's ships—a proce- dure which, it will be remembered, was followed in the case of the Eurydice. A Plymouth correspondent says that Frederick James Gould is a leading seaman, who formerly belonged to the Cambridge gunnery school-ship, and whose mother and sister reside at Knackers Nowle, near Pl 3 mouth. He is a single man, and was on board the Wasp when she was wrecked on the coast of Ireland, and on the Lily when she foundered off Labrador. Benjamin Burton is an able seaman, and formerly belonged to the Royal Naval Barracks, Keyham. He is a married man, and his wife Is at present residing in Birmingham. The name of 11Qt5en 14 not on the official list of those serving on board, but inquiries made disclosed the fact that he was serv- ing as .a captain's steward. PAINFUL SCENES. Painful stories are still coming to hand relative to the distress caused among the relatives of the drowned crew. One woman who heard of the loss of her husband in a shop fell down in a fit, and is still unconscious. Another woman has been prematurely confined of twins. AID FOR THE BEREAVED RELATIVES. Lord St. Levan, the Mayor of Devonport, will call a public meeting to raise funds for the distressed families, of whom there are a great number in the three towns. The co-operation of the Lord Mayor of London will be sought.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 15, 1890.

there, Bohemia and Society were there, and business ex- tended there more and more, and above all it was a great centre of pleasure. As he had often said, he preached every Sunday on the most wicked spot out of hell. More sin was committed within a mile of his pulpit than within thP same distance of any other pulpit in the world. There were facilities in that part of London for sin such as were not even found even in Paris. What a glorious thing it was that God had given him the privi- lege to go to that place, which was the very

_ ESSENCE ON HELL, to preach the old gospel. (Applause.) And If sinners were saved there, as, glory be to God, they were every day—(applause)—what might not be done in Warrington and other places where the difficulties were not a tithe of what they were in London and the resources so much greater. (Hear, hear.) There was one department of the work, which was the most inter•sting and important of all, that was the establishment of the sisterhood. He referred to that for the reason which Mr. Walters had mentioned. Mr. Garnett's niece was one of the most de- voted of the sisters. (Applause.) That was the first time he 'rad ever had the privilege of speaking on behalf of the mission in a town which had furnished them with a sister, and he had come to War- rington partly in order that he might publicly express his gratitude. (Applause.) He had long been dreaming of such a Pis te rhood, but he was told that it was impossible to form one. He was thankful to see that his dream had at last been fulfilled. (Applause). He believed one cultured and refined lady would be worth two parsons. (Laughter.) What was required for the work were ladies who could meet the daughters of well-to-do people in their drawing-rooms on the same social footing. (Hear, hear). Experience in London had shown that the more highly cultivated and refined a woman was, the better qualified was she to work among both rich and poor. (Hear, hear.) Warrington had already given them a devoted sister. What a beautiful thing it would be if it could furnish another. That would be better than the collection. (Laughter.) However, he was pleased to say that their prospects were never brighter than they were at present. He was of opinion that society should be constructed on a Christian basis. They wanted a sweep- ing Liquor Act, which would shut up their public-houses on Sundays. (Applause.) Language failed him to de- precate the evils caused by strong drink. It was the cause of the social misery with which they were dealing. (Applause.) The Rev. W. D. WALTERS thanked the Chairman for presiding, and all who had done anything that tended to promote the success of the gathering that night. The meeting was brought to a conclusion by the Doxo- logy and Benediction.

div.head: REV. HUGH PRICE HUGHES AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: REV. HUGH PRICE HUGHES AT WARRINGTON.
SERMON 111 BOLD-ST. CHAPEL.

An eloquent sermon was preached on Tuesday afternoon, in Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes, M.A., the well known Wesleyan minister, who superintends the work of the West London Mission. The rev, gentleman selected for his text the words---" Your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams," Acts ii. latter part of verse 17. Mr. Hughes said his theme that afternoon was the use of the imagina- tion in religion. It was this imagination which enabled the great saints to do such mighty deeds. Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and all the prophets saw visions and dreamed dreams. They were not paralysed and deceived by the things which were seen and were temporal, but in the strength of a ' beatific vision they accomplished gigantic revolu- tions which had lifted the whole of the human race to a higher level of goodness and happiness. He was afraid it had become true of the Methodists, though they were roUsing themselves again, that the ordinary Christians among them did not see visions and dream dreams. These dear men and women had prayed I for little things and had got them, but they had not had the courage to expect great things, to do daring de.xls in the name of God, to make great incursions into the devil's territory, and to smite gigantic evils. Their dull souls had not realised the Divine possibility. They must divide all christians into two classes—the moles , and the eagles. The moles saw much in front of their noses, but the eagles mounted up and took a great bird's eye view of the situation, realizing what a fool the devil , was after all ; how helpless his servants were ; how mighty Jesus was, and what a forward movement might be made. Some of their christians were content if they could" make both ends meet," like a greengrocer or any other shopkeeper. It would be better under those cir- cumstances for their chapels to be burnt down, and for them to begin again at the beginning and work in the open air, as did Wesley, Whitfield and others. What visions a man of business had ! How quickly he adapted all his arrangements, correspondence, and the peculiarities of his business ! How carefully lie read the money article in the" Times !" flow vividly he grasped the commercial situation so that he might double his fortune, and yet some of these men, when they got into a trustees', leaders', or quarterly meeting seemed to have lost their courage and ability, and all their power to grasp the situation was gone. They were eagles in the counting house, but grovelling moles in the vestry. He contended that a man ought to throw as much soul into religion as he did into business, and if he would do is they would soon have their chapels crowded, and great good would be done. A iittle tact was also required. A friend once told him of a visit he had paid to a certain chapel in an important town. The minister selected as the opening hymm the longest he he could find ; then he prayed 15 or 20 minutes, and afterwards preached 50 or 55 minutes and went through other weary performances. All that was done in a chapel which would seat 1,500 people, and yet on the occasion to which he referred there were only 300 people present, and his friend re- marked to him that that was a great sign of the intelli- gence of the people of the locality. (Laughter.) They should adapt themselves to circumstances. There never was a time when people were so willing to listen to the Gospel as they were now, and what was wanted was a kindling of the imagination into a flame of divine enthus- iasm.
Gos.

div.head: EVENING MEETING.
div.p: EVENING MEETING.

In the evening a public meeting was held in Bold-st. Chapel. which was completely filled. Mr. E. J. Guest, 8.A., J.P., presided, and was supported by the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes and the Rev. W. D. Walters (West London Mission), Rev. John Gunnell, Rev. A. _Freeman,

Rev. Thomas Ross, Rev. John Yonge, Rev. J. Davies, Rev. Thomas, Rev. W. Graham, Mr. Robert Garnett, Mr. John Bennett, and others. The meeting having been opened with the singing of hymns and a prayer by the Rev. J. Yonge, The CHAIRMAN remarked that he owed his position that evening, he believed. to the fact that he took a very deep interest in all mission work. (Hear, hear.) He did not see how it was possible for anyone " who professed and called himself a Christian" to do other than sympathize with any movement which was at work for the extension of the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ. He rejoiced to see that mission work was on the increase, not only in Methodism, but in every section of the Christian Church. (Hear, hear.) Missionary work had been stimulated to a great extent by the Salvation Army. He was glad to see that the Conference had allowed Mr. Hughes and his colleagues to extend their work of evangelization, thus giving them an opportunity of exorcising the talents which God has given them. All the Nonconformist Churches were now more allied to spiritual work than ever they were. That great improvement was largely due to the bloodless revolution of the 18th century, when John Wesley and his assistants went forth to spread practical holiness throughout the land. If Methodism, however, has exerted herself fully, there would have been no need of the Salvation Army. They had an organization suitable to meet the requirements of all classes. Methodism had become rich and respectable during the last 25 years, and five million pounds had been spent in the erection • f houses of prayer. (Hear, hear.) Nonconformist churches were, it was said the churches of the middle, well-to-do, and artizan classes. He believed that that reproach was about to be wiped away. (Hear, hear.) We had now the Forward Movement and the Salvation Army. Mr. Walters and Mr. Hughes were present that night to infuse a spirit of earnestness into them. He trusted they would respond generously to the appeal of the deputation. Last year the London Mission cost £7,500. By support- ting the London mission they were tending to strengthen the very art of Methodism, for was not London the centre of the world? In conclusion, he hoped Warring- ton would be inspired by the great Forward Movement.

(Applause.) The Rev. W. D. WALTERS (secretary of the West Lon- don Mission), in a forcible speech, explained that the deputation that evening represented not only the West London Mission—of which the Rev. Hugh P. Hughes was superintendent—lint the London Mission, of which there were four branches, each with a superintendent. They had ten ministers, scares of lay agents, and over 3,000 persons meeting in "class." (Applause.) The Rev. Howl PRICE HUGHES was very warmly received. He expressed his appreciation of the kindly welcome which had been given Mr. Walters and him- self by the superintendent and other ministers of the circuit. He weot on to say that he was very glad to know that they had with them that evening ministers of other denominations. They did not feel any embarrass- ment in accepting the sympathy of representatives of other churches, for the movement in which they were engaged was entirely unsectarian in character, spirit and I object. (Hear, hear.) They never tried to make any- body a Methodist. They tried to make everybody Christians. (Applause.) He was thankful to know that the enterprise had already been a blessing to other churches as well as the Wesleyan. (Hear, hear.) He had always argued that what was called the forward movement ought really to be called a backward move- ment. (Laughter.) John Wesley originated all that they were saying and doing now. All the things which he (Mr. Hughes) advocated, and which had been denounced, were what John Wesley advocated. His hearers would be astonished to find what an 91d-fashioned Methodist he was—(laughter)—but he agreed with John Wesley more than anyone he had yet met. (Laughter.) He agreed with the Chairman that if they had only been faithful to the teaching and spirit of John Wesley there would have been no occasion for the Salvation Army or the Primitive Methodist body. (Hear, hear.) Wesleyans alone were to blame for those separate organiz- ations. Twice over did General Booth, with all his followers, offer to join the Wesleyan communion, but he was repulsed. He would not be refused if he were to come a third time (laughter) —he would be received with open arms. (Applause.) Nothing had impressed the speaker more, when visiting the principal centres of Salvation Army work, than to find with scarcely an exception that the most effective and successful officers in the Salvation Army were ex-Wesleyans. (Applause.) When hs had asked them why they left the Wesleyan body, their answer was that they had nothing to do. If the Salva- tion Army could do what it was doing, then the Wesleyan Methodists ought to do ten times more. "If," said General Booth to him some time ago, "I had only your organization and resources, what would I not do !" If Wesleyans were only willing to adapt themselves to the opportunities which came within their reach, they would be able to do not only as much as the Salvation Army, but a hundred times more. (Applause.) It was impos- sible to exaf;gerate the latent and unused resources of 'Wesleyan Methodism. (Applause.) Until quite recently they were rich and respectable. They were still rich— as he hoped they would show presently when the collec- tion was made—(laughter)—but they were losing their false respectability. (Hear, hear.) If modern Metho- I dists wished to destroy Methodism, they had only to imitate their grandfathers and have another "spilt." What a mighty church it might have been if, instead of quarrelling with one another 50 years ago, they had un- animously quarrelled with the devil and carried on the work of God. (Applause.) He expected to live to see the day when Methodism in this country would be what it was when John Wesley died—one and indivisible— (applause)—when the Primitive Methodists and the Bible Christians all came home, and they presented a united front to the foe. (Applause.) The questions on which they agreed were the only essential questions. It was a great national scandal that British Methodism should be split up into five separate churches. (Hear, hear.) Sometimes there were three or four wretched little Methodist churches in a village which was suited for one. He hoped to see the day when there would be only one Methodism in this country—(applause)—and, indeed, all the world over. (Hear, hear.) In the meantime, they must be as friendly with one another as they could. (Laughter.) For the first time in history the Wesleyan church had reached the lowest class of all. (Applause.) Coming to his own mission, he might tell them that it was impossible for anyone to understand the condition of affairs in West London who had not lived there. West London was in many respects the most important spat in ha world. Parliament was there, the aristocracy wepe

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION. DEATH OF REV. DR. HANNAY.
div.p: THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION. DEATH OF REV. DR. HANNAY.

The Rev. Alexander Hannay, D.D., the well-known secretary of the Congregational Union of England and Wales, died at his residence at Hornsey at a quarter to three on Wednesday afternoon. A large congregation gathered at the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-st., on Wednesday, to hear an address from the Rev. J. Guinness Rogers on "The Congrega- tionalism of to-day; its difficulties and trials ; its suc- cesses and prospects."—Dr. Joseph Parker presided, and, speaking with much emotion of the death of Dr. Hannav, the secretary of the Congregational Union of England and Wales, said his character was unequalled in many res- pects, and he was perhaps supreme in this, that he never allow any event to prevent his going forward with what he believed to be the duty of the time.—The Rev. Mr. Rogers prefaced his lecture with the observation that the death of Dr. Hannay was a heavier blow than he had felt for many years. Dr. Hannay and he were brothers and comrades in every respect.
LACROSSE. WARRINGTON v. PRESTWICH.

This matcli--WaS played at •Arpley on Saturday. Im- mediately on seeding the visitors commenced to attack, and compelled the home goal-keeper to save, and after ten minutes' play drew first blood. The home team shortly after equalized, and at half-time the score was two goals all. On change of ends Warrington quickly scored a couple of goals. This put the visitors on their mettle and kept the home defence very busy, and made the game four goals all. In tha end the visitors won an even and exciting game, by five goals to four. The visi- tors' attacks played a capital game, and their defence was very good. The Warrington custodian played an excellent game, and saved his side many a dangerous shot. Williamson on the defence played a very safe game, while R. Smith and Bennett on the attack were in good form. Warrington team: Goal, Barker ; point, Wal- lington ; cover point, Kiernan : third man, Dunn; right defence, Garnett, jun. ; left defence, Williamson; centre, Bennett; right attack, Garnett ; left attack Tetlow ; third home, R. Smith ; second home, Proud; first home, Jones. The match on Saturday is against Sale Ist at Arpley.

div.head: FLOODING OF THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE FLOODING OF THE SHIP CANAL.
PROPOSED ERECTION OF A DAM. Continua fr,mi Page 6.

In order to get the water out of the canal, it is, we understand, the intention of the engineers of the Ship Canal to erects dam at Morris Brook, on the Thelwall side of the Latchford locks. The water in the locks will then he pumped over the dam,tind, by this means, it is hoped that the locks cutting will be got clear, and work resumed in the ordinary way in the course at the outside of three or four weeks. The water will be pumped from the locks into the canal on the other side of the locks, and it .will thence flow into the river. At present pump- ing operations are being actively carried on near Lumb Brook, but on Thursday the water again rose about six inches. Up to last night the body of the man who was drowned had not been recovered, and it will probably not be found for some time yet unless it rises to the top of the water. The work of recovering the immersed locomotive Lancaster " on Wednesday was of a rather interesting descrip- tion, as divers and diving bells were employed. Chains were fastened to the locomotive and it was then hauled out of the water by other engines. It I was so little injured by its immersion that it was i working again on Thursday.

div.head: NEW BUTTER EXTRACTOR.
div.p: THE NEW BUTTER EXTRACTOR.

We understand that anew company is about to be established called the Butter Extractor Company. The butter extractor is only just being brought before the public in this country, though it has already gained a good name in America. Last week the extractor was on view at the Holland Park Dairy, Kensington-road, Lon- don, and created no little interest amongst those engaged in the making of butter. In America the extractor is coming into practical use. A number have gone out, and the reports regarding them are eminently satisfactory. The machine is one which is expected to revolutionise the making of butter. The "American Dairyman " of June sth, 1890, has the following article :—" Progress of the extractor.—The first time we witnessed the butter extractor at work we watched it with the same feelings of doubt that we would now indulge in ifycalled upon to examine the work of a new cow-milking machine, but when the but- ter made its appearance, and was laidupon the table, we said to ourselves," Here is a machine that is certain to revolutionise :butter making !" In this spirit we have closly watched its progress, and in not a single step has it disappointed our expectations, but rather to the con- trary, it has met with an enthusiasm in the hands of those who have purchased it that no one could have correctly anticipated. Mr. Taube, the manager of the company, knowing our interest in the machine, has kindly shown us letters from the purchasers, and, without exception, they have said more in favour of the work performed than he ever made bold to claim. There is no humbug- gery and boastfulness about this company, for it is made up of quiet gentlemen whose wealth and commer9ial importance needs no puffing, and who are going quietly along with their work in a manner that assures success. The importance of this machine to the dairy- men of the country is so great that we feel no hesitation in devoting much of our space in putting before them the facts connected with its progress. Many machines are capable of doing good work in the hands of experts that fail in a great measure when handled by those not familiar with them. Such has not been the case with the extractor. For instance, here is what Mr. James C. Stone, jun., of Leavenworth, Kansas, writes :7 • " The machine is doing wonderfully well. I got this • morning of salted butter lib. to 21±lbs. of milk. Remem- ber, this is the milk that, with the separator and churn took 281bs. to make a pound of butter, and it goes. ' Everyone wants it." To show how easy it is to run the ' machine, we will quote from a letter written shortly • after putting it up, wherein Mr. Jones says :—" I ran the machine to-day for the third time. It ran beautifully, ! and we got to-day one pound of salted butter to 221bs. of ; milk. We were getting from this same milk -with a • separator and churn, one pound to 28lbs. of milk." Just to think of it beatinF; the separator, and churn the third I time it is run by a novice, six pounds of milk to the pound of butter, and such good butter as it makes, with- out the need of the skill that is so hard to find." We may add that the prospectus of the new company will shortly ) be advertised.

MANCRESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. There is only a moder- ate trade going through in any quarters, and prices ob- tainable are seldom quite satisfactory to producers. Cotton Is not active, the first estimate of 6,000 bales being quite sufficient to cover the day's business. Yarns steady at Tues- day's prices, but little doing either in twist or weft. Bundles are also steady, but merchants take only small parcels at quotations. Good printers and finishing cloths keep fairly steady, but common sorts are sadly neglected and makers need orders. div.head: ANOTHER RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: ANOTHER RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

-- A Central News telegram from New York on Friday, states that a collision occurred on the Pennsylvania railway near Johnstown. Two passengers were killed, eleven injured, six of thorn mortally. The wreckage caught fire. ANOTHER RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR TAUNTON. Another railway accident occurred Yesterday morning only a few miles from the scene of the Norton Fitzwarren disaster. Shortly before 2 a.m., a fish train ran into a goods train while the latter was being shunted from the up to the down line. Six wagons were thrown off the rails. There were no personal injuries.

div.head: TRE TRIAL OF SLAVIN AND M'AULIFFE.
div.p: TRE TRIAL OF SLAVIN AND M'AULIFFE.

At the Surrey Sessions House, Newington Causeway, yesterday morning, before Sir P. H. Edlin, the chairman, and a bench of magistrates, Frank Slavin and Joseph M'Auliffe surrendered to their recognizarces to answer the charge arising out of the Ormonde Club fight on the 27th September. Inspector Chisholin was then called and gave details as to the fight, and the case was ad- journed until next day.

div.head: O'SHEA DIVORCE CASE„
div.p: THE O'SHEA DIVORCE CASE„

The Exchange Telegraph Company is informed that the O'Shea divorce case, which is down for hearing to- day (Saturnay), will, in all probability, terminate on the same day. Up to the present moment the name of Mr. Parnell's counsel is not known in the courts, but Sir Charles Russell certainly has not a brief in the case. It is rumoured that Mr. Parnell, whose solicitors are , Messrs. Lewis and Lewis, may conduct his own case.

FIRE IN LONDON. TWO LIVES LOST At a quarter to three o'clock yesterday morning flames and smoke were seen bursting from the King of Prussia public-house, Shadwell, London, and it was at once seen that the bar was on fire. The flames spread with rapidity, and before any fire escapes could arrive, the upper win- dows were thrown up, and a Mrs. Lucy Wilson, thirty- seven years of age, jumped from the second floor after appealing piteously for aid for a few moments, and fell heavily to the ground. She was picked up badly injured and removed to the London Hospital. The premises were totally destroyed. Two children were reported miss- ing. and,on a search being instituted,the charred remains , of Agnes Pass, aged seven, and Elizabeth Pass, aged two years. were found among the debris. They were the daughters of the landlord. The cause of the fire is un known. THE TAUNTON RAILWAY ACCIDENT. VERDICT OF THE CORONER'S JURY. Upon the Coroner's jury assembling yesterday morn- ing, the foreman said that the jury had come to the fol- lowing verdict :—The jury consider that the collision on the Great Western Railway which caused the death of ten persons at Norton Fitzwarren on Tuesday morning last arose through George Rice forgetting that he had, owing to the siding being full, placed the down goods train on the main up line, and allowing it to remain there after putting the signals "Line clear" for the coming up special train. We consider the driver of the goods train acted wrongly in removing his head lights before he was on the down line. The jury further considered that had there ;been sufficient siding accommodation between

div.head: WORKMAN'S TRAIN. IN COLLISION.
div.p: WORKMAN'S TRAIN. IN COLLISION.
WARRINGTON MAN KILLED.

A workman's train from Watford for London ran into a goods train in Primrose-hill Tunnel on Thurs- day morning. The train had left Willesden Junc- tion at 7.20, and was proceeding to the city when, in the tunnel between Loudoun-road and Chalk Farm stations, it ran violently into the rear part of a goods train. The shock was very severe. The brake van of the good train was smashed and the brakeman instantly killed The passenger train was crowded with workmen, many of whom were seriously injured. The line was completely blocked and much damage was caused. A breakdown gang was at once despatched and are busy clearing the

line. The brakesman, whose name was John Rigby, residel at 20, Nicholson-st., Warrington. Ile left home at 8.30 on Wednesday morning and pro- ceeded from Dalham by the 8. 5.5 a. m. goods train for Hampden, near London. Deceased, who was 60 years of age, had been in the employment of the London and North Western Company, for upwards of 40 years. His body now lies at Hampden mor- tuary P waiting an inquest, which will take place to- day (Saturday). Deceased leaves a wife and three children, all of whom' fortunately, are grown up. He was well respected in the town' enjoyed a wide circle of friends, and through his demise the rail- way company have lost a true and faithful servant. Ilis remains will be conveyed to Warrington after the inquest, and interred in the cemetery on Tues- day next. AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF ENGINEERS. ANNUAL DINNER.

The annnal meeting in connection with the Newton-le-Willows branch of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, was celebrated by a dinner held at the Pied Bull Hotel, on Saturday evening. The usual headquarters of the club is at the Wel- lington Hotel, Earlestown, but, owing to the large membership roll, Mr. Sharpe was unabla to accomo- date them, and thus arrangements had to be made for the gathering to take place at the Pied Bull. Mrs. Bond provided an excellent dinner, and about 130 members partook thereof. After dinner, the cloth was removed, and the subsequent proceed- ings were presided over by Mr. J. Whittaker of the vacant book office, Manchester. the vice chair being filled by Mr. W. Davies. The usual, loyal toasts were proposed and duly honoured. Mr. D. Williams proposed the toast of "Success to the Amalgamated Society of Engineers." Their Society was considered to be one of the finest organisations in the world. He had not much time to refer to the new union- ism, but there was room for them all, and he trusted it would be able to do as much as their old unionism had done. S 3 far as their movement was concerned they were in a very favourable position. When the various societies of engineers agreed to amalgamate, it was at Warrington where they first carried it out, so that War- rington was really the birthplace of their Society. Since that period it had spread to such an extent that there was not another organisation in the same positioa. It was to the credit of the pioneers who formed the Newton branch that they threw in their lot with the amalgama- tion scheme soon after it was formed, and their branch was No. 37. At the( present time there was 485 branches ot the Society throughout the world. He thought they would all agree with him that Trade Unions were necessary. The condition of things had so changed that the only way of treating with the employers about anything now was by means of organisation. It was usual in the old days for a man to work all his life for one firm, but now, owinc, to the speed at which all industries were worked, they wanted to turn off the old men, but their organisation was there to protect the weak and old amongst its mem- bers. (Applause.) He condemned picketing, and said that although some of them were obliged to wolk over- time, it was not right. He advocated two shifts of men instead of one shift working a great amount of overtime , because more men would then be wanted. Piece work did not induce a man to do his work well, but led to scamped work and bad workmanship, and it increased the elements of dissatisfaction between employers and employed. He had very great pleasure in proposing the toast of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers. (Ap- plause.) Mr. G. Wright sang with excellent taste " Nil desperandum," Mr. Robinson gave a recitation" People will talk," Mr. Wilkinson followed with the song " There is a flower that bloometh." Mr. J. Whittaker (of Manchester) responded to the last toast. Comparing their position with what it was in October 1889, he found they had increased from 58,670 members to 66,103, being a gain in membership of 7,433. (Hear, hear). During that period their branches had increased from 463 to 489 being an increase of 26. That morning he received the last published record of their Society, which was the balancing up -of the quarter be- fore September 1890. Comparing it with September 1889 he found that their funds had increased from £192,543, to £228,660, being an increase af £36,117. If they went back to the time when the wave of pi osperity began to spread over the land, the increase in the funds of the Society had been more remarkable still. He found in the two years, they had gained nearly 13,000 members and had increased in funds nearly £BO,OOO. That was a 'record which was very good for a fossilised Society like the Amalgamated Engineers. (Laughter). Since the docker's strike of last year the question of Unionism had attracted the public attention more than it had done for a very long time, and interest had been intensified by the late conquest at Liverpool. There was one feature in their proceedings which he was sure was not met with the approval of those who had taken an active part in their own Society. He meant the attack which they had made upon the old leaders of trade Union- ism. Ile believed it was essential that their hours of labour should be reduced, but so far as the methods by which they should be reduced were concerned, he belonged to the old school. Ile thought it was generally admitted that they should continue on the lines that they had gained, than that they should throw away their independence by asking the State to assist them in what they fought for, and obtained for themselves. (Applause.) He was not in favour of legislature so far as the shortening of hours was concerned, but when their members wanted eight hours they got it. The members considered that the time was not yet opportune. He thought so too. He should like to see overtime considerably lessened before they went in for the eight hours, but he hoped the day was not far distant when the members would take into con- sideration the shortening of the hours of labour. They must go on educating their members up to the time when they thought it would be opportune for them to go in for the shortening of the hours of labour. He asked them to be cautious of the leaders they followed. A society like theirs had not been built up in a day. It had been Isuilt upon a solid foundation, which had stood the severest storms and adversity. (Applause.) Mr. S. Shaw then sang "The pilot of England," and Mr. E. Bailey sang "I'm afloat." Mr. W. Davies afterwards proposed the toast of" The treasurer," and spoke in eulogistic terms of the genero- sity and courtesy of Mr. Thorp.—Mr. Thorp responded, and remarked that he had held the post for over 21 years, and he hoped he might still go on with them, and act as their treasurer for a further 21 years. (Ap- plause.) Other toasts and smogs followed, and a very pleasant evening was spent.

TO THE ELECTORS OF WHITECROSS WARD. LADIES AND GxxxLtatgar,—l have been requested by a number of my Friends and Neighbours, Burgesses of the Ward, to allow myself to be nominated for the vacancy in the Town Council caused by the resignation of my father. After careful consideration of the responsibilities and duties the position entails, I have decided to comply with their request. I am known personally to most of you, hsving been a reel. dent among you for 20 years. Being connected with one of the principal industries of the town, I am naturally anxious to do everything in my power to promote the material prosperity of the Borough. If favoured- with your confidence. I shall act in all the various questions arising out of the conduct of municipal affairs as I may judge best for the welfare of the town. Requesting the honour of your support, I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Yours truly, P. W. MONKS, Brooklands, 'Warrington, November 14th, 1090,

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE BURGESSES OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—A vacancy having occurred in your Ward through the elevation of your late represent ative, Mr. John Platt, to the Aldermanic Bench, I have been solic- ited by a number of the electors to allow myself to be put in nomination for the vacant seat, and, having consented, I now offer myself for your suffemges. For seventeen years I have been engaged in business in the old North-Bast Ward of which St. John's Ward is a section, and therefore am no stranger amongst you. For several years past I have taken an active interest in the many local questions that have agitated the public mind. The question of the Intercepting Dep6ts is one which I know closely concerns the well-being and comfort of a great number of the electors, and, having ascertained the opinions of those who live in their immediate vicinity,and who should, therefore. be the best judges as to whether they constitute a grievance or not, I should be prepared to support the adoption of any remedy, however drastic, for their improve- ment, and, failing that, I should not hesitate to vote for their abolition. Attention as early as possible should be given by the Coun _ eil to the unsatisfactory state of many of the streets in the Ward, which in rainy weather, are in a deplorable condition. I am desirous of seeing, early in the coming year, the lend- ing department of our Library free, as is the case in some of our neighbouring towns not near solpopulous as our own. Another question is that of the Public Baths, and I shall heartily support any scheme for their improvement, so that the greatest facilities and encouragement may be given to all classes to use them, and particularly the young that they may under favourable conditions acquire the art of swimming., These, and many other questions affecting the economical and efficient government of the town, should you do me the honour to elect me as your representative, shall receive my most earnest attention.--I am, Laeliesland Gentlemen, your obedient servant, FELIX LOUGHLIN. 17, Buttermarket-st., Warrington. Nov. 14, 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. ST. JOHN'S WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—At the request of a large and Influential body of the Ratepayers of the Ward, I have much pleasure in again offering myself as a candidate for election to fill the vacancy caused by Mr. Platt being appointed Alder- man. Should you do me the honour to elect me. my constant object in the Council will be to do all in my power for the improvement of the Town and its Trade, so as to create Labour and Wages for the Working Classes and Business for the Shopkeepers and Commercial Interest. My best attention will be given to the Improvement of your Streets, Workingmen's Houses, the supply of good Gas at as low a rate as possible, the Improvement of the Sanitary Arrangements of the Town, and to full efficiency with due economy in all matters connected with the Ward and Borough. As regards the Intercepting DepOt so cruelly planted in your midst, I shall do all in my power to have it swept away and entirely removed. lam also strongly in favour of the nightsoll being removed during the night, and thus do away with the nuisance of having to meet bad smelling carts lathe streets at all hours of the day. I am a resident in your Ward, your interests and mine are identical, and I shall at all times be at hand and ready to hear the grievance of any Burgess, and, so far as it lies in my power, I shall endeavour to have such grievance remedied. Having lived amongst you for many years and being well known to a very large number of lon. I feel that I may with great confidence ask your votes and active support on the Polling Day. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JAMES HILL. 23, Birchall-street, November 14th, 1890.

After a long discussion, during which some extraor- dinary scenes occurred, the verdict was altered, and the signalman was committed for trial on the charge of manslaughter. EXECUTION OF BIRCHALL. Woonsrocx, FRIDAY.—John Reginald Birchall was ' hanged here at 8.27 this morning for the murder of Mr. Benwell. SCENE IN THE GAOL. NEW YORK, FRIDAY.—AII the arrangements for the execution of Birchall are now complete, and the event will take place at nine o'clock tins morning. The pri- soner preserves the utmost composure, and shows neither signs of fear nor repentence, still persistently de- claring his innocence. The final interview with his wife was the occasion of a very painful scene. Mrs. Birchall completely broke down, and had to be carried out in a dead faint. Her request that the body might be given her for burial in England has been denied, and it will probably be interred within the prison walls at Wood- stock. At six b'clock in the morning Birchall's breakfast was served, consisting of poached eggs, toast, coffee, and fruit. When the gaol cook brought in the meal the prisoner smiled and bade him heartily good morning. Birchall ate with appetite, and then entered into con- versation with Mr. Wade. The scaffold was erected in the western yard, and the hangman proceeded to place the ropes and weight in position. The scaffold worked with a 350 pound weight in the end of the noose, instead of the ordinary drop. The condemned man halted in front of the gallows while the service was being read, and then, at a given signal, lie took his place on the ground beneath the rope. After shaking hands with the hangman, he whispered " Good-bye," as the black cap was being adjusted. As the chaplain was reciting the closing words of the Lord's Prayer, the execu- tioner pulled the rope, which allowed the heavy weight to fall, and Birchall's body shot into the air about ten feet. It swayed for some time, and death resulted from strangulation.
